content:
# String Immutability and the String Pool

**Level: Beginner | Phase 3 | Priority: MUST | Since: Java 1.0 (pool moved to heap Java 7, compact strings Java 9)**

> **30-second interview answer:** A `String` object never changes after creation; methods like `toUpperCase` return new strings. String literals are stored once in the String pool and shared, so `"hi" == "hi"` is true, while `new String("hi")` creates a separate object. Immutability makes strings safe to share between threads, safe as `HashMap` keys (their hash is cached), safe for security checks, and makes pooling possible. Always compare content with `equals`.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
Printed price tags in a shop.

| Price tags | Java |
|---|---|
| A printed tag is never edited | A `String` never changes |
| To change the price you print a new tag | `s.toUpperCase()` returns a new String |
| The shop keeps one master tag for each common price and reuses it | The String pool shares literals |
| Making a photocopy of the master tag | `new String("hi")`: a separate object |
| Checking two tags show the same text | `equals` |
| Checking they are the very same piece of paper | `==` |

### What it is
- `String` is a `final` class holding characters in a private final array (`byte[]` since Java 9).
- **String pool (string constant pool):** a JVM table of unique string objects. Literals and compile-time constant expressions are pooled automatically.
- **`intern()`:** returns the pooled copy of a string, adding it if missing.
- **Compact strings (Java 9):** strings that only use Latin-1 characters store one byte per char instead of two, halving memory for most text.
- **Cached hash:** `String` computes its `hashCode` once and stores it.

### Why it exists
| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Security | File paths, URLs, class names and passwords checked once cannot be changed afterwards by another reference |
| Thread safety | Shared freely without locks |
| Hash keys | Hash code never changes, and it is cached for speed |
| Pooling | Sharing is only safe because nobody can modify a shared string |

## 2. How It Works
```text
String a = "java";             // literal: pooled
String b = "java";             // same literal: same pooled object
String c = new String("java"); // new object on the heap (its content comes from the pool literal)
String d = c.intern();         // returns the pooled object

HEAP
+------------- String pool --------------+
|  "java"  <---- a, b, d                  |
+-----------------------------------------+
   "java" (separate object)  <---- c

a == b  -> true     a == c -> false     a == d -> true     a.equals(c) -> true
```

**Compile-time constants are folded:**
```text
"ja" + "va"           -> compiler makes "java" -> pooled -> == "java" is true
String part = "ja";
part + "va"           -> computed at runtime -> new object -> == "java" is false
final String fp = "ja";
fp + "va"             -> fp is a compile-time constant -> folded -> == is true
```

**How many objects does `new String("hello")` create?** Up to two: the literal `"hello"` in the pool (if not already there, created when the class loads) and one new heap object.

**Concatenation in loops** creates a new String each time, copying all previous characters: O(n²) work for n appends. Use `StringBuilder` (next topic). Since Java 9, a single `a + b + c` expression is compiled to an efficient `invokedynamic` call, so simple concatenations are fine.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
```java
public class StringPoolDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Pool and identity
        String a = "java";
        String b = "java";
        String c = new String("java");
        String d = c.intern();
        System.out.println("a == b      : " + (a == b));
        System.out.println("a == c      : " + (a == c));
        System.out.println("a.equals(c) : " + a.equals(c));
        System.out.println("a == d      : " + (a == d));

        // 2. Compile-time folding vs runtime concatenation
        String part = "ja";
        final String constPart = "ja";
        System.out.println("\"ja\"+\"va\" == a : " + (("ja" + "va") == a));
        System.out.println("part+\"va\" == a  : " + ((part + "va") == a));
        System.out.println("const+\"va\" == a : " + ((constPart + "va") == a));

        // 3. Immutability: methods return new strings
        String original = "  Hello World  ";
        String trimmed = original.trim();
        String upper = trimmed.toUpperCase();
        System.out.println("original    : [" + original + "]");
        System.out.println("upper       : [" + upper + "]");
        original.concat("!!!");                       // result ignored: nothing changes
        System.out.println("after concat: [" + original + "]");

        // 4. Common String API
        String csv = "pen,book,,lamp";
        System.out.println("split       : " + String.join(" | ", csv.split(",")).replace(" | ", "/"));
        System.out.println("parts       : " + csv.split(",").length);
        System.out.println("contains    : " + csv.contains("book"));
        System.out.println("indexOf     : " + csv.indexOf("book"));
        System.out.println("substring   : " + csv.substring(4, 8));
        System.out.println("charAt      : " + csv.charAt(0));
        System.out.println("replace     : " + "a-b-c".replace("-", "+"));
        System.out.println("isBlank     : " + "   ".isBlank() + ", isEmpty: " + "   ".isEmpty());
        System.out.println("strip       : [" + "  hi  ".strip() + "]");
        System.out.println("repeat      : " + "ab".repeat(3));
        System.out.println("lines       : " + "a\nb\nc".lines().count());
        System.out.println("format      : " + String.format("%-5s|%5.2f|%03d", "id", 3.14159, 7));
        System.out.println("formatted   : " + "%s has %d items".formatted("cart", 3));
        System.out.println("equalsIgnoreCase: " + "JAVA".equalsIgnoreCase(a));
        System.out.println("compareTo   : " + "apple".compareTo("banana"));

        // 5. Safe comparison with possible null
        String input = null;
        System.out.println("literal first: " + "yes".equals(input));   // no NPE
        System.out.println("Objects.equals: " + java.util.Objects.equals(input, "yes"));

        // 6. hashCode is cached and depends only on content
        System.out.println("same hash   : " + (a.hashCode() == c.hashCode()));
    }
}
```

### Walkthrough
- Part 1: two literals share one pooled object; `new String` creates a separate object; `intern()` returns the pooled one.
- Part 2: `"ja" + "va"` is folded by the compiler into the literal `"java"`. `part + "va"` happens at runtime and creates a new object. A `final` local initialized with a literal is a compile-time constant, so it is folded too.
- Part 3: `trim`, `toUpperCase` and `concat` all return new strings. Ignoring the return value of `concat` changes nothing, a common beginner bug.
- Part 4: the most used methods. `split(",")` on `"pen,book,,lamp"` gives 4 parts including an empty string. `strip` (Java 11) removes Unicode whitespace that `trim` does not. `isBlank`, `repeat`, `lines` are Java 11; `formatted` is Java 15.
- Part 5: `"yes".equals(input)` is null-safe because the literal is never null.

### Output
```text
a == b      : true
a == c      : false
a.equals(c) : true
a == d      : true
"ja"+"va" == a : true
part+"va" == a  : false
const+"va" == a : true
original    : [  Hello World  ]
upper       : [HELLO WORLD]
after concat: [  Hello World  ]
split       : pen/book//lamp
parts       : 4
contains    : true
indexOf     : 4
substring   : book
charAt      : p
replace     : a+b+c
isBlank     : true, isEmpty: false
strip       : [hi]
repeat      : ababab
lines       : 3
format      : id   | 3.14|007
formatted   : cart has 3 items
equalsIgnoreCase: true
compareTo   : -1
literal first: false
Objects.equals: false
same hash   : true
```

### Compare
| `==` | `equals` |
|---|---|
| Same object? | Same characters? |
| True for two identical literals (pooled) | True for any two strings with equal content |
| Unreliable for strings from input, concatenation or `new` | Always correct |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **Why is String immutable?**
   For security, thread safety, safe use as hash keys with a cached hash code, and to make the String pool possible.
2. **What is the String pool?**
   A JVM-managed table of unique string instances. Literals are interned there so identical literals share one object. Since Java 7 it lives on the heap.
3. **Difference between `==` and `equals` for strings?**
   `==` compares references; `equals` compares characters. Always use `equals` for content.

**Follow-up**
4. **How many objects does `String s = new String("abc");` create?**
   Up to two: the pooled literal `"abc"` (if not already present) and a new heap object referenced by `s`.
5. **What does `intern()` do?**
   Returns the pooled instance with the same content, adding this string to the pool if needed.
6. **Why is concatenation in a loop slow?**
   Each `+=` creates a new String and copies all previous characters, giving quadratic time. Use `StringBuilder`.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **Why are passwords often stored in `char[]` instead of `String`?**
   A String cannot be wiped and may linger in memory (and the pool) until garbage collected; a `char[]` can be overwritten with zeros right after use. `JPasswordField.getPassword()` returns `char[]` for this reason.
8. **What does `"a" + 1 + 2` give, and `1 + 2 + "a"`?**
   `"a12"` and `"3a"`: evaluation is left to right, and once a String appears, `+` means concatenation.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you know why `==` sometimes "works" for strings and why you still must not rely on it.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Comparing strings with `==` | Works for literals, fails for input | `equals` |
| Ignoring the return value: `s.trim();` | String unchanged | `s = s.trim();` |
| `input.equals("yes")` with null input | `NullPointerException` | `"yes".equals(input)` |
| `+=` in big loops | Slow, lots of garbage | `StringBuilder` |
| `split(".")` | Regex: `.` matches everything, returns an empty array | `split("\\.")` or `Pattern.quote(".")` |

### Best practices
- Prefer `isBlank` and `strip` (Unicode-aware) over `trim().isEmpty()`.
- Use `String.join`, `String.format` or text blocks (Phase 6) for readable building.
- Use `equalsIgnoreCase` or `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` for case-insensitive checks; avoid locale surprises.

### Compare with
| Type | Mutable? | Thread-safe? |
|---|---|---|
| `String` | No | Yes (immutable) |
| `StringBuilder` | Yes | No |
| `StringBuffer` | Yes | Yes (synchronized) |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
Write `isPalindrome(String s)` that ignores case, spaces and punctuation (`"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"` is true). Then write `countWords(String text)` that counts words separated by any whitespace, ignoring leading and trailing spaces.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
public class StringExercises {
    static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        String clean = s.toLowerCase().replaceAll("[^a-z0-9]", "");  // keep letters and digits
        int i = 0, j = clean.length() - 1;
        while (i < j) {
            if (clean.charAt(i++) != clean.charAt(j--)) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    static int countWords(String text) {
        String t = text.strip();
        return t.isEmpty() ? 0 : t.split("\\s+").length;   // \\s+ = one or more whitespace
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")); // true
        System.out.println(isPalindrome("race a car"));                     // false
        System.out.println(countWords("  Java   is\tfun \n"));              // 3
        System.out.println(countWords("   "));                              // 0
    }
}
```
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What does `"java" == new String("java")` evaluate to?
A: false, because `new String` creates a separate object.

Q: Where has the String pool lived since Java 7?
A: On the heap.

Q: What does `String.intern()` return?
A: The pooled instance with the same content.

Q: Why is `"yes".equals(input)` safer than `input.equals("yes")`?
A: The literal is never null, so it cannot throw `NullPointerException`.

Q: Name three reasons `String` is immutable.
A: Security, thread safety, and safe hashing/pooling (cached hash code).

**Related:** [[StringBuilder and StringBuffer]] · [[Immutable Class Design]] · [[var, Switch Expressions and Text Blocks]]

# Phase 3 review: Exceptions and Core APIs

## Cheat sheet

| Idea | Remember |
|---|---|
| Hierarchy | Throwable → Error and Exception; RuntimeException = unchecked |
| Checked | Must catch or declare (`IOException`, `SQLException`, `InterruptedException`) |
| Unchecked | Bugs and invalid input (`NPE`, `IllegalArgumentException`) |
| Catch order | Specific before general |
| finally | Always runs except JVM halt; never return from it |
| try-with-resources | `AutoCloseable`, reverse-order close, suppressed exceptions |
| Custom exceptions | Extend RuntimeException, keep the cause, add context |
| Spring rollback | Unchecked by default; checked needs `rollbackFor` |
| String | Immutable, pooled literals, `equals` not `==` |
| `new String("x")` | Up to two objects |
| StringBuilder | Mutable, fast, not synchronized; StringBuffer is synchronized |
| BigDecimal | From String, assign results, divide with scale and rounding, compare with `compareTo` |
| java.time | Immutable; Instant for moments, LocalDate for dates, ZonedDateTime for zones |
| Duration vs Period | Time-based vs date-based |
| Files | `readString`, `lines` in try-with-resources, `walk`, explicit UTF-8 |

### Key code snippets
```java
// try-with-resources plus exception translation
try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    return reader.readLine();
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw new ImportFailedException("Cannot read " + path, e);   // keep the cause
}
```

```java
// Custom unchecked exception
public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public OrderNotFoundException(long id) { super("Order " + id + " not found"); }
}
```

```java
// Strings
boolean same = "yes".equals(input);                    // null-safe
String joined = String.join(", ", items);
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.append("a").append(1);
```

```java
// Money and time
BigDecimal total = price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(qty)).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
Instant createdAt = Instant.now(clock);
LocalDate delivery = LocalDate.now(clock).plusDays(3);
```

## The 10 most likely interview questions

1. **Checked vs unchecked exceptions?** Compiler-enforced vs not; recoverable conditions vs bugs.
2. **Error vs Exception?** JVM-level failures you should not catch vs conditions you may handle.
3. **Does finally always run?** Yes, except when the JVM stops; returning from finally swallows exceptions.
4. **What is try-with-resources?** Automatic closing of `AutoCloseable` resources, with suppressed exceptions.
5. **How do you design custom exceptions?** Unchecked, specific names, context in messages, keep causes, map centrally.
6. **Why is String immutable?** Security, thread safety, hashing, pooling.
7. **String pool and `new String`?** Literals are shared; `new` creates a separate object.
8. **String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?** Immutable vs mutable vs mutable and synchronized.
9. **Why BigDecimal for money?** Exact decimal arithmetic; double is binary and inexact.
10. **LocalDateTime vs Instant?** No zone vs exact UTC moment; store Instant.

## Rapid-fire flashcards

Q: Is `IllegalStateException` checked or unchecked?
A: Unchecked.

Q: What does multi-catch syntax look like?
A: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` (types written with a vertical bar between them).

Q: What does `e.getSuppressed()` return?
A: Exceptions from closing resources that were suppressed in favour of the primary exception.

Q: What does `"ja" + "va" == "java"` evaluate to?
A: true, because constant expressions are folded and pooled at compile time.

Q: What is the default capacity of `StringBuilder`?
A: 16.

Q: What does `new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))` return?
A: false, because the scales differ.

Q: Which rounding mode is banker's rounding?
A: `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN`.

Q: Which java.time class should a "created at" timestamp use?
A: `Instant` (or `OffsetDateTime`).

Q: Which `Files` method streams a file lazily line by line?
A: `Files.lines(path)`.

Q: Why prefer `Path.resolve` over string concatenation for paths?
A: It handles separators correctly across operating systems and avoids traversal mistakes.

**Shared analogy: running a library.** Knowing the furniture (lists, sets, maps) is not enough; you also need house rules. # Comparable vs Comparator

**Level: Beginner | Phase 4 | Priority: MUST | Since: Java 1.2 (both interfaces), Java 8 (Comparator.comparing, thenComparing, reversed, nullsFirst)**

> **30-second interview answer:** `Comparable<T>` defines a class's **natural ordering** through one method, `compareTo(T other)`, implemented inside the class itself (`String`, `Integer`, `LocalDate` do this). `Comparator<T>` is a separate object with `compare(T a, T b)` that defines **any other ordering** without touching the class. Both return a negative number, zero or a positive number for less than, equal, or greater than. Since Java 8 you build comparators with `Comparator.comparing(...)`, chain them with `thenComparing`, flip them with `reversed()` and handle nulls with `nullsFirst`/`nullsLast`. Sorted collections like `TreeSet` and `TreeMap` treat a comparison result of 0 as "duplicate".

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
Shelving books in a library.

| Library | Java |
|---|---|
| Every book has a default shelving rule printed inside the cover: by title | `Comparable`: `compareTo` lives in the class |
| A curator builds a temporary display "by year, newest first" without reprinting books | `Comparator`: ordering defined outside the class |
| "By author, then by title for the same author" | `thenComparing` chain |
| "Same rule, opposite direction" | `reversed()` |
| Books with no year go at the end of the display | `nullsLast` |
| Two books judged "same position" by the rule share one slot on a strict display | `TreeSet` drops elements whose comparison is 0 |

### What it is
- **`Comparable<T>`** (`java.lang`): `int compareTo(T o)`. One per class; defines the natural order used by `Collections.sort(list)`, `TreeSet`, `TreeMap`, `Arrays.sort(objects)`.
- **`Comparator<T>`** (`java.util`): `int compare(T a, T b)`. A functional interface, so it can be a lambda or method reference. Unlimited orderings per class, usable for classes you cannot change.
- **The contract** (both): sign of `compare(a, b)` is the opposite of `compare(b, a)`; it is transitive (a > b and b > c means a > c); and ideally `compare(a, b) == 0` exactly when `a.equals(b)` ("consistent with equals").

Key `Comparator` factory and default methods:

| Method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Comparator.comparing(Employee::name)` | Compare by an extracted `Comparable` key |
| `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary)` | Same for an int key, without boxing |
| `.thenComparing(Employee::name)` | Tie-breaker when the first comparison is 0 |
| `.thenComparing(key, Comparator.reverseOrder())` | Tie-breaker with its own direction |
| `.reversed()` | Flip the whole chain built so far |
| `Comparator.naturalOrder()` and `reverseOrder()` | Natural ascending or descending |
| `Comparator.nullsFirst(c)` and `nullsLast(c)` | Wrap another comparator to tolerate null |

### Why it exists
Sorting and sorted collections need a way to ask "which of these two comes first?". Putting one answer in the class (natural order) covers the common case; a separate comparator covers every other business rule (sort products by price, then by rating, descending) and classes you do not own, like a third-party DTO.

## 2. How It Works
```text
compare(a, b) result:
   < 0   a comes before b
   = 0   a and b rank equally (a TreeSet or TreeMap treats them as the same element)
   > 0   a comes after b

Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary, reverseOrder())
   compare(maya, zoe):
      step 1: "Eng".compareTo("Eng") = 0     -> tie, go to the next comparator
      step 2: reverseOrder: compare(120, 95) -> negative (120 before 95)
      result: maya before zoe
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need to order objects"] --> B{"Is there one obvious natural order and you own the class?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["implements Comparable: compareTo"]
    B -->|"No, or several orders needed"| D["Comparator via comparing and thenComparing"]
    C --> E["Collections.sort(list), TreeSet, TreeMap"]
    D --> F["list.sort(cmp), new TreeSet with cmp, stream sorted(cmp)"]
```

**Sorting algorithm facts:** `List.sort` and `Collections.sort` on objects use TimSort, a stable merge sort (equal elements keep their previous relative order) running in O(n log n). `Arrays.sort` on primitives uses dual-pivot quicksort, which is not stable, but stability does not matter for primitives.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class SortingDemo {
    // Natural order: by name
    record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary) implements Comparable<Employee> {
        @Override
        public int compareTo(Employee other) {
            return name.compareTo(other.name);
        }
    }

    static String names(List<Employee> list) {
        return list.stream().map(Employee::name).toList().toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
                new Employee("Maya", "Eng", 120),
                new Employee("Ali", "Sales", 80),
                new Employee("Zoe", "Eng", 95),
                new Employee("Ben", "Sales", 80),
                new Employee("Kim", "HR", 70)));

        // 1. Natural order (Comparable)
        Collections.sort(staff);
        System.out.println("by name      : " + names(staff));

        // 2. Comparator by salary (stable: Ali stays before Ben)
        staff.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary));
        System.out.println("by salary    : " + names(staff));

        // 3. Salary descending, then name ascending
        staff.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary).reversed()
                             .thenComparing(Employee::name));
        System.out.println("salary desc  : " + names(staff));

        // 4. Department ascending, then salary descending
        staff.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
                             .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder()));
        System.out.println("dept, salary : " + names(staff));

        // 5. Null handling
        List<String> withNulls = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("pear", null, "apple"));
        withNulls.sort(Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println("nullsLast    : " + withNulls);

        // 6. The subtraction trap: overflow gives the wrong sign
        Comparator<Integer> broken = (a, b) -> a - b;
        Comparator<Integer> correct = Integer::compare;
        System.out.println("broken       : " + broken.compare(Integer.MAX_VALUE, -1));
        System.out.println("correct      : " + correct.compare(Integer.MAX_VALUE, -1));

        // 7. A comparator decides key equality in a TreeMap
        Map<String, Integer> caseless = new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
        caseless.put("Java", 1);
        caseless.put("JAVA", 2);
        System.out.println("caseless map : " + caseless);

        // 8. Length, then reverse alphabetical
        List<String> words = new ArrayList<>(List.of("banana", "fig", "cherry", "kiwi"));
        words.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
                             .thenComparing(Comparator.<String>reverseOrder()));
        System.out.println("words        : " + words);
    }
}
```

### Walkthrough
- **Record with `Comparable`:** the record implements `compareTo` by name, delegating to `String.compareTo` (which is itself a natural ordering). `Collections.sort(staff)` uses it.
- **Part 2:** `comparingInt` extracts the int salary with no boxing. TimSort is stable, so Ali and Ben (both 80) stay in their previous order (Ali first, from the name sort).
- **Part 3:** `reversed()` flips only what is to its left: salary descending. `thenComparing(Employee::name)` added after it stays ascending.
- **Part 4:** for a descending tie-breaker, pass a second comparator to `thenComparing(key, Comparator.reverseOrder())` instead of calling `reversed()` (which would flip the department order too).
- **Part 5:** natural ordering cannot compare null; `nullsLast` wraps it and puts nulls at the end.
- **Part 6:** `Integer.MAX_VALUE - (-1)` overflows to `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, a negative number claiming MAX_VALUE is smaller than -1. `Integer.compare` never overflows.
- **Part 7:** the comparator says "Java" and "JAVA" are equal, so the second `put` replaces the value but keeps the original key object.
- **Part 8:** the explicit type witness `Comparator.<String>reverseOrder()` helps the compiler; equal lengths 6 are ordered cherry before banana.

### Output
```text
by name      : [Ali, Ben, Kim, Maya, Zoe]
by salary    : [Kim, Ali, Ben, Zoe, Maya]
salary desc  : [Maya, Zoe, Ali, Ben, Kim]
dept, salary : [Maya, Zoe, Kim, Ali, Ben]
nullsLast    : [apple, pear, null]
broken       : -2147483648
correct      : 1
caseless map : {Java=2}
words        : [fig, kiwi, cherry, banana]
```

### Compare
The pre-Java-8 way versus the modern way:

| Task | Old (anonymous class) | Modern |
|---|---|---|
| Sort by salary | `new Comparator<Employee>() { public int compare(Employee a, Employee b) { return Integer.compare(a.salary(), b.salary()); } }` | `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary)` |
| Then by name | Nested if on the first result | `.thenComparing(Employee::name)` |
| Descending | Swap a and b by hand | `.reversed()` |
| Nulls | Manual null checks | `Comparator.nullsLast(...)` |

| | Comparable | Comparator |
|---|---|---|
| Package | `java.lang` | `java.util` |
| Method | `compareTo(T o)` | `compare(T a, T b)` |
| Where | Inside the class | Separate object or lambda |
| How many | One natural order | Any number |
| Classes you do not own | Not possible | Possible |
| Used by | `Collections.sort(list)`, `TreeSet()` | `list.sort(cmp)`, `new TreeSet<>(cmp)`, `stream.sorted(cmp)` |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **Comparable vs Comparator?**
   `Comparable` is implemented by the class itself and defines one natural order through `compareTo`. `Comparator` is an external strategy with `compare(a, b)`, allowing many different orders and sorting classes you cannot modify. Both return negative, zero or positive.
2. **What does `compareTo` return?**
   A negative int if this object is less than the argument, zero if equal in ordering, and a positive int if greater. Only the sign matters, not the magnitude.
3. **How do you sort a list in descending order?**
   `list.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder())` for naturally ordered elements, or `Comparator.comparing(key).reversed()` for a key.

**Follow-up**
4. **What does "consistent with equals" mean and why care?**
   `compare(a, b) == 0` should hold exactly when `a.equals(b)`. Sorted collections use the comparator, not `equals`, for identity, so an inconsistent comparator makes a `TreeSet` drop elements that `equals` considers different, and `TreeSet` and `HashSet` disagree on the same data.
5. **Why is `(a, b) -> a - b` a bad comparator?**
   Subtraction overflows for large values of opposite sign, giving the wrong sign and corrupting sort order (sometimes TimSort even throws "Comparison method violates its general contract"). Use `Integer.compare` or `Comparator.comparingInt`.
6. **Is Java's object sort stable, and why does it matter?**
   Yes, `List.sort` uses TimSort, which keeps equal elements in their existing order. That lets you sort by a secondary key first and then by a primary key, and keeps UI lists from shuffling equal rows.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **`comparing(Employee::dept).reversed().thenComparing(Employee::name)`: which parts are descending?**
   Only the department. `reversed()` applies to the chain built so far; the `thenComparing` added afterwards stays ascending.
8. **You put employees into a `TreeSet` with `comparingInt(Employee::salary)` and two people earn the same. What happens?**
   The second one is not added because the comparator returns 0, so the set considers them duplicates. Add tie-breakers like `.thenComparing(Employee::id)`.
9. **A class from a library does not implement Comparable, but you need a `TreeMap` keyed by it. What do you do?**
   Pass a `Comparator` to the `TreeMap` constructor, built from its getters with `Comparator.comparing(...)`. Without a comparator, the first `put` throws `ClassCastException`.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you can write correct, readable sort logic with the Java 8 comparator API and understand how comparators affect sorted collections.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `return a.value - b.value;` | Overflow, wrong order, contract violation | `Integer.compare(a.value, b.value)` |
| Comparator without tie-breakers in a TreeSet | Elements silently lost | `.thenComparing(...)` down to a unique key |
| Misplaced `reversed()` | Wrong fields descending | Use `thenComparing(key, reverseOrder())` for one key |
| Natural ordering with null elements | `NullPointerException` | `nullsFirst` or `nullsLast` |
| Comparing `Double` with subtraction cast to int | 0.3 and 0.7 compare equal | `Double.compare` or `comparingDouble` |
| `compareTo` inconsistent with `equals` (like `BigDecimal`) | `TreeSet` and `HashSet` disagree | Know it, choose the set deliberately |

### Best practices
- Implement `Comparable` only when there is one obvious natural order (ids, dates, versions); use comparators for business sorting.
- Build comparators from method references; keep them as `static final` constants when reused (`static final Comparator<Product> BY_PRICE = ...`).
- Use primitive specializations (`comparingInt`, `comparingLong`, `comparingDouble`) to avoid boxing.
- In databases-backed apps, sort in SQL (`ORDER BY`) when possible; sort in Java when the data is already in memory.

### Compare with
| Need | Code |
|---|---|
| Natural ascending | `list.sort(null)` or `Collections.sort(list)` |
| Natural descending | `list.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder())` |
| By field | `Comparator.comparing(Person::name)` |
| Multi-field | `comparing(A).thenComparing(B)` |
| Case-insensitive strings | `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER` |
| Stream sorting | `stream.sorted(cmp)` |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
Create a record `Product(String sku, String name, BigDecimal price, double rating)` and a list of at least five products. Then:
1. Make `Product` implement `Comparable` by `sku` (natural order).
2. Sort by price ascending, then rating descending, then name.
3. Build a `TreeSet<Product>` using a comparator on `name` only, and show what happens when two products share a name; then fix it with a tie-breaker.
4. Find the cheapest product with `Collections.min` and a comparator.

Acceptance criteria: no subtraction in comparators; `BigDecimal` compared with `compareTo` (via `Comparator.comparing`).

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.*;

public class ProductSorting {
    record Product(String sku, String name, BigDecimal price, double rating) implements Comparable<Product> {
        @Override
        public int compareTo(Product o) { return sku.compareTo(o.sku); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Product> products = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
                new Product("P3", "Mouse", new BigDecimal("25.00"), 4.5),
                new Product("P1", "Keyboard", new BigDecimal("45.00"), 4.7),
                new Product("P5", "Mouse", new BigDecimal("25.00"), 4.8),
                new Product("P2", "Monitor", new BigDecimal("180.00"), 4.6),
                new Product("P4", "Cable", new BigDecimal("5.00"), 4.0)));

        Collections.sort(products);
        System.out.println(products.stream().map(Product::sku).toList());   // [P1, P2, P3, P4, P5]

        products.sort(Comparator.comparing(Product::price)
                .thenComparing(Product::rating, Comparator.reverseOrder())
                .thenComparing(Product::name));
        System.out.println(products.stream().map(Product::sku).toList());   // [P4, P5, P3, P1, P2]

        Set<Product> byNameOnly = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(Product::name));
        byNameOnly.addAll(products);
        System.out.println(byNameOnly.size());                               // 4: one "Mouse" lost

        Set<Product> fixed = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(Product::name).thenComparing(Product::sku));
        fixed.addAll(products);
        System.out.println(fixed.size());                                    // 5

        Product cheapest = Collections.min(products, Comparator.comparing(Product::price));
        System.out.println(cheapest.name());                                 // Cable
    }
}
```
Both mice cost 25.00, so the rating tie-breaker puts P5 (4.8) before P3 (4.5).
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What single method does `Comparable` declare?
A: `int compareTo(T other)`.

Q: What does a `Comparator` let you do that `Comparable` cannot?
A: Define many orderings outside the class, including for classes you cannot modify.

Q: Why should a comparator never use `a - b`?
A: Integer overflow can produce the wrong sign.

Q: In a chain `comparing(x).reversed().thenComparing(y)`, which key is descending?
A: Only x; `reversed()` flips the chain built before it.

Q: What does a `TreeSet` do with two elements whose comparator returns 0?
A: Treats them as duplicates and keeps only the first.

Q: Is `List.sort` stable in Java?
A: Yes, it uses TimSort, a stable merge sort.

**Related:** [[HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet]] · [[Queue, Deque and PriorityQueue]] · [[Lambdas and Functional Interfaces]]

# Phase 4 review: Collections

## Cheat sheet

| Idea | Remember |
|---|---|
| Hierarchy | `Collection` → `List`, `Set`, `Queue`/`Deque`; `Map` is separate |
| Default picks | `ArrayList`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `ArrayDeque` |
| ArrayList | Resizable array, O(1) get, amortized O(1) append, grows 50% |
| LinkedList | Doubly linked nodes, O(n) get, rarely the right choice |
| Hash sets and maps | O(1) average, need `equals` + `hashCode`, no order |
| Linked variants | Same speed, insertion order (LinkedHashMap can do access order: LRU) |
| Tree variants | O(log n), sorted, need `Comparable` or `Comparator`, navigation methods |
| Nulls | HashMap one null key; TreeMap no null key; ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue, `List.of` no nulls |
| Queue methods | `offer`/`poll`/`peek` return special values; `add`/`remove`/`element` throw |
| Stack | `ArrayDeque` with `push`/`pop`, never `Stack` |
| PriorityQueue | Min-heap, head ordered, iteration not sorted, O(log n) offer and poll |
| Fail-fast | `modCount` check in `next()`, throws `ConcurrentModificationException` |
| Fail-safe | `CopyOnWriteArrayList` snapshot, `ConcurrentHashMap` weakly consistent |
| Safe removal | `removeIf`, `Iterator.remove`, `entrySet().removeIf` |
| Comparable | `compareTo` inside the class, one natural order |
| Comparator | External, `comparing`, `thenComparing`, `reversed`, `nullsLast` |
| Sorting | TimSort for objects (stable), dual-pivot quicksort for primitives |
| `Arrays.asList` | Fixed-size view, `set` writes through, `add` throws |
| Unmodifiable vs immutable | View that reflects changes vs fixed snapshot |
| `List.of` | Immutable, no nulls; `Set.of`/`Map.of` reject duplicates |

### Key code snippets
```java
// Counting and grouping with the modern Map API
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
for (String w : words) counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);

Map<String, List<String>> byDept = new TreeMap<>();
for (Employee e : staff) byDept.computeIfAbsent(e.dept(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e.name());
```

```java
// Sorting with comparators
staff.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
        .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
        .thenComparing(Employee::name));
```

```java
// Queue, stack and heap
Queue<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();   queue.offer("a"); queue.poll();
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();  stack.push(1);    stack.pop();
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
```

```java
// Safe removal and LRU
list.removeIf(x -> x < 0);
map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0);
Map<String, Integer> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, Integer> e) { return size() > 100; }
};
```

```java
// Immutability and defensive copies
record Order(String id, List<String> lines) {
    Order { lines = List.copyOf(lines); }
}
List<Integer> result = stream.map(x -> x * 2).toList();   // unmodifiable
```

```java
// TreeMap navigation
NavigableMap<Integer, String> bands = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0, "F", 60, "D", 70, "C", 80, "B", 90, "A"));
String grade = bands.floorEntry(85).getValue();            // "B"
```

## The 10 most likely interview questions

1. **ArrayList vs LinkedList?** Array with O(1) index access vs linked nodes with O(1) end operations; ArrayList wins in practice thanks to cache locality and lower memory.
2. **HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap?** No order and O(1); insertion or access order and O(1); sorted keys and O(log n) with navigation.
3. **How does a HashSet guarantee uniqueness?** It is a HashMap underneath; `hashCode` picks the bucket and `equals` confirms duplicates.
4. **What is fail-fast iteration?** Iterators check `modCount` and throw `ConcurrentModificationException` on outside structural changes; fix with `removeIf` or `Iterator.remove`.
5. **Fail-fast vs fail-safe?** Throw on modification vs iterate a snapshot or weakly consistent view (`CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `ConcurrentHashMap`).
6. **Comparable vs Comparator?** Natural order inside the class vs any number of external orders built with `Comparator.comparing`.
7. **Why not use `a - b` in a comparator?** Integer overflow flips the sign; use `Integer.compare`.
8. **`List.of` vs `Collections.unmodifiableList` vs `Arrays.asList`?** Immutable and null-free vs read-only view vs fixed-size array-backed view where `set` works.
9. **Which class should you use as a stack or queue?** `ArrayDeque`; `Stack` is synchronized legacy and `LinkedList` is memory-heavy.
10. **How do you find the top k elements efficiently?** A min-heap `PriorityQueue` of size k: O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.

## Rapid-fire flashcards

Q: Which collection keeps unique elements in insertion order?
A: `LinkedHashSet`.

Q: What is the average time complexity of `HashMap.get`?
A: O(1).

Q: What does `TreeMap.ceilingKey(k)` return?
A: The smallest key greater than or equal to k, or null.

Q: What is the default ordering of a `PriorityQueue<Integer>`?
A: Smallest first (a min-heap).

Q: What does `queue.peek()` return on an empty `ArrayDeque`?
A: null.

Q: Does `list.set(i, x)` inside a for-each loop throw `ConcurrentModificationException`?
A: No, replacing an element is not a structural modification.

Q: What does `Map.of("a", 1, "a", 2)` throw?
A: `IllegalArgumentException` for the duplicate key.

Q: Is the result of `Collectors.toList()` guaranteed to be mutable?
A: No guarantee; use `Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new)` if you need mutability.

Q: How do you get a typed array from a `List<String>`?
A: `list.toArray(new String[0])` or `list.toArray(String[]::new)`.

Q: Why must `HashMap` keys be immutable?
A: If a key's hash code changes after insertion, lookups search the wrong bucket and the entry is lost.

# Phase 5: Spring Boot Foundations (Beginner)

This phase takes you from "I know Java" to "I can build and explain a small REST API with Spring Boot". You will learn what Spring and Spring Boot actually do for you, how Maven builds the project, what each generated file is for, what `@SpringBootApplication` hides, how to write controllers that read path variables, query parameters and JSON bodies, how configuration files work, and how to split code into controller, service and repository layers with DTOs at the edge. You also start **OrderHub**, the running project of this guide: by the end of the phase it has in-memory CRUD for products.

Interviewers care because almost every Java backend job today is a Spring Boot job. Beginner rounds always include "What is Spring Boot and how is it different from Spring?", "What does `@SpringBootApplication` do?" and "Walk me through what happens when a request hits your controller". Clear answers here signal you can be productive from week one. The deep internals (how the container really works, proxies, auto-configuration classes) come in Phases 10 and 18; this phase builds the mental model they rest on.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["What Spring and Spring Boot Are"] --> B["Maven Basics"]
    B --> C["Spring Initializr and Project Structure"]
    C --> D["@SpringBootApplication Explained"]
    D --> E["First REST Controller"]
    E --> F["Path Variables, Request Params and Request Body"]
    D --> G["application.properties and application.yml"]
    F --> H["Layered Architecture"]
    H --> I["DTOs and Mapping"]
    I --> J["Lombok: Uses and Risks"]
    H --> K["OrderHub v1: in-memory CRUD"]
    G --> K
```

**Prerequisites:** Phase 2 (classes, interfaces, records, encapsulation), Phase 3 (exceptions, `BigDecimal`), Phase 4 (`List`, `Map`, `ConcurrentHashMap` idea). You need JDK 21, Maven (or the Maven wrapper), an IDE and `curl` or an HTTP client (setup in Phase 0).

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. What is the difference between Spring and Spring Boot?
2. What does `@SpringBootApplication` do?
3. `@Controller` vs `@RestController`, and `@PathVariable` vs `@RequestParam`?
4. Why split an application into controller, service and repository layers?
5. Why use DTOs instead of returning domain objects or entities directly?

# First steps

**Shared analogy: moving into a furnished flat.** Plain Java is an empty plot of land: you can build anything, but you lay every pipe yourself. The **Spring Framework** is a building contractor that connects the pipes and wires between rooms for you (dependency injection). **Spring Boot** is a fully furnished flat from that contractor: the kitchen (web server), heating (JSON conversion) and locks (sensible defaults) are already installed, and you just move your furniture (business code) in. **Maven** is the moving company's checklist and delivery truck: it fetches every box you listed (dependencies) and runs the same steps every time (compile, test, package). **Spring Initializr** is the brochure where you tick the rooms you want, and `@SpringBootApplication` is the front-door key that switches everything on.

The four topics in this group answer: what am I using, how is it built, what did the generator give me, and what happens when I press run.

name: What Spring and Spring Boot Are
description: IoC container, dependency injection, the Spring ecosystem, and what Boot adds: starters, auto-configuration, embedded server
content:
# What Spring and Spring Boot Are

**Level: Beginner | Phase 5 | Priority: MUST | Since: Spring Framework 1.0 (2004), Spring Boot 1.0 (2014); baseline Spring Boot 3.5 on Spring Framework 6.2 and Java 17+ (we use Java 21); Boot 4 / Framework 7 released November 2025**

> **30-second interview answer:** The Spring Framework is a Java framework whose core is an **IoC container**: instead of my classes creating their own dependencies with `new`, Spring creates the objects (called **beans**), wires them together through constructors (**dependency injection**) and manages their lifecycle. On top of that core Spring offers modules for web (Spring MVC), data access, transactions, security and more. **Spring Boot** is an opinionated layer on top of Spring that removes setup work: **starters** bring a tested set of dependencies, **auto-configuration** creates the usual beans based on what is on the classpath and in your properties, and an **embedded server** (Tomcat by default) lets the app run as a plain `java -jar`. Spring is the engine; Boot is the engine pre-installed in a car with sensible defaults.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
Building a restaurant.

| Restaurant | Spring |
|---|---|
| A chef who must grow vegetables, build the oven and hire waiters before cooking | Plain Java: every class creates its own dependencies with `new` |
| A restaurant manager who hires staff and hands each chef the tools they need | Spring IoC container: creates beans and injects dependencies |
| The chef says "I need a knife and an oven" on their job application | Constructor parameters declare dependencies |
| Staff list kept by the manager | `ApplicationContext`, the registry of beans |
| A franchise kit: kitchen installed, menu template, suppliers pre-arranged | Spring Boot: starters, auto-configuration, embedded server |
| You can still swap the oven if you want a different brand | Your own beans override Boot's defaults |
| The restaurant opens with one switch | `SpringApplication.run(...)` |

### What it is
- **Spring Framework:** a set of libraries for building Java applications. Its core is the container plus modules: Spring MVC (web), Spring WebFlux (reactive web), JDBC and transactions, AOP, testing support.
- **IoC (Inversion of Control):** a design principle where a framework, not your code, controls object creation and the flow between components. "Don't call us, we'll call you."
- **DI (Dependency Injection):** the main IoC technique. A class receives its collaborators (through its constructor) instead of creating them. This makes classes easy to test (pass a fake) and easy to change.
- **Bean:** any object created and managed by the Spring container. You mark classes with `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository` or `@RestController`, or declare them with `@Bean` methods.
- **ApplicationContext:** the container itself. It reads configuration, creates beans in the right order, injects them and destroys them at shutdown.
- **Spring Boot:** a project that makes Spring applications quick to start and production-ready by default:
  - **Starters:** dependency bundles such as `spring-boot-starter-web` (Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON, embedded Tomcat) with versions that work together.
  - **Auto-configuration:** conditional configuration classes that create beans only when needed ("Jackson is on the classpath and you have not defined an `ObjectMapper`, so I will create one").
  - **Embedded server:** Tomcat, Jetty or Undertow inside your jar; no separate application server to install.
  - **Externalized configuration:** `application.yml`, environment variables and command-line arguments.
  - **Production features:** Actuator health checks and metrics (Phase 21).
- **Spring ecosystem:** Spring Data (repositories), Spring Security, Spring Cloud (microservices), Spring Batch, Spring AI, and more, all integrating with Boot.

### Why it exists
In early-2000s enterprise Java (J2EE), you wrote heavy EJB components, XML deployment descriptors and deployed to big application servers. Spring (2004) showed that plain Java objects plus dependency injection were simpler and more testable. But Spring itself then needed a lot of configuration: XML or Java config for the web layer, JSON converters, data sources, transaction managers, and you still deployed a WAR to an external Tomcat. Spring Boot (2014) removed that boilerplate with defaults and auto-configuration, so a working REST service is one class plus one dependency.

## 2. How It Works
What happens when you run a Spring Boot application:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Main as "main()"
    participant SA as "SpringApplication"
    participant Ctx as "ApplicationContext"
    participant AC as "Auto-configuration"
    participant Tomcat as "Embedded Tomcat"
    Main->>SA: "SpringApplication.run(App.class, args)"
    SA->>SA: "load application.yml, env vars, args"
    SA->>Ctx: "create context"
    Ctx->>Ctx: "component scan: find @Component, @Service, @RestController"
    Ctx->>AC: "evaluate auto-config conditions (classpath, properties, missing beans)"
    AC-->>Ctx: "register beans: ObjectMapper, DispatcherServlet, Tomcat factory"
    Ctx->>Ctx: "create beans, inject constructor dependencies"
    Ctx->>Tomcat: "start on port 8080"
    Tomcat-->>Main: "application ready"
```

Then, for every HTTP request:
```text
HTTP GET /greet?name=Ann
   -> Tomcat thread receives the request
   -> DispatcherServlet (the front controller, auto-configured by Boot)
   -> finds the @GetMapping("/greet") method on GreetingController
   -> converts query param "name" to a String argument
   -> calls the method; the controller calls GreetingService (injected by Spring)
   -> return value converted to JSON by Jackson (HttpMessageConverter)
   -> HTTP 200 with body {"message":"Hello, Ann!"}
```

**Spring vs Spring Boot, layer by layer:**
```text
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Your code: controllers, services, repositories            |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Spring Boot: starters, auto-config, embedded server,      |
|              externalized config, Actuator                |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Spring Framework: IoC container, MVC, transactions, AOP   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Java 21 + JVM                                             |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
```

## 3. Code Example
### Code
First, the problem Spring solves, in plain Java (manual wiring):
```java
import java.time.LocalTime;

public class ManualWiring {
    interface Clock { LocalTime now(); }

    static class SystemClock implements Clock {
        public LocalTime now() { return LocalTime.of(9, 30); }   // fixed for a predictable demo
    }

    static class GreetingService {
        private final Clock clock;
        GreetingService(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; }     // dependency passed in

        String greet(String name) {
            String part = clock.now().getHour() < 12 ? "morning" : "afternoon";
            return "Good " + part + ", " + name + "!";
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Without Spring, main() must build the whole object graph by hand, in the right order
        Clock clock = new SystemClock();
        GreetingService service = new GreetingService(clock);
        System.out.println(service.greet("Ann"));
    }
}
```

The same idea as a Spring Boot web application (Maven project with `spring-boot-starter-web`):

`pom.xml` (the important parts; full file in [[Maven Basics: pom.xml, Lifecycle and Scopes]]):
```xml
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.0</version>
</parent>

<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
</properties>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

`src/main/java/com/orderhub/OrderHubApplication.java`:
```java
package com.orderhub;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication                     // config + auto-configuration + component scan
public class OrderHubApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderHubApplication.class, args);   // starts the container and Tomcat
    }
}
```

`src/main/java/com/orderhub/greeting/GreetingClock.java`:
```java
package com.orderhub.greeting;

import java.time.LocalTime;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component                                 // Spring creates one instance (a singleton bean)
public class GreetingClock {
    public LocalTime now() {
        return LocalTime.now();
    }
}
```

`src/main/java/com/orderhub/greeting/GreetingService.java`:
```java
package com.orderhub.greeting;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class GreetingService {
    private final GreetingClock clock;

    // Single constructor: Spring injects the GreetingClock bean automatically (no @Autowired needed)
    public GreetingService(GreetingClock clock) {
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public String greet(String name) {
        String part = clock.now().getHour() < 12 ? "morning" : "afternoon";
        return "Good " + part + ", " + name + "!";
    }
}
```

`src/main/java/com/orderhub/greeting/GreetingController.java`:
```java
package com.orderhub.greeting;

import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController                            // methods return data (JSON), not HTML views
public class GreetingController {
    private final GreetingService service;

    public GreetingController(GreetingService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping("/greet")
    public Map<String, String> greet(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "world") String name) {
        return Map.of("message", service.greet(name));    // Jackson turns the Map into JSON
    }
}
```

`src/main/resources/application.yml`:
```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: orderhub
server:
  port: 8080
```

### Walkthrough
- **ManualWiring:** the service does not create its clock; it receives it. That is dependency injection done by hand. In a real application with hundreds of classes, `main` would become a huge, fragile wiring method. Spring automates exactly this step.
- **pom.xml:** the parent manages versions of every Spring and third-party library; the single web starter brings Spring MVC, Jackson and embedded Tomcat.
- **OrderHubApplication:** `@SpringBootApplication` turns on component scanning of `com.orderhub` and its sub-packages, plus auto-configuration. `SpringApplication.run` creates the `ApplicationContext` and starts Tomcat.
- **GreetingClock, GreetingService, GreetingController:** the stereotype annotations mark them as beans. During startup Spring sees that `GreetingController` needs a `GreetingService`, which needs a `GreetingClock`, and creates them in that order. You never write `new GreetingService(...)`.
- **`@GetMapping` and `@RequestParam`:** Spring MVC maps `GET /greet` to the method and fills `name` from the query string (default "world").
- **application.yml:** externalized configuration; Boot reads it automatically.

### Output
Manual wiring program:
```text
Good morning, Ann!
```

Starting the Spring Boot app with `./mvnw spring-boot:run` (key log lines, trimmed):

( ( )\___ | '_ | '_| | '_ \/ _` | \ \ \ \

 =========|_|==============|___/=/_/_/_/

INFO  --- [orderhub] [main] com.orderhub.OrderHubApplication : Starting OrderHubApplication using Java 21

### Compare
| | Plain Java | Spring Framework (no Boot) | Spring Boot |
|---|---|---|---|
| Object creation | `new` everywhere, manual wiring | Container creates and injects beans | Same container |
| Web setup | Write a server or use servlets by hand | Configure `DispatcherServlet`, converters, deploy WAR | Auto-configured, embedded Tomcat |
| Dependency versions | Choose and align yourself | Choose and align yourself | Managed by the Boot parent and starters |
| Configuration | Your own property loading | XML or Java config classes | `application.yml` plus auto-config |
| Run | `java Main` | Deploy to an external server | `java -jar app.jar` |
| Production features | Build yourself | Add libraries yourself | Actuator starter |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **What is Spring Framework?**
   A Java framework built around an IoC container that creates and wires application objects (beans) through dependency injection. It also provides modules for web applications, data access, transactions, security integration, messaging and testing, all designed to work with plain Java objects.
2. **What is Spring Boot and how is it different from Spring?**
   Spring Boot is built on Spring and removes configuration work. It adds starters (curated dependency sets), auto-configuration (beans created automatically based on the classpath and properties), an embedded server so the app runs with `java -jar`, externalized configuration and production features like Actuator. Spring gives the capabilities; Boot gives sensible defaults and packaging.
3. **What are IoC and dependency injection?**
   Inversion of Control means the framework controls object creation and lifecycle instead of your code. Dependency injection is how Spring does it: a class declares what it needs (usually as constructor parameters) and the container supplies those objects. This decouples classes and makes them easy to unit test with fakes.

**Follow-up**
4. **What is a bean?**
   An object whose lifecycle is managed by the Spring container. Beans are found through component scanning of classes annotated with `@Component` and its specializations, or declared with `@Bean` methods in `@Configuration` classes. By default each bean is a singleton within the context.
5. **What does a starter contain?**
   A starter is a mostly empty jar whose `pom` lists dependencies that belong together. `spring-boot-starter-web` brings `spring-webmvc`, Jackson, validation-ready support and `spring-boot-starter-tomcat`. Versions come from Boot's dependency management, so you rarely write a version number.
6. **How does auto-configuration decide what to create?**
   Auto-configuration classes are ordinary `@Configuration` classes guarded by conditions such as `@ConditionalOnClass` (a library is on the classpath), `@ConditionalOnProperty` and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (you have not defined your own). If you define your own bean, Boot backs off. Running with `--debug` prints which conditions matched.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **Does Spring Boot replace Spring Framework?**
   No. Boot uses Spring Framework underneath; every Boot app is a Spring app. Boot only automates configuration, dependency management and packaging, and you can still configure anything manually.
8. **A teammate says "Spring Boot is slow and magic". How do you respond?**
   The "magic" is explicit conditional configuration you can inspect with the conditions report (`--debug`) or the Actuator `conditions` endpoint, and you can override any default by defining your own bean or property. Startup cost is mostly classpath scanning and bean creation; for very fast startup there are options like lazy initialization, AOT and GraalVM native images (Phase 18).
9. **What changed in Spring Boot 3 that interviewers ask about?**
   Boot 3 (Spring Framework 6) requires Java 17+, moved from `javax.*` to `jakarta.*` packages (Jakarta EE 9+), added native image support and Micrometer observation. Boot 4 (Framework 7, November 2025) moves further to Jakarta EE 11, Jackson 3, modularized auto-configuration and null-safety annotations (JSpecify).

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you understand the container and dependency injection as the core idea, and can explain Boot's value without calling it magic.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Creating services with `new` inside controllers | Not a bean: no injection, no transactions, hard to test | Inject through the constructor |
| Thinking Boot and Spring are different frameworks | Confusing interview answers | Boot is configuration and packaging on top of Spring |
| Adding many starters "just in case" | Unwanted auto-config (for example a DataSource demanding a database URL) | Add only what you use |
| Writing versions for Boot-managed dependencies | Version conflicts at runtime | Let the parent or BOM manage versions |
| Mixing `javax.*` and `jakarta.*` imports in Boot 3 | `ClassNotFoundException` or annotations ignored | Use `jakarta.*` only |

### Best practices
- Use constructor injection with `final` fields; with one constructor no `@Autowired` is needed.
- Keep the main class in the root package (`com.orderhub`) so scanning covers every feature package.
- Start from Spring Initializr with the current Boot release; upgrade regularly (each Boot minor version gets about 13 months of open-source support).
- Learn to read the startup log and the conditions report; they explain the "magic".

### Compare with
| | Spring Boot | Jakarta EE (application server) | Quarkus | Micronaut |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DI style | Runtime reflection plus AOT option | CDI, runtime | Build-time DI | Compile-time DI |
| Startup | About 1 to 3 seconds typical | Server already running, deploy WARs | Very fast, native-first | Very fast |
| Ecosystem | Largest | Standard specs | Growing | Growing |
| Job market | Dominant | Legacy enterprise | Niche | Niche |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
Start **OrderHub**. Using the code above as a template, create the project skeleton and a health-style endpoint:
1. `com.orderhub.OrderHubApplication` with `@SpringBootApplication`.
2. A `@Service` called `com.orderhub.info.AppInfoService` that returns the app name and the start time (an `Instant` captured in the constructor).
3. A `@RestController` `com.orderhub.info.AppInfoController` exposing `GET /api/info` that returns `{"name":"orderhub","startedAt":"..."}`.
4. Prove dependency injection: the controller must not contain the word `new` for the service.

Acceptance criteria: `curl localhost:8080/api/info` returns HTTP 200 with JSON containing both fields; the service is injected through a constructor.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
package com.orderhub.info;

import java.time.Instant;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class AppInfoService {
    private final Instant startedAt = Instant.now();   // created once: the bean is a singleton

    public String name() { return "orderhub"; }

    public Instant startedAt() { return startedAt; }
}
```

```java
package com.orderhub.info;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
public class AppInfoController {
    private final AppInfoService info;

    public AppInfoController(AppInfoService info) {   // injected by Spring
        this.info = info;
    }

    @GetMapping("/info")
    public Map<String, Object> info() {
        Map<String, Object> body = new LinkedHashMap<>();   // keeps field order in JSON
        body.put("name", info.name());
        body.put("startedAt", info.startedAt());
        return body;
    }
}
```

```http
GET /api/info HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080

HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json

{"name":"orderhub","startedAt":"2026-11-24T09:30:12.345678Z"}
```
Boot configures Jackson's Java time module, so the `Instant` is written as an ISO-8601 string.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What is the core of the Spring Framework?
A: The IoC container, which creates beans and wires them together with dependency injection.

Q: What three things does Spring Boot add on top of Spring?
A: Starters for dependencies, auto-configuration of beans, and an embedded server (plus externalized config and Actuator).

Q: What is dependency injection in Spring?
A: The container passes a class its collaborators (usually via the constructor) instead of the class creating them with `new`.

Q: When does Spring Boot auto-configuration back off?
A: When its conditions fail, for example when you define your own bean of that type (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`).

Q: Which Java version and package namespace does Spring Boot 3 require?
A: Java 17 or later and `jakarta.*` instead of `javax.*`.

**Related:** [[@SpringBootApplication Explained]] · [[IoC and Dependency Injection]] · [[Auto-Configuration Internals]]

content:
# Maven Basics: pom.xml, Lifecycle and Scopes

**Level: Beginner | Phase 5 | Priority: MUST | Since: Maven 2 (2005), Maven 3.x current (3.9 line), Maven Wrapper bundled by Spring Initializr; Spring Boot 3.5 requires Maven 3.6.3+**

> **30-second interview answer:** Maven is a build tool that uses a declarative `pom.xml` to describe a project: its coordinates (`groupId:artifactId:version`), its dependencies, and its plugins. Maven downloads dependencies, including transitive ones, from Maven Central into the local `~/.m2` repository. Builds follow a fixed **lifecycle** of phases (`validate`, `compile`, `test`, `package`, `verify`, `install`, `deploy`); running one phase runs all earlier ones. **Scopes** control where a dependency is visible: `compile` (default, everywhere), `provided` (compile but not packaged), `runtime` (not needed to compile), `test` (tests only). In Spring Boot, the `spring-boot-starter-parent` manages versions and the `spring-boot-maven-plugin` builds an executable fat jar.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
A recipe card and a kitchen routine.

| Kitchen | Maven |
|---|---|
| The recipe card listing ingredients and steps | `pom.xml` (Project Object Model) |
| A unique product code on the finished dish: brand, dish name, edition | Coordinates `groupId:artifactId:version` |
| Ingredients ordered from a central wholesaler | Dependencies downloaded from Maven Central |
| Your home pantry where delivered ingredients are kept | Local repository `~/.m2/repository` |
| "Flour" automatically brings "yeast" because the flour mix needs it | Transitive dependencies |
| A fixed routine: wash, chop, cook, plate, serve | Lifecycle phases: validate, compile, test, package, install |
| Asking for "plate" means all earlier steps happen first | Running `mvn package` runs compile and test first |
| Ingredients only for tasting, not served | `test` scope |
| Cutlery the restaurant already provides | `provided` scope |
| A franchise rule book fixing which supplier versions to use | `spring-boot-starter-parent` dependency management |

### What it is
- **POM (`pom.xml`):** XML file at the project root describing the project. Maven combines it with a built-in "super POM" and any parent POM into the **effective POM** (`mvn help:effective-pom`).
- **Coordinates:** `groupId` (organization, reverse domain: `com.orderhub`), `artifactId` (project name: `orderhub`), `version` (`0.0.1-SNAPSHOT`). `SNAPSHOT` means "work in progress, may change"; releases are fixed.
- **Packaging:** `jar` (default) or `war`; for Spring Boot, `jar`.
- **Dependency:** another artifact your code needs. **Transitive dependency:** a dependency of your dependency, pulled in automatically. Conflicts are solved by "nearest wins" in the tree.
- **Repository:** local (`~/.m2`) and remote (Maven Central, or a company Nexus/Artifactory).
- **Plugin and goal:** all actual work is done by plugins (compiler, surefire for tests, jar). A goal is one task of a plugin (`compiler:compile`). Lifecycle phases are bound to plugin goals.
- **Lifecycles:** `clean` (delete `target/`), `default` (build), `site` (reports).

Default lifecycle phases (the ones you use):

| Phase | What happens | Plugin goal bound by default |
|---|---|---|
| `validate` | Check the POM is correct | - |
| `compile` | Compile `src/main/java` into `target/classes` | `compiler:compile` |
| `test-compile` | Compile `src/test/java` | `compiler:testCompile` |
| `test` | Run unit tests | `surefire:test` |
| `package` | Build the jar in `target/` | `jar:jar` (plus Boot `repackage`) |
| `verify` | Run integration tests and checks | `failsafe:verify` if configured |
| `install` | Copy the jar to `~/.m2` for other local projects | `install:install` |
| `deploy` | Upload to a remote repository | `deploy:deploy` |

Dependency scopes:

| Scope | Compile main code | Run tests | Packaged in the app | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `compile` (default) | Yes | Yes | Yes | `spring-boot-starter-web` |
| `provided` | Yes | Yes | No (the environment provides it) | Servlet API when deploying a WAR, Lombok |
| `runtime` | No | Yes | Yes | JDBC driver `postgresql` |
| `test` | No | Yes | No | `spring-boot-starter-test` |
| `system` | Yes | Yes | No | Local jar path (avoid) |
| `import` | Only in `dependencyManagement` with type `pom` | - | - | Importing a BOM like `spring-cloud-dependencies` |

### Why it exists
Before Maven (and its predecessor Ant), every project had its own build scripts and a `lib/` folder of jars copied by hand, with unknown versions and conflicts. Maven standardized the project layout (`src/main/java`, `src/test/java`), the build steps and dependency resolution, so any Java developer can clone any Maven project and run `mvn package`. Gradle is the main alternative (Groovy or Kotlin build scripts, faster incremental builds); Spring Initializr supports both, and interviews usually expect Maven basics.

## 2. How It Works
```text
mvn clean package
  clean lifecycle:   pre-clean -> clean (delete target/)
  default lifecycle: validate -> compile -> test-compile -> test -> package
                                                                    |
                            spring-boot-maven-plugin:repackage  <---+
                            target/orderhub-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar  (executable fat jar)

Dependency resolution for spring-boot-starter-web (no version written):
  pom.xml: <parent> spring-boot-starter-parent 3.5.0
             -> extends spring-boot-dependencies 3.5.0 (a BOM: hundreds of managed versions)
  Maven looks in ~/.m2/repository -> missing? download from Maven Central -> cache it
  then reads that artifact's own pom and repeats for its dependencies (transitive)
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["pom.xml"] --> B["Effective POM: super POM + parent + yours"]
    B --> C["Resolve dependencies"]
    C --> D["~/.m2 local repo"]
    D -->|"missing"| E["Maven Central"]
    B --> F["Lifecycle: compile, test, package"]
    F --> G["target/orderhub.jar"]
```

**The fat jar:** Spring Boot's `repackage` goal puts your classes in `BOOT-INF/classes`, all dependency jars in `BOOT-INF/lib`, and a launcher (`org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher`) as the `Main-Class`. That is why `java -jar orderhub.jar` works without a classpath.

**Maven Wrapper (`mvnw`, `mvnw.cmd`, `.mvn/wrapper/`):** scripts that download the exact Maven version the project expects, so nobody needs Maven installed and every machine and CI server uses the same version.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
`pom.xml` for OrderHub:
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- Inherit plugin config and dependency versions from Spring Boot -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.5.0</version>
        <relativePath/> <!-- look up the parent in the repository, not in ../pom.xml -->
    </parent>

    <!-- Coordinates of this project -->
    <groupId>com.orderhub</groupId>
    <artifactId>orderhub</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <name>orderhub</name>
    <description>Order management backend</description>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>  <!-- used by the parent to set the compiler release -->
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- compile scope (default): Spring MVC, Jackson, embedded Tomcat -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <!-- runtime scope: needed when the app runs, not to compile it (used from Phase 12) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
            <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>

        <!-- test scope: JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, Spring Test; never packaged -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Builds the executable fat jar and provides mvn spring-boot:run -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

A plain class under `src/main/java/com/orderhub/pricing/PriceCalculator.java`:
```java
package com.orderhub.pricing;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;

public class PriceCalculator {
    public BigDecimal totalWithTax(BigDecimal net, int quantity, BigDecimal taxRate) {
        BigDecimal gross = net.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(quantity));
        return gross.add(gross.multiply(taxRate)).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }
}
```

Its unit test under `src/test/java/com/orderhub/pricing/PriceCalculatorTest.java` (compiles only because `spring-boot-starter-test` is on the test classpath):
```java
package com.orderhub.pricing;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class PriceCalculatorTest {
    @Test
    void addsTaxAndRounds() {
        PriceCalculator calc = new PriceCalculator();
        assertThat(calc.totalWithTax(new BigDecimal("9.99"), 3, new BigDecimal("0.20")))
                .isEqualByComparingTo("35.96");
    }
}
```

./mvnw test                       # compile and run tests only
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests  # build without running tests (still compiles them)
./mvnw spring-boot:run            # run the app from sources
java -jar target/orderhub-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
./mvnw dependency:tree            # show direct and transitive dependencies
./mvnw help:effective-pom         # the full POM after inheritance

### Walkthrough
- **parent:** inherits `spring-boot-dependencies`, a bill of materials (BOM) listing compatible versions of Spring, Jackson, Tomcat, JUnit, PostgreSQL driver and hundreds more. That is why the dependencies have no `<version>`.
- **coordinates:** identify the jar this project produces: `target/orderhub-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar`.
- **`java.version`:** the parent passes it to the compiler plugin as `--release 21`.
- **Scopes:** the web starter is needed everywhere; the PostgreSQL driver only at runtime (code talks to JDBC interfaces); the test starter only for tests.
- **spring-boot-maven-plugin:** hooks the `repackage` goal into `package` to make the fat jar and adds `spring-boot:run`.
- **PriceCalculator and its test:** `src/main/java` goes into the jar; `src/test/java` is compiled and run by the `test` phase but never packaged. If the test fails, `package` stops: the build is protected by tests.
- **Commands:** `-DskipTests` skips running tests (`-Dmaven.test.skip=true` would also skip compiling them).
