# TreeMap and Red-Black Trees

**Level: Intermediate | Phase 8 | Priority: SHOULD | Since: Java 1.2 (NavigableMap Java 6, SequencedMap Java 21)**

> **30-second interview answer:** `TreeMap` stores its entries in a red-black tree, a binary search tree that rebalances itself with recolouring and rotations so its height stays at most about 2 log n. That gives guaranteed O(log n) `get`, `put` and `remove`, keys always in sorted order, and navigation methods like `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `headMap` and `subMap`. Ordering comes from `Comparable` or a `Comparator`, and that ordering, not `equals`, decides whether two keys are the same.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
A library card catalogue sorted alphabetically, with a librarian who keeps the drawers balanced.

| Card catalogue | TreeMap |
|---|---|
| Cards sorted A to Z | Keys kept in sorted order |
| "Go left if earlier in the alphabet, right if later" | Binary search tree navigation, O(log n) |
| The librarian reshuffles drawers so no drawer grows much deeper than the others | Red-black rebalancing (recolour and rotate) |
| "What is the last card before M?" | `floorKey` or `lowerKey` |
| "Give me every card from C to F" | `subMap("C", true, "F", true)` |
| The sorting rule printed on the drawer | The `Comparator` (or `Comparable`) |

### What it is
- **Binary search tree (BST):** every node's left subtree has smaller keys and its right subtree larger keys. Search walks down one path.
- **Red-black tree:** a BST where each node is coloured red or black and these rules hold:
  1. Every node is red or black.
  2. The root is black.
  3. A red node never has a red child (no two reds in a row).
  4. Every path from a node down to a null leaf passes through the same number of black nodes (the black height).
  Together, rules 3 and 4 mean the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so height is at most `2 log2(n + 1)`.
- **Rotation:** a local rearrangement of three nodes that keeps BST order but changes the shape (left rotation, right rotation).
- **`NavigableMap`:** the interface (Java 6) with `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `lowerKey`, `higherKey`, `headMap`, `tailMap`, `subMap`, `descendingMap`, `pollFirstEntry`, `pollLastEntry`.
- **Consistent with equals:** a comparator where `compare(a, b) == 0` exactly when `a.equals(b)`. `TreeMap` only uses `compare`.

### Why it exists
A plain BST degenerates into a linked list if keys arrive sorted (1, 2, 3, ...), giving O(n) operations. A hash map has no order at all. `TreeMap` gives sorted order and range queries with a guaranteed O(log n) worst case, which matters for things like price tiers, time windows and leaderboards.

## 2. How It Works
**Node layout:** each `TreeMap.Entry` has `key`, `value`, `left`, `right`, `parent` and a `boolean color`. That is more memory per entry than a `HashMap` node.

**Why balancing matters:** inserting 10, 20, 30 in order.

```text
Plain BST (degenerates)        Red-black tree after fix-up
   10                               20(B)
     \                             /     \
      20                       10(R)     30(R)
        \
         30                    height 2 instead of 3; with 1,000,000 sorted keys:
                               plain BST height 1,000,000, red-black at most about 40
```

**Insert algorithm:**
1. Walk down as in any BST using `compare(key, node.key)`. If a comparison returns 0, replace the value and stop (the key object already in the map is kept).
2. Attach a new **red** node as a leaf (red does not change any black height, so only rule 3 can break).
3. Fix up while the parent is red:
   - Uncle red: recolour parent and uncle black, grandparent red, move up to the grandparent.
   - Uncle black: one or two rotations around the grandparent plus recolouring, then stop.
4. Colour the root black.

Insertion needs at most 2 rotations, deletion at most 3; recolouring can travel up the tree, but everything is O(log n).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["put(key, value)"] --> B{"root null?"}
    B -- "yes" --> C["root = new black node"]
    B -- "no" --> D["walk down using compare()"]
    D --> E{"compare == 0?"}
    E -- "yes" --> F["replace value, keep existing key"]
    E -- "no" --> G["attach new red leaf"]
    G --> H{"parent red?"}
    H -- "no" --> I["done"]
    H -- "yes, uncle red" --> J["recolour, move up to grandparent"]
    J --> H
    H -- "yes, uncle black" --> K["rotate once or twice, recolour, done"]
```

**Range views:** `headMap`, `tailMap` and `subMap` return live views backed by the same tree, not copies. Writing through the view writes the map; putting a key outside the view's range throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

**Null keys:** with natural ordering, `put(null, v)` throws `NullPointerException` because it calls `compareTo` on the key. A custom comparator such as `Comparator.nullsFirst(...)` can allow nulls.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
```java
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class TreeMapDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Price tiers: floorEntry finds the tier that applies to an amount
        TreeMap<Integer, String> tiers = new TreeMap<>();
        tiers.put(0, "STANDARD");
        tiers.put(50, "FREE_SHIPPING");
        tiers.put(200, "GOLD");
        for (int amount : new int[] {10, 50, 120, 999}) {
            System.out.println("order " + amount + " -> " + tiers.floorEntry(amount).getValue());
        }

        // 2. Navigation on a score board
        TreeMap<Integer, String> scores = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(85, "Ava", 70, "Ben", 55, "Cara", 92, "Dan"));
        System.out.println("sorted: " + scores);
        System.out.println("floorKey(80)=" + scores.floorKey(80) + " ceilingKey(80)=" + scores.ceilingKey(80));
        System.out.println("higherKey(85)=" + scores.higherKey(85) + " lowerKey(55)=" + scores.lowerKey(55));
        System.out.println("headMap(85)=" + scores.headMap(85));
        System.out.println("tailMap(85, inclusive)=" + scores.tailMap(85, true));
        System.out.println("subMap[60, 90]=" + scores.subMap(60, true, 90, true));
        System.out.println("descending=" + scores.descendingMap());
        System.out.println("pollFirstEntry=" + scores.pollFirstEntry() + " remaining=" + scores);

        // 3. The comparator decides equality, not equals()
        TreeMap<String, Integer> caseless = new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
        caseless.put("Apple", 1);
        caseless.put("apple", 2);
        System.out.println("case-insensitive map: " + caseless + " size=" + caseless.size());

        // 4. Consistent hashing ring: the first node clockwise from a hash
        TreeMap<Integer, String> ring = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0, "node-A", 100, "node-B", 200, "node-C"));
        for (int hash : new int[] {42, 150, 250}) {
            Map.Entry<Integer, String> e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash);
            String node = (e != null ? e : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();   // wrap around
            System.out.println("hash " + hash + " -> " + node);
        }

        // 5. Natural ordering rejects a null key
        try {
            new TreeMap<String, Integer>().put(null, 1);
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("null key: NullPointerException");
        }
    }
}
```

### Walkthrough
- Part 1: `floorEntry(amount)` returns the greatest key less than or equal to the amount. With tiers at 0, 50 and 200, an order of 120 falls in the 50 tier. This replaces a chain of `if` statements and stays O(log n) as tiers grow.
- Part 2: `Map.of` has no order, but the `TreeMap` copy is sorted. `floor` and `ceiling` include the key itself, `lower` and `higher` are strict. `headMap(85)` excludes 85 by default; `tailMap(85, true)` includes it. `pollFirstEntry` removes and returns the smallest entry.
- Part 3: with a case-insensitive comparator, `"apple"` compares equal to `"Apple"`, so the second `put` replaces the value but keeps the original key object. The map has one entry even though `"Apple".equals("apple")` is false.
- Part 4: a consistent-hashing ring (used by caches and sharded databases) maps a hash to the first server at or after it, wrapping to the first server. `ceilingEntry` plus `firstEntry` is the whole algorithm.
- Part 5: natural ordering calls `compareTo` on the key, so a `null` key fails fast.

### Output
```text
order 10 -> STANDARD
order 50 -> FREE_SHIPPING
order 120 -> FREE_SHIPPING
order 999 -> GOLD
sorted: {55=Cara, 70=Ben, 85=Ava, 92=Dan}
floorKey(80)=70 ceilingKey(80)=85
higherKey(85)=92 lowerKey(55)=null
headMap(85)={55=Cara, 70=Ben}
tailMap(85, inclusive)={85=Ava, 92=Dan}
subMap[60, 90]={70=Ben, 85=Ava}
descending={92=Dan, 85=Ava, 70=Ben, 55=Cara}
pollFirstEntry=55=Cara remaining={70=Ben, 85=Ava, 92=Dan}
case-insensitive map: {Apple=2} size=1
hash 42 -> node-B
hash 150 -> node-C
hash 250 -> node-A
null key: NullPointerException
```

### Compare
| Approach to "which tier does 120 fall into?" | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Chain of `if (amount >= 200) ... else if` | O(tiers) | Code change for every new tier |
| Sort a list, linear scan | O(n) | Easy to get boundaries wrong |
| `TreeMap.floorEntry(amount)` | O(log n) | Data-driven, tiers can come from config or a database |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **How does `TreeMap` store entries?**
   In a red-black tree, a self-balancing binary search tree. Each entry node has key, value, left, right, parent and a colour bit, and the tree is ordered by the comparator or the keys' natural order.
2. **What is the time complexity of `TreeMap` operations?**
   `get`, `put`, `remove`, `containsKey`, `floorKey` and the other navigation methods are O(log n) in the worst case. Iterating all entries in order is O(n). `firstKey` and `lastKey` are O(log n) because they walk down one edge of the tree.
3. **When would you choose `TreeMap` over `HashMap`?**
   When you need keys in sorted order or range queries: "the nearest key below X", "all keys between A and B", the smallest or largest key. If you only need lookup by exact key, `HashMap` is faster.

**Follow-up**
4. **What are the red-black tree rules, and why do they keep the tree balanced?**
   Nodes are red or black, the root is black, a red node cannot have a red child, and every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes. The shortest possible path is all black and the longest alternates red and black, so no path is more than twice as long as another, which bounds the height at about 2 log n.
5. **How does `TreeMap` decide that two keys are equal?**
   Only by `compare` or `compareTo` returning 0; `equals` and `hashCode` are never called. If the comparator is inconsistent with `equals`, the map can treat different objects as the same key (or equal objects as different keys).
6. **Why are newly inserted nodes coloured red?**
   A red leaf does not change the black height of any path, so rule 4 still holds. Only rule 3 (no red parent with red child) can be broken, and that is fixed locally with recolouring and at most two rotations.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **We used a `TreeSet<Employee>` with a comparator on salary, and employees with equal salaries disappeared. Why?**
   Two employees with the same salary compare as 0, so the set treats the second as a duplicate and ignores it. Add tie-breakers to the comparator, for example `Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary).thenComparing(Employee::id)`.
8. **Is `headMap` a copy?**
   No, it is a live view backed by the original tree. Changes in either are visible in the other, and inserting a key outside the view's range through the view throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Use `new TreeMap<>(map.headMap(k))` if you need an independent copy.
9. **Java 8 `HashMap` also uses red-black trees. How is that different from `TreeMap`?**
   `HashMap` only treeifies a single overloaded bucket, as a fallback against collisions, and orders that small tree by hash (then `Comparable`). `TreeMap` is one tree for the whole map, ordered by the comparator, giving a global sort order.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you know when sorted structures beat hash structures, can explain why balancing guarantees O(log n), and understand that the comparator defines key identity.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Comparator inconsistent with `equals` (for example only comparing salary) | Distinct keys silently overwrite each other | Add tie-breakers with `thenComparing` |
| Mutating a field used by the comparator after insertion | Tree order is broken, lookups fail | Use immutable keys |
| Using `TreeMap` when order is not needed | O(log n) and more memory instead of O(1) | Use `HashMap` |
| Assuming `subMap` or `headMap` is a copy | Unexpected changes in the original map | Copy explicitly with `new TreeMap<>(view)` |
| Inserting `null` keys with natural ordering | `NullPointerException` | Avoid null keys or use `Comparator.nullsFirst` |
| Using `TreeMap` from several threads | Corrupted tree | `ConcurrentSkipListMap` for a concurrent sorted map |

### Best practices
- Reach for `floorEntry`, `ceilingEntry` and `subMap` whenever you see range logic or tier tables; it turns if-chains into data.
- Build comparators with `Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...)` so they are consistent with `equals`.
- For a concurrent sorted map use `ConcurrentSkipListMap`, which offers the same `NavigableMap` API with lock-free operations.
- Prefer `pollFirstEntry` over `firstKey` plus `remove` when consuming entries in order.

### Compare with
| Structure | Order | Complexity | Thread-safe | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TreeMap | Sorted | O(log n) | No | Red-black tree, `NavigableMap` |
| HashMap | None | O(1) average | No | Fastest exact lookup |
| LinkedHashMap | Insertion or access | O(1) average | No | No range queries |
| ConcurrentSkipListMap | Sorted | O(log n) expected | Yes, lock-free | Skip list instead of a tree |
| PriorityQueue | Only the head is ordered | O(log n) offer and poll | No | Not a map; no range queries |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
OrderHub needs a meeting-room style booking for delivery slots. Write `SlotBooker` with `boolean book(int start, int end)` (half-open interval `[start, end)`) that returns `false` if the new slot overlaps any existing booking. Use a `TreeMap<Integer, Integer>` from start to end. Acceptance criteria:
- Each `book` call is O(log n).
- Booking `[10, 20)`, `[20, 30)` succeed; `[15, 25)` and `[5, 11)` fail; `[0, 10)` succeeds.
- Print all bookings in order at the end.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class SlotBooker {
    private final TreeMap<Integer, Integer> slots = new TreeMap<>();   // start -> end

    public boolean book(int start, int end) {
        Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> before = slots.floorEntry(start);    // starts at or before
        if (before != null && before.getValue() > start) return false;   // it ends after we start
        Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> after = slots.ceilingEntry(start);   // starts at or after
        if (after != null && after.getKey() < end) return false;         // it starts before we end
        slots.put(start, end);
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SlotBooker booker = new SlotBooker();
        int[][] requests = {{10, 20}, {20, 30}, {15, 25}, {5, 11}, {0, 10}};
        for (int[] r : requests) {
            System.out.println("[" + r[0] + ", " + r[1] + ") -> " + booker.book(r[0], r[1]));
        }
        System.out.println("bookings: " + booker.slots);
    }
}
```
Output:
```text
[10, 20) -> true
[20, 30) -> true
[15, 25) -> false
[5, 11) -> false
[0, 10) -> true
bookings: {0=10, 10=20, 20=30}
```
Only the two neighbours of the new start can overlap it, so two O(log n) lookups are enough.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What data structure backs TreeMap?
A: A red-black tree, a self-balancing binary search tree with guaranteed O(log n) operations.

Q: What are the four red-black tree rules?
A: Every node is red or black, the root is black, a red node has no red child, and every path from a node to its null leaves has the same number of black nodes.

Q: How does TreeMap decide whether two keys are the same?
A: Only by the comparator or `compareTo` returning 0; `equals` and `hashCode` are not used.

Q: What is the difference between TreeMap `floorKey` and `lowerKey`?
A: `floorKey` returns the greatest key less than or equal to the argument; `lowerKey` returns the greatest key strictly less.

Q: Which class gives a thread-safe sorted map with the NavigableMap API?
A: `ConcurrentSkipListMap`.

**Related:** [[HashMap Internals]] · [[Comparable vs Comparator]] · [[HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet]] · [[Concurrent Collections and BlockingQueue]]

# Edge cases

**Shared analogy: the rules of a shared notebook.** A normal collection is a notebook with one rule: if someone rewrites a page while you are reading through it, you stop and shout (that shout is `ConcurrentModificationException`). The special maps are notebooks with house rules of their own: `EnumMap` is a printed form with one fixed box per option, `WeakHashMap` is a notebook whose entries fade once nobody else remembers the person they are about, and `IdentityHashMap` is a guest list that checks faces, not names, so two people called "Sam" are two different guests.

These topics are where interviewers check whether you know *why* a rule exists, because each one deliberately bends a rule from the topics before it.

# Phase 8 review: Collections Internals

## Cheat sheet

| Idea | Remember |
|---|---|
| HashMap layout | `Node[] table`, node = hash, key, value, next |
| Bucket index | `(n - 1) & (h ^ (h >>> 16))`; n is a power of two |
| Defaults | Capacity 16, load factor 0.75, threshold 12; table created on first put |
| Resize | Doubles; each node stays at i or moves to i + oldCap (one bit decides) |
| Treeify | Bucket of 8+ nodes and table of 64+ becomes a red-black tree; back to list at 6 |
| Java 7 vs 8 | Head insertion and possible infinite loop vs tail insertion and trees; still not thread-safe |
| Keys | Immutable, `equals` and `hashCode` consistent; mutated key = lost entry |
| Pre-sizing | `HashMap.newHashMap(n)` (Java 19+) avoids resizes |
| LinkedHashMap | HashMap plus before and after links; insertion or access order |
| LRU | `super(16, 0.75f, true)` plus `removeEldestEntry` returning `size() > cap` |
| SequencedMap | Java 21: `firstEntry`, `lastEntry`, `pollFirstEntry`, `putFirst`, `reversed()` |
| TreeMap | Red-black tree, O(log n), sorted, `NavigableMap` (floor, ceiling, subMap) |
| Red-black rules | Red or black, black root, no red-red, equal black height |
| Comparator | Defines key identity in TreeMap; keep it consistent with `equals` |
| ConcurrentHashMap 8+ | Lock-free get, CAS on empty bin, `synchronized` on bin head, cooperative resize |
| ConcurrentHashMap 7 | 16 segments with `ReentrantLock` each |
| No nulls | ConcurrentHashMap and Hashtable reject null keys and values |
| Atomic ops | `merge`, `compute`, `computeIfAbsent`, `putIfAbsent`, `replace(k, old, new)` |
| CME | `modCount != expectedModCount` in `next()`; fix with `removeIf` or `iterator.remove()` |
| Second-to-last trap | Removing it in for-each ends the loop silently, last element skipped |
| EnumMap | Array by ordinal, declaration order, no null key |
| WeakHashMap | Weak keys, strong values; value referencing key leaks |
| IdentityHashMap | `==` and identity hash, linear probing; for object graphs |

### Key code snippets
```java
// Bucket index, exactly as HashMap computes it
static int index(Object key, int capacity) {
    int h;
    int hash = key == null ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
    return hash & (capacity - 1);
}
```

```java
// LRU cache
class Lru<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int cap;
    Lru(int cap) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.cap = cap; }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) { return size() > cap; }
}
```

```java
// TreeMap navigation
TreeMap<Integer, String> tiers = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0, "STANDARD", 50, "FREE_SHIPPING", 200, "GOLD"));
String tier = tiers.floorEntry(amount).getValue();
SortedMap<Integer, String> cheap = tiers.headMap(50);          // live view, keys below 50
```

```java
// ConcurrentHashMap: atomic updates only
counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);
views.computeIfAbsent(productId, id -> new LongAdder()).increment();
cache.computeIfAbsent(id, this::loadQuickly);                   // keep the function short
```

```java
// Safe removal while iterating
list.removeIf(x -> x.isExpired());
map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0);
for (Iterator<Order> it = orders.iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) if (it.next().isCancelled()) it.remove();
```

```java
// Special maps
EnumMap<Status, Integer> byStatus = new EnumMap<>(Status.class);
Set<Object> visited = Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>());
```

## The 10 most likely interview questions

1. **How does HashMap work internally?** Array of buckets; index from spread `hashCode` and a bitmask; collisions chained, compared by hash then `equals`; resize at 75% full; trees for long buckets.
2. **What happens on a hash collision?** Nodes chain in the bucket; `equals` finds the right key; 8+ nodes (table 64+) become a red-black tree, so worst case O(log n).
3. **Why is capacity a power of two?** Cheap `&` instead of `%`, and resize splits each bucket into exactly two.
4. **What if a key's hashCode changes after insertion?** Lookups go to the wrong bucket or fail `equals`; the entry is stuck. Use immutable keys.
5. **How do you build an LRU cache?** Access-ordered `LinkedHashMap` plus `removeEldestEntry`; or hash map plus doubly linked list by hand; Caffeine in production.
6. **TreeMap vs HashMap?** Sorted and O(log n) with range queries vs unordered and O(1); comparator defines equality in TreeMap.
7. **ConcurrentHashMap vs Hashtable vs synchronizedMap?** Per-bin locks, CAS and lock-free reads vs one lock for everything.
8. **Why no nulls in ConcurrentHashMap?** `get` returning null must mean absent; no atomic way to disambiguate.
9. **What causes ConcurrentModificationException and how do you avoid it?** Structural change outside the iterator; use `removeIf`, `iterator.remove()`, or concurrent collections.
10. **When would you use EnumMap, WeakHashMap or IdentityHashMap?** Enum keys; metadata tied to the key's lifetime; identity tracking in object graphs.

## Rapid-fire flashcards

Q: What is the default initial capacity and load factor of HashMap?
A: 16 and 0.75, so the first resize happens when the 13th entry is added.

Q: What is HashMap's TREEIFY_THRESHOLD?
A: 8 nodes in one bucket, provided the table capacity is at least 64 (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY).

Q: In HashMap resize, where can a node from bucket 5 of a 16-slot table go?
A: Bucket 5 or bucket 21 of the 32-slot table, depending on bit 16 of its hash.

Q: Which LinkedHashMap constructor argument enables access order?
A: The third one, `accessOrder = true`, in `new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true)`.

Q: What is the worst-case time complexity of TreeMap `get`?
A: O(log n), guaranteed by red-black balancing.

Q: Which TreeMap method returns the greatest key strictly less than a given key?
A: `lowerKey`.

Q: How does Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap handle a write to an empty bucket?
A: A CAS from null to the new node, with no lock.

Q: Which ConcurrentHashMap method returns the size as a long?
A: `mappingCount()`.

Q: What does `ArrayList` iterator's `hasNext()` compare?
A: Only `cursor != size`; the `modCount` check happens in `next()`.

Q: Which map compares keys with == instead of equals?
A: `IdentityHashMap`.

# Phase 9: Concurrency Fundamentals (Intermediate)

This phase teaches you how Java runs several things at once and how to keep shared data correct while it does. You start with threads themselves (what they are, their states, `Runnable` vs `Callable`), move to the problems shared state causes (race conditions, visibility, deadlock) and the tools that fix them (`synchronized`, `volatile`, `wait` and `notify`, atomic classes), and finish with the modern, high-level toolkit every Spring developer uses daily: executors and thread pools, `Future` and `CompletableFuture`, and concurrent collections such as `BlockingQueue`.

Why interviewers care: every Spring Boot service is concurrent. Tomcat serves each request on a pool thread, so two requests can hit the same singleton bean at the same moment. Interviewers ask concurrency questions to find out whether you will write the bug where two customers get the last item in stock, or the thread pool that brings production down. The questions range from definitions ("process vs thread") to output prediction ("what does this counter print?") to design ("how would you call three services in parallel?").

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Processes, Threads and Thread Lifecycle"] --> B["Runnable vs Callable"]
    A --> C["Race Conditions and synchronized"]
    C --> D["volatile and Visibility"]
    C --> E["wait, notify and notifyAll"]
    C --> F["Deadlock, Livelock and Starvation"]
    D --> G["Atomic Classes and CAS"]
    B --> H["ExecutorService and Thread Pools"]
    H --> I["Future and CompletableFuture"]
    E --> J["Concurrent Collections and BlockingQueue"]
    G --> J
    I --> K["Practice: coding drill and Phase 9 review"]
    J --> K
```

**Prerequisites:** Phase 2 (objects, interfaces, `final`), Phase 7 (lambdas, because every task is a lambda), and Phase 8 ([[ConcurrentHashMap Internals]] previews CAS and per-bin locking). Phase 16 builds on this phase with explicit locks, synchronizers, virtual threads and advanced `CompletableFuture` composition; Phase 15 covers the formal Java Memory Model.

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. What is a race condition, and how do `synchronized` and atomic classes fix it?
2. What does `volatile` guarantee, and why is `count++` on a volatile field still unsafe?
3. What is a deadlock, and how do you prevent one?
4. How does a `ThreadPoolExecutor` decide whether to run, queue or reject a task?
5. `Future` vs `CompletableFuture`: how do you call several services in parallel and combine the results?

# Threads

**Shared analogy: a restaurant kitchen.** The restaurant is a *process*: it has its own building, pantry and money (memory, file handles). The cooks are *threads*: they share the same pantry and the same kitchen, which is why they can cooperate quickly and also why they bump into each other. A cook is hired (NEW), starts working (RUNNABLE), waits for the only oven (BLOCKED), waits for a waiter to call them (WAITING), takes a timed break (TIMED_WAITING), and finally goes home (TERMINATED). An order ticket is a *task*: a `Runnable` ticket just says "do this", while a `Callable` ticket says "do this and bring me back the result, or tell me what went wrong".

# Shared state

**Shared analogy: one whiteboard in a busy office.** Everyone can read and write the same whiteboard (the heap). If two people update the same number at once, one update is lost (a race condition), so the office uses a marker that only one person may hold at a time (`synchronized`). Some people copy the board into their notebook and keep reading the stale copy (visibility), unless the board has a "always look at the real board" sign (`volatile`). People can wait by the board until someone rings a bell (`wait` and `notify`), two people each holding one marker and waiting for the other's can freeze forever (deadlock), and some numbers can be changed with a single tamper-proof stroke that never needs the marker at all (atomic classes and CAS).

Every topic in this group answers the same question: when two threads touch the same data, how do we keep it correct?

# Executors

**Shared analogy: a delivery company.** You do not hire a new driver for every parcel; you keep a fleet of drivers (a thread pool) and a sorting area where parcels wait (the work queue). When you hand over a parcel you get a tracking number (a `Future`); a smarter tracking number can also say "when this arrives, send the invoice, and if it fails, refund" (`CompletableFuture`). The sorting area itself must be safe for many drivers and clerks to use at once, with shelves that make a clerk wait when they are full and a driver wait when they are empty (concurrent collections and `BlockingQueue`).

This group is what you actually use in Spring Boot code: `@Async` runs on an executor, `RestClient` calls are fanned out with `CompletableFuture`, and Kafka consumers and schedulers are built on queues and pools.

name: Practice — Phase 9 review: Concurrency Fundamentals
description: Cheat sheet, key snippets, top 10 questions and rapid-fire flashcards for Phase 9
content:
# Phase 9 review: Concurrency Fundamentals

## Cheat sheet

| Idea | Remember |
|---|---|
| Process vs thread | Own memory vs shared heap with own stack and program counter |
| Thread states | NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED |
| start vs run | `start` makes a new thread; `run` is a plain call; start only once |
| Interruption | Cooperative; blocking calls throw `InterruptedException`; restore the flag if you cannot rethrow |
| Runnable vs Callable | `void run()` vs `V call() throws Exception` |
| submit vs execute | Exception stored in the `Future` vs uncaught handler kills the worker |
| Race condition | Read-modify-write (`count++`) or check-then-act |
| synchronized | Mutual exclusion plus visibility; instance method locks `this`, static locks the `Class`; reentrant |
| Lock object | `private final Object lock`; never string literals or boxed values |
| volatile | Visibility and ordering, not atomicity; flags, publication, DCL |
| wait and notify | Hold the monitor, `while` loop, prefer `notifyAll`; `wait` releases the lock, `sleep` does not |
| Deadlock | Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait; fix with lock ordering or `tryLock` timeouts |
| Livelock vs starvation | Busy but no progress vs some thread never gets a turn |
| CAS | Set only if still equal to expected; retry loop; lock-free |
| Atomics | `incrementAndGet`, `compareAndSet`, `updateAndGet` (pure function), `LongAdder` for hot counters |
| ABA | Value returns to the old one; `AtomicStampedReference` |
| Pool admission | Core threads, then queue, then max threads, then reject |
| Executors traps | Fixed and single have unbounded queues; cached has unbounded threads |
| Pool sizing | CPU: cores; I/O: cores x (1 + wait / compute) |
| Shutdown | `shutdown`, `awaitTermination`, `shutdownNow`; `close()` in Java 19+ |
| CompletableFuture | `thenApply` (map), `thenCompose` (flatMap), `thenCombine`, `allOf`, `exceptionally`, `handle` |
| Common pool | Default for `supplyAsync`; pass your own executor for I/O |
| Timeouts | `orTimeout`, `completeOnTimeout` (Java 9); they do not stop the task |
| BlockingQueue | `put` and `take` block; `offer` and `poll` return; bound it for back-pressure |
| CopyOnWriteArrayList | Snapshot iteration, O(n) writes; read-mostly lists |

### Key code snippets
```java
// Race fixed three ways
synchronized void increment() { count++; }                    // lock
private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();     // CAS
count.incrementAndGet();
map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);                              // atomic map update
```

```java
// Guarded block with wait and notifyAll
synchronized (lock) {
    while (!condition) lock.wait();
    // act
}
synchronized (lock) { changeState(); lock.notifyAll(); }
```

```java
// Lock ordering against deadlock
Account first = a.id() < b.id() ? a : b;
Account second = first == a ? b : a;
synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { /* transfer */ } }
```

```java
// A production-style thread pool
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),
        r -> new Thread(r, "orderhub-worker"),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
```

```java
// Parallel calls with fallback and timeout
CompletableFuture<Integer> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(id), io)
        .exceptionally(ex -> cataloguePrice)
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
CompletableFuture<Integer> stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventory.get(id), io);
ProductPage page = price.thenCombine(stock, ProductPage::new).join();
```

```java
// Producer-consumer with a bounded queue and poison pill
BlockingQueue<Job> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);
queue.put(job);                 // producer blocks when full
Job next = queue.take();        // consumer blocks when empty
if (next == POISON) return;
```

## The 10 most likely interview questions

1. **Process vs thread?** A process has its own memory; threads share the process heap but have their own stacks, so they communicate cheaply and need synchronization.
2. **What is a race condition and how do you fix it?** Timing-dependent results from unsynchronized shared state; fix with `synchronized`, atomics, atomic collection methods or immutability.
3. **What does `volatile` guarantee?** Visibility and ordering of one variable, not atomicity; `count++` on a volatile still races.
4. **`synchronized` vs `volatile` vs atomics?** Mutual exclusion plus visibility vs visibility only vs lock-free single-variable atomic updates.
5. **What is a deadlock and how do you prevent it?** Threads waiting on each other's locks in a cycle; consistent lock ordering, `tryLock` with timeouts, fewer nested locks.
6. **`wait` vs `sleep`?** `wait` needs and releases the monitor and waits for a notify; `sleep` keeps locks and waits for time.
7. **Runnable vs Callable?** No result and no checked exceptions vs a result and checked exceptions via `Future.get`.
8. **How does `ThreadPoolExecutor` handle a new task?** Core thread, then queue, then extra thread up to max, then rejection policy.
9. **Future vs CompletableFuture?** Blocking `get` only vs non-blocking composition, combination, error handling and timeouts.
10. **What is a `BlockingQueue` used for?** Producer-consumer hand-off with back-pressure; it is the work queue inside thread pools.

## Rapid-fire flashcards

Q: Which thread state means waiting to enter a synchronized block?
A: BLOCKED.

Q: What exception does calling `start()` twice on the same Thread throw?
A: `IllegalThreadStateException`.

Q: What does a static synchronized method lock on?
A: The `Class` object of its class.

Q: Does `Thread.sleep()` release monitors the thread holds?
A: No.

Q: What does `future.get()` throw when the task threw an exception?
A: `ExecutionException`, with the original exception as its cause.

Q: Which atomic class detects the ABA problem?
A: `AtomicStampedReference`.

Q: What queue does `Executors.newFixedThreadPool` use?
A: An unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue`.

Q: Which rejection policy runs the task on the submitting thread?
A: `ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy`.

Q: What does `CompletableFuture.allOf` return?
A: A `CompletableFuture<Void>` that completes when all given futures complete.

Q: Which BlockingQueue has zero capacity?
A: `SynchronousQueue`.

# Phase 10: Spring Core in Depth (Intermediate)

In Phase 5 you used Spring Boot as a black box: annotate a class, and it "just works". This phase opens the box. You learn what the IoC container is, how it turns classes into bean definitions and then into objects, how dependencies are wired, how scopes and lifecycle callbacks work, and how Boot decides which beans exist at all (profiles, properties and conditions). Finally you see the container's built-in event bus.

Interviewers care because every Spring question above junior level rests on this: "Why does `@Transactional` not work on a private method?", "Why is my prototype bean behaving like a singleton?", "How does auto-configuration back off when I define my own bean?" You cannot answer those without a clear picture of the container.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["IoC and DI"] --> B["ApplicationContext and Bean Definitions"]
    B --> C["Constructor vs Setter vs Field Injection"]
    C --> D["@Qualifier, @Primary"]
    B --> E["Stereotype Annotations"]
    B --> F["@Configuration and @Bean"]
    F --> G["Bean Scopes"]
    G --> H["Bean Lifecycle Callbacks"]
    B --> I["Profiles"]
    I --> J["@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties"]
    J --> K["Conditional Beans"]
    B --> L["Application Events"]
```

**Prerequisites:** Phase 2 (interfaces, polymorphism), Phase 5 (your first Spring Boot app and the OrderHub product CRUD), Phase 9 helps for thread-safety of singletons.

**OrderHub in this phase:** the Phase 5 project has `com.orderhub.product` with `Product`, `ProductController`, `ProductService` and an in-memory `ProductRepository`. In Phase 10 you refactor it to constructor injection everywhere, introduce a `PaymentGateway` interface with two implementations, move settings into a typed `OrderHubProperties` class, add `dev` and `prod` profiles, a conditional notification sender, and an `OrderPlacedEvent`.

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. What are IoC and dependency injection, and why does Spring use them?
2. Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
3. What bean scopes exist, and what happens when you inject a prototype bean into a singleton?
4. Describe the Spring bean lifecycle from definition to destruction.
5. What is the difference between `@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties`?

# Phase 11: Building REST APIs (Intermediate)

Phase 5 gave OrderHub a working CRUD API. This phase makes it an API you could put in front of real clients: correct HTTP semantics and status codes, idempotent operations, precise request mapping, meaningful headers, validated input, one consistent error format (RFC 9457 `ProblemDetail`), pagination and sorting, a versioning strategy, generated OpenAPI documentation, file upload and download, CORS for the browser frontend, and finally calling other services with `RestClient` and HTTP interfaces.

Interviewers love this phase because almost every backend job is "build and maintain REST APIs". Expect questions such as "PUT vs PATCH?", "Which status code for a validation error?", "How do you handle exceptions globally?", "What is idempotency and how would you make POST idempotent?" and "Why does my browser get a CORS error when Postman works?".

# REST design

**Shared analogy: a well-run library.** Every book has a permanent shelf address (a resource URI). You do a small set of standard things with any book: look at it (GET), add a new one to the catalogue (POST), replace its catalogue card (PUT), correct one detail on the card (PATCH), withdraw it (DELETE). The librarian answers with standard slips: "here it is" (200), "added, it is on shelf 12" (201 with `Location`), "no such book" (404), "your form is filled in wrong" (400). Looking at a book never changes it (safe), and asking twice to withdraw the same book has the same result as asking once (idempotent).

- **REST Principles, HTTP Methods and Status Codes:** the shelf addresses, the standard actions and the standard answer slips.
- **Idempotency and Safe Methods:** which actions are harmless to repeat, and how to make "add a book" safe to retry.

# CORS

**Level: Intermediate | Phase 11 | Priority: MUST | Since: CORS W3C recommendation 2014 (now in the WHATWG Fetch standard); @CrossOrigin Spring 4.2; CorsConfigurationSource in Spring Security 4.x**

> **30-second interview answer:** Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: JavaScript from `https://shop.orderhub.example` may not read responses from `https://api.orderhub.example` unless the API allows it with CORS headers. For non-simple requests (JSON bodies, `Authorization` headers, PUT or DELETE) the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` preflight; the server answers with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods`, `-Headers` and optionally `-Allow-Credentials` and `-Max-Age`. In Spring I configure it globally via `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings` or a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean, and with Spring Security I enable `http.cors()` so preflights are not rejected by the security filter. CORS is a browser protection, not server security: Postman and curl ignore it.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
A members-only club with a guest list.

| Club | CORS |
|---|---|
| The club only serves its own members by default | Same-origin policy |
| A visitor from another club arrives | A request from another origin (scheme, host, port) |
| The bouncer phones ahead: "Can a guest from Club Shop come in with a bag?" | Preflight `OPTIONS` request with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `-Headers` |
| The club answers: "Yes, guests from Club Shop, with bags, for the next hour" | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Allow-Headers`, `-Max-Age` |
| The bouncer works for the visitor's safety, not the club's | The browser enforces CORS to protect the user |
| Someone who climbs in through the kitchen ignores the bouncer | curl, Postman and servers are not restricted by CORS |

### What it is
- **Origin:** scheme plus host plus port. `http://localhost:5173` and `http://localhost:8080` are different origins; so are `http` and `https`.
- **Same-origin policy:** browsers block JavaScript from *reading* cross-origin responses (the request may still reach the server).
- **Simple request:** GET, HEAD or POST with only safelisted headers and a `Content-Type` of `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. Sent directly; the browser checks `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the response.
- **Preflighted request:** anything else (JSON `Content-Type`, `Authorization` header, PUT, PATCH, DELETE). The browser first sends `OPTIONS` with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`.
- **Response headers:**
  - `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`: the allowed origin (or `*`).
  - `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`: for preflights.
  - `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`: allows cookies or HTTP auth; then the origin cannot be `*`.
  - `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`: response headers JavaScript may read beyond the safelisted ones (`Location`, `X-Total-Count`, `ETag`).
  - `Access-Control-Max-Age`: how long the browser caches the preflight result.
- **Spring options:** `@CrossOrigin` on a controller or method, global `addCorsMappings` in `WebMvcConfigurer`, a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean (used by Spring Security and `CorsFilter`), or the gateway.

### Why it exists
Without the same-origin policy, any website you visit could use your logged-in cookies to read your bank or email data through JavaScript. CORS is the controlled exception: the API declares which other origins may read its responses, so legitimate frontends on other domains (or `localhost:5173` during development) can work.

## 2. How It Works
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant JS as "Browser JS on http://localhost:5173"
    participant B as "Browser"
    participant S as "OrderHub API http://localhost:8080"
    JS->>B: fetch PUT /api/v1/products/7, JSON body, Authorization header
    B->>S: OPTIONS /api/v1/products/7 (Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT, -Request-Headers: authorization,content-type)
    S-->>B: 200, Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173, Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,DELETE, Allow-Headers: authorization,content-type, Max-Age: 3600
    B->>S: PUT /api/v1/products/7 (Origin header included)
    S-->>B: 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173, body
    B-->>JS: response readable
    Note over B: Missing or wrong Allow-Origin: request may have run on the server, but JS gets a CORS error
```

Inside Spring:
- Spring MVC: `AbstractHandlerMapping` checks the CORS configuration for the matched handler. For a preflight it answers directly without calling your controller; for actual requests `DefaultCorsProcessor` adds headers or rejects with 403 "Invalid CORS request".
- Spring Security: its filter chain runs **before** MVC. A preflight carries no credentials, so without `http.cors(...)` security returns 401 and the browser reports a CORS error. `http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())` adds a `CorsFilter` early in the chain that uses your `CorsConfigurationSource` bean (or falls back to the MVC configuration).
- `allowedOriginPatterns("https://*.orderhub.example")` supports wildcards and works with credentials, unlike `allowedOrigins("*")`.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
```yaml
# File: src/main/resources/application.yml
orderhub:
  cors:
    allowed-origins:
      - http://localhost:5173
      - https://shop.orderhub.example
```

```java
// File: src/main/java/com/orderhub/config/CorsProperties.java
package com.orderhub.config;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotEmpty;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "orderhub.cors")
public record CorsProperties(@NotEmpty List<String> allowedOrigins) { }

// File: src/main/java/com/orderhub/config/CorsConfig.java
package com.orderhub.config;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfiguration;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfigurationSource;
import org.springframework.web.cors.UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class CorsConfig {

    // One source of truth, used by Spring Security's CorsFilter (and by MVC if no security)
    @Bean
    CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource(CorsProperties props) {
        CorsConfiguration api = new CorsConfiguration();
        api.setAllowedOrigins(props.allowedOrigins());                    // exact origins, no "*"
        api.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
        api.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type", "Idempotency-Key", "If-Match"));
        api.setExposedHeaders(List.of("Location", "ETag", "X-Total-Count"));   // readable by JS
        api.setAllowCredentials(true);                                    // cookies or auth allowed
        api.setMaxAge(Duration.ofHours(1));                              // cache preflight

        UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
        source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", api);
        return source;
    }
}

// File: src/main/java/com/orderhub/config/SecurityConfig.java  (minimal until Phase 14)
package com.orderhub.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())                 // uses the CorsConfigurationSource bean
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                    // stateless JSON API (Phase 14 explains)
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().permitAll());
        return http.build();
    }
}
```

Without Spring Security, the MVC-only equivalent:

```java
// File: src/main/java/com/orderhub/config/WebCorsConfig.java  (alternative when Spring Security is absent)
package com.orderhub.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.CorsRegistry;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;

@Configuration
public class WebCorsConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins("http://localhost:5173")
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE")
                .allowedHeaders("Authorization", "Content-Type")
                .exposedHeaders("Location", "ETag")
                .maxAge(3600);
    }
}
```

### Walkthrough
- Allowed origins come from typed configuration, so dev, staging and prod each list their own frontends without code changes.
- The `CorsConfiguration` allows specific methods and headers, including the custom `Idempotency-Key` and `If-Match` headers from earlier topics. Forgetting a custom header in `allowedHeaders` makes every preflight fail.
- `exposedHeaders` lets the frontend read `Location`, `ETag` and `X-Total-Count`.
- `allowCredentials(true)` permits cookies; it requires explicit origins (or `allowedOriginPatterns`), never `*`.
- `maxAge` lets browsers cache the preflight for an hour, halving request count for frequent writes.
- In the security configuration, `http.cors(...)` places a `CorsFilter` before authentication so preflights get CORS headers instead of 401.
- `WebCorsConfig` is the simpler alternative for apps without Spring Security; do not configure CORS in two places with different rules.

### Output
Preflight from the dev frontend:
```http
OPTIONS /api/v1/products/7 HTTP/1.1
Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type
```
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Vary: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, Access-Control-Request-Headers
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE,OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 3600
```
Preflight from an unknown site:
```http
OPTIONS /api/v1/products/7 HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://evil.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: DELETE
```
```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

Invalid CORS request
```
Browser console for a fetch from an origin that is not allowed:
```text
Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/7' from origin 'https://evil.example' has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
```

### Compare
| Where to configure | Scope | Works with Spring Security | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@CrossOrigin` on controller or method | Local | Yes, if `http.cors()` enabled | Scattered, easy to forget |
| `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings` | Global MVC | Partly (security may block preflight first) | Fine without Security |
| `CorsConfigurationSource` bean + `http.cors()` | Global, before security | Yes | Recommended with Security |
| API gateway or reverse proxy | Edge | Independent | Good for many services; avoid duplicating headers |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **What is CORS?**
   Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser mechanism that relaxes the same-origin policy: the server uses `Access-Control-*` headers to tell the browser which other origins may read its responses, with which methods and headers.
2. **What is an origin?**
   The combination of scheme, host and port. `https://shop.example` and `https://api.example` are different origins, and so are `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8080`.
3. **What is a preflight request?**
   An automatic `OPTIONS` request the browser sends before a non-simple request (JSON content type, custom or `Authorization` headers, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to ask the server whether the actual request is allowed.

**Follow-up**
4. **Why does my API work in Postman but not from the browser?**
   CORS is enforced only by browsers. Postman, curl and server-to-server calls do not check `Access-Control-*` headers. Configure CORS on the server for the frontend's origin.
5. **Why can you not combine `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials?**
   The specification forbids it, because it would let any site make authenticated requests with the user's cookies and read the results. With credentials you must echo a specific allowed origin. Spring's `allowedOriginPatterns` lets you use wildcard patterns safely by echoing the matching origin.
6. **How do you configure CORS when using Spring Security?**
   Define a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean and call `http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())`. This puts a `CorsFilter` before the authentication filters, so preflights (which carry no credentials) are answered instead of rejected with 401.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **Is CORS a security feature that protects your API?**
   No. It protects users' browsers from malicious sites reading data with their credentials. Attackers can call your API directly with any tool. You still need authentication, authorisation, CSRF protection for cookie-based auth and rate limiting.
8. **The frontend gets a CORS error only on error responses (500), not on success. Why?**
   The error response is produced by a path that does not add CORS headers, for example the servlet container's error page or a filter that fails before the `CorsFilter` runs. Without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, the browser hides the response and reports CORS. Make sure CORS headers are added early (a filter at high precedence) so every response has them.
9. **Requests work but JavaScript reads `null` for the `Location` header. Why?**
   Only CORS-safelisted response headers are exposed to JavaScript. Add `Location` (and `ETag`, `X-Total-Count`) to `exposedHeaders`.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you understand that CORS is browser-enforced, how preflight works, and how it interacts with Spring Security.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `allowedOrigins("*")` with `allowCredentials(true)` | Startup error or rejected by browsers | Explicit origins or `allowedOriginPatterns` |
| CORS configured in MVC only, with Spring Security | Preflights get 401 | `http.cors()` with a `CorsConfigurationSource` |
| Custom header missing from `allowedHeaders` | Every preflight fails | List all headers clients send |
| Not exposing `Location` or pagination headers | Frontend cannot read them | `exposedHeaders` |
| Treating CORS as API security | Direct calls bypass it | Real authentication and authorisation |
| Configuring CORS in both gateway and service | Duplicate headers, browser rejects | One place only |

### Best practices
- Keep allowed origins in configuration per environment; never `*` for authenticated APIs.
- Configure CORS once (service or gateway), globally, in a filter that runs before security.
- Set `maxAge` to reduce preflight traffic.
- In development, a frontend dev-server proxy (Vite `server.proxy`) avoids CORS entirely by making calls same-origin.

### Compare with
| Mechanism | Protects | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| Same-origin policy and CORS | Users' data from other websites' JavaScript | Browser |
| CSRF protection | Users from forged state-changing requests using cookies | Server (tokens, SameSite cookies) |
| Authentication and authorisation | API resources from unauthorised callers | Server |
| Content Security Policy | Pages from injected scripts | Browser, configured by server |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
**OrderHub task.** Make the OrderHub API usable from the Vue frontend:
1. Add `CorsProperties` with per-profile origins: `dev` allows `http://localhost:5173`; `prod` allows `https://shop.orderhub.example` and `https://admin.orderhub.example`.
2. Register a `CorsConfigurationSource` for `/api/**` with the methods and headers OrderHub uses (`Authorization`, `Content-Type`, `Idempotency-Key`, `If-Match`), exposing `Location`, `ETag` and `X-Total-Count`, credentials enabled, max age one hour.
3. Enable `http.cors()` in the security chain.
4. Write a `MockMvc` test that sends a preflight from the dev origin and asserts the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, and one from `https://evil.example` that expects 403.

Acceptance criteria: both tests pass; no `@CrossOrigin` annotations remain.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```yaml
# File: src/main/resources/application-dev.yml
orderhub:
  cors:
    allowed-origins:
      - http://localhost:5173
```

```yaml
# File: src/main/resources/application-prod.yml
orderhub:
  cors:
    allowed-origins:
      - https://shop.orderhub.example
      - https://admin.orderhub.example
```

```java
// File: src/test/java/com/orderhub/config/CorsTest.java
package com.orderhub.config;

import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.options;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.*;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.context.ActiveProfiles;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@ActiveProfiles("dev")
class CorsTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @Test
    void preflightFromFrontendIsAllowed() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(options("/api/v1/products/1")
                        .header("Origin", "http://localhost:5173")
                        .header("Access-Control-Request-Method", "PUT")
                        .header("Access-Control-Request-Headers", "authorization,content-type,if-match"))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(header().string("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "http://localhost:5173"))
                .andExpect(header().string("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true"))
                .andExpect(header().string("Access-Control-Max-Age", "3600"));
    }

    @Test
    void preflightFromUnknownOriginIsRejected() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(options("/api/v1/products/1")
                        .header("Origin", "https://evil.example")
                        .header("Access-Control-Request-Method", "DELETE"))
                .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }
}
```
`CorsConfig` and `SecurityConfig` are exactly as in the Code section; the configuration source reads `CorsProperties`, so each profile gets its own origins. With `prod` active the localhost origin would get 403.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What makes two URLs different origins for CORS?
A: A different scheme, host or port.

Q: When does a browser send a CORS preflight request?
A: For non-simple requests, such as JSON bodies, custom or `Authorization` headers, or methods like PUT, PATCH and DELETE.

Q: Why does an API work in Postman but fail with a CORS error in the browser?
A: CORS is enforced only by browsers; Postman ignores it, so the server must send the right `Access-Control-*` headers for the frontend origin.

Q: How do you enable CORS correctly when Spring Security is used?
A: Provide a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean and call `http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())` so a `CorsFilter` runs before authentication.

Q: Which CORS header lets browser JavaScript read a custom response header like `Location`?
A: `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`.

**Related:** [[ResponseEntity and Headers]] · [[@RestController and Request Mapping Deep Dive]] · [[Security Filter Chain Architecture]]

content:
# Calling other APIs

**Shared analogy: ordering from suppliers.** So far OrderHub has been the shop counter that answers customers. Now it also has to phone suppliers: ask the inventory service whether stock exists, ask the payment provider to charge a card. You can dial by hand and read out every detail (`RestClient` with a fluent builder), use a switchboard that handles many calls at once without waiting on hold (`WebClient`, reactive), or keep a speed-dial card where each button is already set up for one supplier request (HTTP interfaces with `@HttpExchange`). In every case you must decide how long to wait on hold (timeouts) and what to do when the supplier does not answer (error handling, retries).

- **RestClient, WebClient and HTTP Interfaces:** the three ways to call out, and how to make the calls robust.

# Phase 12: Data Access with Spring Data JPA (Intermediate)

Almost every Spring Boot backend talks to a relational database, and almost every Spring interview spends 10 to 20 minutes on it. This phase takes OrderHub from in-memory maps to **PostgreSQL**: first with plain JDBC so you see what the frameworks hide, then with JPA and Hibernate, relationships between products, customers, orders and order lines, Spring Data repositories, transactions, isolation, locking, schema migrations with Flyway, and auditing.

Interviewers love this area because it separates people who "used JPA" from people who understand it. The classic questions are traps: the N+1 problem, `LazyInitializationException`, `@Transactional` that silently does nothing, the owning side of a relationship, lost updates under concurrency. Every one of them is explained here with the SQL that Hibernate actually logs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["JDBC, JdbcTemplate, JdbcClient"] --> B["JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA"]
    B --> C["Entity Mapping"]
    C --> D["Relationships"]
    D --> E["Owning side, cascade, orphanRemoval"]
    D --> F["Fetch types and N+1"]
    C --> G["Repositories and derived queries"]
    G --> H["@Query, JPQL, native"]
    G --> I["Projections and DTO queries"]
    F --> H
    B --> J["Persistence context and entity states"]
    J --> K["@Transactional and propagation"]
    K --> L["Isolation levels"]
    L --> M["Optimistic vs pessimistic locking"]
    C --> N["Flyway migrations"]
    C --> O["Auditing"]
```

**What OrderHub gains in this phase**

| Piece | What you build |
|---|---|
| Database | PostgreSQL 17 in Docker (from the orientation `docker-compose.yml`) |
| Schema | Flyway migrations `V1__init.sql`, `V2__customer.sql` and onwards instead of `ddl-auto` |
| Entities | `Product`, `Category`, `Customer`, `CustomerProfile`, `Order`, `OrderLine`, `Payment` |
| Repositories | `ProductRepository`, `OrderRepository`, `CustomerRepository` with derived queries, JPQL, projections |
| Services | `OrderService.placeOrder` in one transaction, stock decrement with locking |
| Cross-cutting | Optimistic locking with `@Version`, auditing of `createdAt` and `updatedAt` |

**Prerequisites:** Phase 5 (layered architecture, DTOs), Phase 10 (beans, DI, configuration properties), Phase 11 (REST controllers, validation, pagination). Basic SQL: `SELECT`, `JOIN`, `WHERE`, indexes and foreign keys.

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?
2. What is the difference between JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA?
3. How does `@Transactional` work, and when does it not work (self-invocation, private methods, checked exceptions)?
4. Explain propagation `REQUIRED` vs `REQUIRES_NEW` and the isolation levels with their read phenomena.
5. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: how do you prevent two users from overselling the last item in stock?

content:
# Foundations

**Shared analogy: sending letters abroad.** Raw JDBC is writing the letter yourself in the foreign language, buying the stamp and walking to the post office. `JdbcTemplate` and `JdbcClient` are a post office clerk: you still write the letter (the SQL), but the clerk handles envelopes, stamps and returns (connections, statements, exceptions). JPA is the international postal standard, Hibernate is the postal company that implements it, and Spring Data JPA is the concierge who sends standard letters for you when you only say "find the order with this id". Entity mapping is the address format that tells the system which table and column each field goes to.

content:
# Relationships

**Shared analogy: a family tree in a city records office.** Each person has one birth certificate (one-to-one), a mother can have many children while each child has one mother (one-to-many and many-to-one), and people join many clubs while clubs have many members (many-to-many, recorded in a membership register). Only one document is the legal record of each link: the child's birth certificate names the mother, not the other way round. That legal record is the **owning side**. Cascade is "when you register the family, register the children too", orphan removal is "a child removed from the family file is removed from the register", and fetch type is whether the clerk brings the whole family file or just the person's card until you ask for more.

# Repositories

**Shared analogy: a library help desk.** The repository is the help desk: you never walk into the stacks yourself. For common requests you just say the request in a standard phrase ("books by author Rowling, sorted by title") and the librarian understands it from the wording alone (derived queries). For unusual requests you hand over a written request slip in the library's own catalogue language (JPQL with `@Query`) or, if you know the shelf layout, in raw shelf codes (native SQL). And if you only need the titles and not the whole books, the librarian photocopies just that page (projections), which is lighter to carry.

# Transactions and state

**Shared analogy: a bank's teller counter.** A transaction is one visit to the counter: either every slip you hand over is processed or none is (atomicity). Propagation is what happens when a second clerk is called in during your visit: does she work on the same visit or open her own? Isolation is how much you can see of other customers' half-finished visits. The persistence context is the teller's working tray: everything you touched during the visit lies there and is written to the ledger when the visit ends. Locking decides what happens when two tellers try to change the same account at once, Flyway is the numbered list of renovations done to the bank building, and auditing is the stamp on every form saying who changed it and when.
