# Schema Migrations with Flyway

**Level: Intermediate | Phase 12 | Priority: MUST | Since: Flyway 1.0 (2010), Boot auto-configuration since Boot 1.x; Boot 3.5 ships Flyway 11**

> **30-second interview answer:** Flyway manages the database schema as numbered SQL scripts in `db/migration`, like `V1__init.sql` and `V2__add_payment.sql`. At startup it compares the scripts with its `flyway_schema_history` table, applies the pending ones in order inside transactions, and records each with a checksum, so every environment ends up with the same schema. Applied migrations are never edited; every change is a new version. I set Hibernate to `ddl-auto: validate` so Hibernate only checks the schema Flyway created.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
A building's renovation logbook.

| Building | Flyway |
|---|---|
| Numbered renovation work orders: 1 foundation, 2 walls, 3 add a balcony | Versioned migrations `V1__`, `V2__`, `V3__` |
| The logbook at the reception listing what was done and when | `flyway_schema_history` table |
| A new building copy follows all work orders in order | A new database gets every migration from V1 |
| You never rewrite an old work order; you file a new one | Never edit applied migrations; add a new version |
| The inspector checks the log matches the papers | Checksum validation at startup |
| Repainting every year, not numbered | Repeatable migrations `R__` re-run when changed |

### What it is
- **Migration:** a script that changes the schema or data. Versioned (`V<version>__<description>.sql`) or repeatable (`R__<description>.sql`, re-applied when its checksum changes, applied after versioned ones; good for views and functions).
- **Naming:** prefix `V`, version (`1`, `1.1`, `20261124.1`), two underscores, description with underscores. Default location `classpath:db/migration`.
- **`flyway_schema_history`:** table with version, description, script, checksum, installed_on, execution time, success.
- **Validate:** at startup Flyway checks that applied scripts still have the same checksum; editing an applied script fails validation.
- **Baseline:** start using Flyway on an existing database (`spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate=true`, `baseline-version`).
- **Java migrations:** classes extending `BaseJavaMigration` for complex data changes.
- **Boot integration:** with `flyway-core` (and for PostgreSQL `flyway-database-postgresql`, required since Flyway 10) on the classpath, `FlywayAutoConfiguration` runs migrations before the `EntityManagerFactory` is created.
- **Liquibase:** the main alternative, with changelogs in XML, YAML or SQL and rollback support.

### Why it exists
`ddl-auto: update` cannot rename columns, never drops anything, cannot migrate data, is not reviewed and differs between environments. Hand-run scripts get forgotten. Flyway makes schema changes code: reviewed in pull requests, versioned in Git, applied automatically and identically everywhere.

## 2. How It Works
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as "Spring Boot startup"
    participant F as "Flyway"
    participant DB as "PostgreSQL"
    participant H as "Hibernate (ddl-auto: validate)"
    B->>F: "FlywayAutoConfiguration: migrate() before EntityManagerFactory"
    F->>DB: "create flyway_schema_history if missing, take advisory lock"
    F->>DB: "read applied versions and checksums"
    F->>F: "scan classpath:db/migration, validate checksums"
    loop "each pending version in order"
        F->>DB: "BEGIN; run script; insert history row; COMMIT"
    end
    F-->>B: "schema at latest version"
    B->>H: "build EntityManagerFactory"
    H->>DB: "validate entities against tables and columns"
```

State of the history table after OrderHub's migrations:
```text
installed_rank | version | description     | script                 | checksum    | success
---------------+---------+-----------------+------------------------+-------------+--------
1              | 1       | init            | V1__init.sql           | 1739812345  | t
2              | 2       | customer        | V2__customer.sql       | -88213001   | t
3              | 3       | relationships   | V3__relationships.sql  | 455120987   | t
4              | 4       | payment         | V4__payment.sql        | 90233411    | t
5              | 5       | stock check     | V5__stock_check.sql    | -12093344   | t
6              | 6       | locking         | V6__locking.sql        | 300119882   | t
```

Safe production changes (expand and contract), because during a rolling deployment old and new app versions run against the same schema:
```text
Rename column full_name -> display_name without downtime:
release 1: V7  add column display_name; backfill; app writes both, reads old
release 2: app reads display_name
release 3: V8  drop column full_name
```

PostgreSQL runs DDL inside transactions, so a failed migration rolls back cleanly. On MySQL, DDL auto-commits, so a failure halfway leaves a partial change and a failed history row that you must repair (`flyway repair`).

## 3. Code Example
### Code
`pom.xml`:
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>   <!-- required for PostgreSQL since Flyway 10 -->
</dependency>
```

`application.yml`:
```yaml
spring:
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    baseline-on-migrate: false        # true only when adopting Flyway on an existing database
    clean-disabled: true              # never allow "clean" (drop everything) by accident
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate              # Flyway owns the schema
```

Project layout:
```text
src/main/resources/db/migration/
  V1__init.sql
  V2__customer.sql
  V3__relationships.sql
  V4__payment.sql
  V5__stock_check.sql
  V6__locking.sql
  V7__order_number_index.sql
  R__order_summary_view.sql
```

`V7__order_number_index.sql` (a production-safe index build):
```sql
-- flyway:executeInTransaction=false is needed because CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction
create index concurrently if not exists idx_orders_status_created on orders (status, created_at);
```
With the matching script configuration file `V7__order_number_index.sql.conf`:
```properties
executeInTransaction=false
```

Repeatable view, re-applied whenever its content changes:
```sql
-- R__order_summary_view.sql
create or replace view order_summary as
select o.id, o.order_number, c.email, o.status, o.total, o.created_at
from orders o
join customer c on c.id = o.customer_id;
```

A Java migration for a data backfill that SQL alone makes awkward:
```java
package db.migration;

import org.flywaydb.core.api.migration.BaseJavaMigration;
import org.flywaydb.core.api.migration.Context;

import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.Statement;

// Class name follows the same convention: V8__Backfill_order_numbers
public class V8__Backfill_order_numbers extends BaseJavaMigration {
    @Override
    public void migrate(Context context) throws Exception {
        try (Statement select = context.getConnection().createStatement();
             ResultSet rs = select.executeQuery("select id from orders where order_number is null order by id");
             PreparedStatement update = context.getConnection()
                     .prepareStatement("update orders set order_number = ? where id = ?")) {
            while (rs.next()) {
                long id = rs.getLong(1);
                update.setString(1, String.format("OH-%06d", id));
                update.setLong(2, id);
                update.addBatch();
            }
            update.executeBatch();
        }
    }
}
```

Running Flyway outside the app (CI or ops) with the Maven plugin:
```bash
./mvnw flyway:info -Dflyway.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orderhub -Dflyway.user=orderhub -Dflyway.password=orderhub
./mvnw flyway:migrate -Dflyway.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orderhub -Dflyway.user=orderhub -Dflyway.password=orderhub
```

### Walkthrough
- `flyway-database-postgresql` is a separate module since Flyway 10; without it Boot fails with "Unsupported Database: PostgreSQL 17".
- `clean-disabled: true` protects against `flyway clean`, which drops every object in the schema.
- `ddl-auto: validate` lets Hibernate fail fast if an entity and the migrated schema disagree.
- `V7` builds an index with `concurrently` so writes are not blocked during the build; that statement cannot run inside a transaction, so the script's `.conf` file disables the transaction for this one migration.
- `R__order_summary_view.sql` is re-run whenever its checksum changes, which suits views and functions that are replaced as a whole.
- `V8__Backfill_order_numbers` is a Java migration found in the `db.migration` package; Flyway records it in the history like a SQL migration.

### Output
First startup against an empty database:
```text
INFO  o.f.c.i.license.VersionPrinter      : Flyway Community Edition 11.7.2 by Redgate
INFO  o.f.c.i.database.base.BaseDatabaseType : Database: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orderhub (PostgreSQL 17.2)
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbValidate : Successfully validated 9 migrations (execution time 00:00.031s)
INFO  o.f.c.i.s.JdbcTableSchemaHistory    : Creating Schema History table "public"."flyway_schema_history"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Current version of schema "public": << Empty Schema >>
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "1 - init"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "2 - customer"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "3 - relationships"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "4 - payment"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "5 - stock check"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "6 - locking"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "7 - order number index" [non-transactional]
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" to version "8 - Backfill order numbers"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Migrating schema "public" with repeatable migration "order summary view"
INFO  o.f.core.internal.command.DbMigrate : Successfully applied 9 migrations to schema "public", now at version v8 (execution time 00:00.412s)
```
Someone edits `V3__relationships.sql` after it was applied:
```text
org.flywaydb.core.api.exception.FlywayValidateException: Validate failed: Migrations have failed validation
Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 3
-> Applied to database : 455120987
-> Resolved locally    : -1290033412
Either revert the changes to the migration, or run repair to update the schema history.
```

### Compare
| | `ddl-auto: update` | Flyway | Liquibase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Format | Generated by Hibernate | Plain SQL (or Java) | XML, YAML, JSON or SQL changelogs |
| Reviewable | No | Yes | Yes |
| Renames, data migration | No | Yes | Yes |
| Rollback | No | Undo only in paid editions; write a new forward migration | Rollback blocks supported |
| History table | None | `flyway_schema_history` | `databasechangelog` |
| Production use | Never | Yes | Yes |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **What is Flyway and why use it?**
   A database migration tool that applies versioned SQL scripts in order and records them in a history table. It makes schema changes repeatable, reviewable and identical across environments, replacing `ddl-auto` and manual scripts.
2. **What is the naming convention for Flyway migrations?**
   `V<version>__<description>.sql` for versioned migrations, such as `V3__add_payment_table.sql`, with two underscores. `R__<description>.sql` for repeatable migrations, re-applied when their checksum changes. Undo migrations use `U` (paid editions).
3. **How does Spring Boot run Flyway?**
   When `flyway-core` is on the classpath and a `DataSource` exists, `FlywayAutoConfiguration` creates a `Flyway` bean and runs `migrate()` during startup, before JPA's `EntityManagerFactory` is initialised. Settings come from `spring.flyway.*`.

**Follow-up**
4. **What happens if you modify a migration that was already applied?**
   The checksum stored in `flyway_schema_history` no longer matches the file, so validation fails at startup and the app does not start. Revert the change and add a new migration; use `flyway repair` only to realign checksums when you deliberately accept the edit (for example a comment change in development).
5. **How do you introduce Flyway to an existing production database?**
   Export the current schema as `V1__baseline.sql` for new environments, and on existing databases baseline at version 1 (`baseline-on-migrate=true`, `baseline-version=1`), so Flyway marks V1 as applied without running it. Subsequent changes start at V2.
6. **What is the relationship between Flyway and `ddl-auto`?**
   Flyway creates and evolves the schema; Hibernate should only validate it with `ddl-auto: validate` (or `none`). Running both `update` and Flyway leads to drift: Hibernate makes changes that are not in any migration.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **You need to rename a column used by the running application without downtime. How?**
   Expand and contract: add the new column and backfill it, deploy code that writes both and reads the new one, then in a later release drop the old column. A single rename migration would break the old app instances still running during a rolling deployment.
8. **Two developers create a `V7__` migration (`V7__coupon.sql` and `V7__tags.sql`) on different branches. What happens and how do teams avoid it?**
   After merging, Flyway sees two migrations with version 7 and fails with "Found more than one migration with version 7". Teams use timestamps as versions (`V20261124_1015__add_tags.sql`), or a CI check, and enable `outOfOrder` carefully if migrations can be merged late.
9. **A migration adds an index on a 200 million row table and production writes stall during deployment. Why, and what do you do?**
   A plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes for the whole build. Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in a non-transactional migration, or run it separately ahead of the deployment. Also review migrations for long locks (adding a column with a volatile default, changing a column type) before release.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you treat schema changes as versioned code and know how to change a live database safely.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Editing an applied migration | Checksum mismatch, startup fails | Add a new migration |
| `ddl-auto: update` alongside Flyway | Schema drift | `ddl-auto: validate` |
| Missing `flyway-database-postgresql` with Flyway 10+ | "Unsupported Database" at startup | Add the database module |
| Destructive changes in one release | Old app instances break during rollout | Expand and contract |
| `CREATE INDEX` on huge tables inside a migration | Writes blocked | `CONCURRENTLY` in a non-transactional migration |
| Leaving `clean` enabled | One command wipes the schema | `spring.flyway.clean-disabled: true` |

### Best practices
- One logical change per migration, small and reviewed like code.
- Test migrations against real PostgreSQL in CI with Testcontainers (Phase 13).
- Use repeatable migrations for views and functions.
- Never put environment-specific data in versioned migrations; use separate locations per profile if needed.
- Check `flyway info` as part of deployment pipelines.

### Compare with
| Approach | Who changes the schema | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Manual DBA scripts | People | Forgotten or inconsistent steps |
| Hibernate `ddl-auto` | ORM at startup | Unreviewed, no data migration |
| Flyway | Versioned SQL in Git | Low, if migrations are reviewed |
| Liquibase | Versioned changelogs | Low; more abstraction and rollback support |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
OrderHub needs a `discount_code` on orders and a `coupon` table. Write the migrations for:
1. `coupon(id, code unique, percent between 1 and 90, valid_until)`.
2. `orders.coupon_id` foreign key (nullable), indexed.
3. A repeatable view `active_coupons` listing coupons still valid.
Then map `Coupon` and add `@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) Coupon coupon` to `Order`.

Acceptance criteria: app starts with `ddl-auto: validate`; history table shows the new versions; the view is re-applied when edited.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```sql
-- V9__coupon.sql
create sequence coupon_seq start with 1 increment by 50;
create table coupon (
    id          bigint primary key,
    code        varchar(30) not null unique,
    percent     integer not null check (percent between 1 and 90),
    valid_until timestamp with time zone not null
);

-- V10__order_coupon.sql
alter table orders add column coupon_id bigint references coupon(id);
create index idx_orders_coupon on orders(coupon_id);
```

```sql
-- R__active_coupons_view.sql
create or replace view active_coupons as
select id, code, percent, valid_until
from coupon
where valid_until > now();
```

```java
package com.orderhub.coupon;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.Instant;

@Entity
@Table(name = "coupon")
public class Coupon {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "coupon_gen")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "coupon_gen", sequenceName = "coupon_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 30)
    private String code;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private int percent;

    @Column(name = "valid_until", nullable = false)
    private Instant validUntil;

    protected Coupon() { }
    public Coupon(String code, int percent, Instant validUntil) {
        this.code = code; this.percent = percent; this.validUntil = validUntil;
    }
    public boolean isValidAt(Instant now) { return now.isBefore(validUntil); }
    public int getPercent() { return percent; }
}
```

```java
// inside Order
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "coupon_id")
private com.orderhub.coupon.Coupon coupon;
```
Starting the app logs "Migrating schema "public" to version "9 - coupon"" and "10 - order coupon", then the repeatable migration. Hibernate validation passes because the column types match the mapping (`integer` for `int`, `timestamp with time zone` for `Instant`).
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What is the Flyway naming convention for versioned and repeatable migrations?
A: `V<version>__<description>.sql` for versioned and `R__<description>.sql` for repeatable migrations.

Q: What does Flyway store in flyway_schema_history?
A: Each applied migration's version, description, script, checksum, install time, execution time and success flag.

Q: What happens when an applied Flyway migration is edited?
A: Checksum validation fails at startup; add a new migration instead (or `repair` deliberately).

Q: Which ddl-auto value should be used together with Flyway?
A: `validate` (or `none`), so Hibernate checks but never changes the schema.

Q: How do you rename a column with Flyway without downtime?
A: Expand and contract: add and backfill the new column, switch the code, then drop the old column in a later release.

**Related:** [[Entity Mapping]] · [[Testcontainers]] · [[Query Performance and Indexes]] · [[CI/CD Pipeline for a Spring App]]

content:
# Phase 13: Testing (Intermediate)

Every serious Java team expects you to write tests, and interviewers check it in two ways: they ask concept questions ("mock vs stub", "`@SpringBootTest` vs `@WebMvcTest`", "how do you test a repository?") and they ask you to write a test live, often for code they just had you write. This phase gives OrderHub a real test suite: fast unit tests for the domain and services with JUnit 5 and Mockito, slice tests for controllers (MockMvc) and repositories (`@DataJpaTest`), integration tests against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers, and the strategy that ties them together (test pyramid and TDD).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["JUnit 5 Essentials"] --> B["Mockito: mocks, stubs, verification"]
    A --> C["@SpringBootTest vs test slices"]
    C --> D["MockMvc for controllers (@WebMvcTest)"]
    C --> E["@DataJpaTest for repositories"]
    E --> F["Testcontainers: real PostgreSQL"]
    C --> F
    B --> G["Test pyramid and TDD"]
    D --> G
    F --> G
```

**What OrderHub gains in this phase**

| Layer | Test type | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| Domain (`Order`, `PriceCalculator`) | Plain unit tests | JUnit 5, AssertJ |
| Services (`OrderService`) | Unit tests with test doubles | Mockito |
| Controllers | Web slice tests | `@WebMvcTest`, MockMvc, `@MockitoBean` |
| Repositories | JPA slice tests on real PostgreSQL | `@DataJpaTest`, Testcontainers, Flyway |
| Whole app | A few end-to-end integration tests | `@SpringBootTest`, Testcontainers, `@ServiceConnection` |

**Prerequisites:** Phase 5 (layered architecture), Phase 10 (DI and beans: tests replace beans), Phase 11 (controllers, validation, `ProblemDetail`), Phase 12 (JPA, repositories, transactions, Flyway).

**Versions:** Spring Boot 3.5 ships JUnit Jupiter 5.12, Mockito 5, AssertJ 3.27 and Testcontainers 1.21 through `spring-boot-starter-test` and `spring-boot-testcontainers`. `@MockBean` is deprecated since Boot 3.4 in favour of Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean`; `Boot 4` removes `@MockBean`, moves test slice annotations into per-technology modules, and supports JUnit 6.

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. What is the difference between a mock, a stub and a spy, and when do you use `verify`?
2. `@SpringBootTest` vs `@WebMvcTest` vs `@DataJpaTest`: what does each load and when do you use it?
3. How do you test a REST controller, including validation errors?
4. How do you test a repository? Why is H2 not enough, and what is Testcontainers?
5. What is the test pyramid, and do you practise TDD?

content:
# Unit tests

**Shared analogy: a car-parts test bench.** Before a gearbox goes into a car, engineers clamp it to a bench, spin the input shaft and measure the output. They do not need the engine or the wheels; a motor and a sensor stand in for them. JUnit 5 is the bench with its clamps, gauges and test schedule. Mockito makes the stand-in parts: a fake engine that spins exactly as told (stub) and a sensor that records what the gearbox did (mock with verification). Unit tests are cheap, fast and precise, so you run thousands of them on every build.

# Spring tests

**Shared analogy: rehearsing a theatre play.** A full dress rehearsal on the main stage with lights, orchestra and costumes is `@SpringBootTest`: realistic but expensive, so you do it rarely. Most rehearsals are partial: the actors rehearse only Act 2 in a small room with a stand-in for the orchestra (a test slice such as `@WebMvcTest` with mocked services), or the lighting crew tests only the lights (`@DataJpaTest`). MockMvc is a pretend audience that reacts like a real one without opening the doors. Testcontainers brings in the real orchestra, in a portable box, whenever you need the real sound. The director reuses the same set between rehearsals if nothing changed: Spring's test context cache.

# Phase 14: Spring Security (Intermediate)

Spring Security is the framework that decides **who you are** (authentication) and **what you may do** (authorization) for every request that reaches a Spring application. It does this with a chain of servlet filters that run before your controllers. Almost every backend interview has at least one security question, because a developer who cannot explain how a request gets authenticated cannot be trusted with production APIs. Interviewers also use security to test whether you understand Spring internals: filters, proxies, `ThreadLocal` context and auto-configuration all show up here.

In this phase OrderHub gains real security: users with BCrypt passwords stored in PostgreSQL, a `/api/auth/login` endpoint that issues a signed JWT, stateless request authentication with Spring's OAuth2 resource server support, role-based URL rules (`CUSTOMER`, `ADMIN`), method security with `@PreAuthorize` (a customer can only read their own orders), CORS for the frontend and correct CSRF settings for a token-based API. Everything uses the **Spring Security 6 lambda DSL** with a `SecurityFilterChain` bean. `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` was deprecated in 5.7 and removed in 6.0; if an interviewer shows you code that extends it, say so.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Authentication vs Authorization"] --> B["Security Filter Chain Architecture"]
    B --> C["UserDetailsService and Password Encoding"]
    B --> D["SecurityFilterChain Configuration"]
    C --> E["JWT Stateless Authentication"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["OAuth2 and OpenID Connect"]
    D --> G["Method Security with @PreAuthorize"]
    D --> H["CSRF, CORS and Common Vulnerabilities"]
    E --> I["Practice: Secure OrderHub"]
    G --> I
    H --> I
```

**Prerequisites:** Phase 10 (beans, proxies, configuration classes), Phase 11 (REST controllers, global error handling), Phase 12 (JPA entities and repositories for the `users` table), Phase 13 (MockMvc tests, which you will extend with `spring-security-test`). From Phase 9, remember that a `ThreadLocal` is a per-thread variable: the security context lives in one.

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and between HTTP 401 and 403?
2. Walk me through what happens inside Spring Security when a request arrives (DelegatingFilterProxy, FilterChainProxy, filters, SecurityContextHolder).
3. How do you store passwords, and why BCrypt instead of SHA-256?
4. How does JWT authentication work, what is inside a token, and how do you log a user out or revoke a token?
5. Should you disable CSRF for a REST API, and how is CORS different from CSRF?

name: Architecture
description: Who you are, what you may do, and the filter machinery that decides it
content:
# Architecture

**Shared analogy: an office building with a security desk.** At the entrance there is a row of checkpoints (the filter chain). One guard checks your badge or ID card and writes your name on a visitor slip (authentication, the `SecurityContext`). The receptionist looks up who you are in the staff register and compares your signature (the `UserDetailsService` and `PasswordEncoder`). Further in, each floor has a sign saying who may enter (authorization rules in the `SecurityFilterChain` configuration). If you have no badge you are sent back to the front desk (401); if your badge is valid but you try the executive floor, you are turned away (403). This group covers the building plan: the difference between identity and permission, the checkpoints, the staff register, and how you write the rules.

# Security Filter Chain Architecture

**Level: Intermediate | Phase 14 | Priority: MUST | Since: Spring Security 3.1 (FilterChainProxy with multiple chains); SecurityContextHolderFilter and AuthorizationFilter Spring Security 5.7/6.0**

> **30-second interview answer:** Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters. The servlet container calls one filter, `DelegatingFilterProxy`, which hands the request to the Spring bean `FilterChainProxy`. That bean picks the first `SecurityFilterChain` whose matcher fits the request and runs its filters in a fixed order: load the security context, CORS, CSRF, logout, an authentication filter, anonymous, exception translation, and finally `AuthorizationFilter`. Only if all of them pass does the request reach the `DispatcherServlet` and your controller.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
An airport security lane.

| Airport security | Spring Security |
|---|---|
| The airport building has one entrance door for everyone | The servlet container's filter chain |
| A sign at the door: "security handled by the airport authority" | `DelegatingFilterProxy`, a container filter that delegates to a Spring bean |
| The airport authority's control room choosing a lane: crew lane or passenger lane | `FilterChainProxy` choosing a `SecurityFilterChain` by request matcher |
| The checkpoints in the lane, always in the same order: ID check, bag scan, body scanner, gate | Security filters in their fixed order |
| The ID officer stamps your card | An authentication filter populating the `SecurityContext` |
| The supervisor who decides "back to check-in" or "you are banned" | `ExceptionTranslationFilter` (401 or 403) |
| The final gate agent | `AuthorizationFilter` |
| The plane | `DispatcherServlet` and your controller |

### What it is
- **Servlet filter:** a `jakarta.servlet.Filter` that sees every request before the servlet and can stop it or pass it on with `chain.doFilter(request, response)`.
- **`DelegatingFilterProxy`:** a plain servlet filter registered with the container (Spring Boot registers it as `springSecurityFilterChain`). The container knows nothing about Spring beans, so this proxy looks up the bean lazily and delegates.
- **`FilterChainProxy`:** the Spring bean that holds a list of `SecurityFilterChain`s, picks one per request, runs its filters, and clears the security context afterwards. It is also the place to put a breakpoint when debugging.
- **`SecurityFilterChain`:** a request matcher plus an ordered list of filters. You declare it as a `@Bean` built with `HttpSecurity`.
- **`SecurityContextHolder`:** the static holder of the current `SecurityContext` (by default a `ThreadLocal`).
- **`SecurityContextRepository`:** where the context is saved between requests: `HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository` for session apps, nothing for stateless JWT apps.

### Why it exists
Security must run before any controller, apply uniformly to every URL (including static files and error pages), and stay out of business code. Servlet filters are the natural place. But filters registered with the container cannot use dependency injection, so Spring adds one proxy filter that bridges into the Spring world, where filters are beans that can use services, encoders and repositories. Multiple chains let one app treat `/api/**` (stateless, JWT) differently from `/admin/**` (form login, session) or `/actuator/**`.

## 2. How It Works
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["HTTP request"] --> T["Tomcat filter chain"]
    T --> DFP["DelegatingFilterProxy"]
    DFP --> FCP["FilterChainProxy (bean)"]
    FCP -->|"matches /api/**"| C1["SecurityFilterChain 1"]
    FCP -->|"matches everything else"| C2["SecurityFilterChain 2"]
    C1 --> DS["DispatcherServlet"]
    C2 --> DS
    DS --> CTRL["@RestController"]
```

The important filters of one chain, in order (Spring Security 6.x; you only see the ones you enable):

```text
 #  Filter                                  Job
 1  DisableEncodeUrlFilter                  stop session ids leaking into URLs
 2  WebAsyncManagerIntegrationFilter        carry the context into async MVC
 3  SecurityContextHolderFilter             load SecurityContext from the repository
 4  HeaderWriterFilter                      X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, HSTS, Cache-Control
 5  CorsFilter                              answer preflight, add CORS headers
 6  CsrfFilter                              reject state-changing requests without a valid token
 7  LogoutFilter                            handle POST /logout
 8  UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter    form login (POST /login)
 9  BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter         Authorization: Bearer <jwt> (resource server)
10  BasicAuthenticationFilter               Authorization: Basic
11  RequestCacheAwareFilter                 resume the saved request after login
12  SecurityContextHolderAwareRequestFilter request.isUserInRole(), getRemoteUser()
13  AnonymousAuthenticationFilter           put AnonymousAuthenticationToken if still empty
14  SessionManagementFilter / session stuff session fixation, concurrency control
15  ExceptionTranslationFilter              turn security exceptions into 401 or 403
16  AuthorizationFilter                     final access decision for the URL
```

What happens in memory and between threads:
1. Tomcat takes a worker thread from its pool and calls the filter chain.
2. `SecurityContextHolderFilter` asks the `SecurityContextRepository` for a context (from the HTTP session, or an empty one) and sets a deferred supplier in the `ThreadLocal`.
3. An authentication filter, if it recognizes credentials, calls the `AuthenticationManager` and on success creates a new `SecurityContext` containing the `Authentication`.
4. `ExceptionTranslationFilter` wraps the rest of the chain in a try/catch. When `AuthorizationFilter` throws `AccessDeniedException`, it catches it: anonymous user goes to the `AuthenticationEntryPoint`, otherwise to the `AccessDeniedHandler`.
5. After the response, `FilterChainProxy` clears the `ThreadLocal`. This is essential because the same Tomcat thread will serve another user next.

Since Spring Security 6, the context is **not** saved automatically to the session after authentication: authentication filters explicitly call `securityContextRepository.saveContext()`. That is why a custom login endpoint must save the context itself if you want a session, and why stateless JWT apps simply skip it.

Exception path:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant ETF as "ExceptionTranslationFilter"
    participant AZF as "AuthorizationFilter"
    participant EP as "AuthenticationEntryPoint"
    participant ADH as "AccessDeniedHandler"
    ETF->>AZF: "chain.doFilter()"
    AZF-->>ETF: "throws AccessDeniedException"
    alt "Authentication is anonymous"
        ETF->>EP: "commence() returns 401 or redirect to /login"
    else "Authentication is real"
        ETF->>ADH: "handle() returns 403"
    end
```

## 3. Code Example
### Code
Two chains in OrderHub (actuator health public with its own chain, API secured), a custom logging filter inserted in the right place, and a debug switch to print the chain.

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

/** Logs who made each request. Runs after authentication so the user is known. */
public class AuditLoggingFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(AuditLoggingFilter.class);

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
        String user = (auth == null) ? "none" : auth.getName();
        chain.doFilter(request, response);                       // let the rest of the chain run
        log.info("{} {} user={} status={}", request.getMethod(), request.getRequestURI(),
                 user, response.getStatus());
    }
}
```

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.security.web.access.intercept.AuthorizationFilter;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity(debug = false)      // true prints every request and the filter list (never in prod)
public class ChainsConfig {

    @Bean
    @Order(1)                                         // checked first
    SecurityFilterChain actuatorChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .securityMatcher("/actuator/**")             // this chain only handles /actuator/**
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**", "/actuator/info").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().hasRole("OPS"))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .build();
    }

    @Bean
    @Order(2)                                         // fallback chain: no securityMatcher = any request
    SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .addFilterBefore(new AuditLoggingFilter(), AuthorizationFilter.class)  // after auth, before access decision
            .build();
    }
}
```

```yaml
# application.yml: see the chain decisions in the log while learning
logging:
  level:
    org.springframework.security: TRACE
```

### Walkthrough
- `@Order(1)` with `securityMatcher("/actuator/**")` makes `FilterChainProxy` try the actuator chain first. Only one chain handles a request: the first whose matcher fits.
- The API chain has no `securityMatcher`, so it matches everything; it must have the highest order number. If you put a catch-all chain first, the second chain is never used (Spring Security 6 fails fast at startup when a chain matching any request is followed by another chain).
- `addFilterBefore(new AuditLoggingFilter(), AuthorizationFilter.class)` places the custom filter after authentication filters, so `auth.getName()` already has the user. Placing it before `SecurityContextHolderFilter` would always log `none`.
- The filter is created with `new`, not as a `@Component`. A `Filter` `@Component` is also auto-registered by Spring Boot in the **servlet container** chain, so it would run twice (once outside Spring Security, once inside). If you need it as a bean, add a `FilterRegistrationBean` with `setEnabled(false)`.
- `OncePerRequestFilter` guarantees one execution per request even with forwards and error dispatches.
- TRACE logging shows lines such as which chain was chosen and every filter invoked, the single best debugging tool for "why do I get 403?".

### Output
```text
GET /actuator/health   (no credentials)
-> 200 OK  {"status":"UP"}

GET /api/orders        (no credentials)
-> 401 Unauthorized

GET /api/orders        Authorization: Basic YWxpY2U6YWxpY2UtcGFzcw==
-> 200 OK
log: INFO  c.o.security.AuditLoggingFilter : GET /api/orders user=alice status=200

TRACE log excerpt for the authenticated request:
o.s.security.web.FilterChainProxy : Trying to match request against DefaultSecurityFilterChain [RequestMatcher=Or [Mvc [pattern='/actuator/**']], Filters=[...]] (1/2)
o.s.security.web.FilterChainProxy : Securing GET /api/orders
o.s.security.web.FilterChainProxy : Invoking SecurityContextHolderFilter (3/12)
o.s.security.web.FilterChainProxy : Invoking BasicAuthenticationFilter (6/12)
o.s.s.w.a.www.BasicAuthenticationFilter : Set SecurityContextHolder to UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken [Principal=org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User [Username=alice, ...]]
o.s.security.web.FilterChainProxy : Invoking AuthorizationFilter (12/12)
o.s.security.web.FilterChainProxy : Secured GET /api/orders
```
(Exact filter numbers depend on which features are enabled; the bracketed filter list in Spring's log line is abbreviated here.)

### Compare
| Old style (Spring Security 5.6 and earlier) | Modern style (6.x) |
|---|---|
| `class SecurityConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` | One or more `SecurityFilterChain` `@Bean`s |
| `antMatchers("/api/**")` | `requestMatchers("/api/**")` |
| `authorizeRequests()` with `FilterSecurityInterceptor` | `authorizeHttpRequests()` with `AuthorizationFilter` |
| `SecurityContextPersistenceFilter` saves automatically | `SecurityContextHolderFilter`; saving is explicit |
| `.and()` chaining | Lambda DSL, each feature in its own lambda (`.and()` removed in `Boot 4` / Security 7) |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **What is `DelegatingFilterProxy` and why is it needed?**
   It is a standard servlet filter registered with the container that delegates to a Spring bean named `springSecurityFilterChain`. The container instantiates filters itself and cannot inject Spring beans, so the proxy bridges the two worlds and allows lazy lookup after the application context starts.
2. **What does `FilterChainProxy` do?**
   It holds all `SecurityFilterChain`s, selects the first one whose request matcher fits, runs that chain's filters, and clears the `SecurityContextHolder` at the end. It also applies the HTTP firewall (`StrictHttpFirewall`) that rejects suspicious URLs such as encoded slashes or path traversal.
3. **Name the main filters in order.**
   `SecurityContextHolderFilter`, `HeaderWriterFilter`, `CorsFilter`, `CsrfFilter`, `LogoutFilter`, the authentication filters (form, bearer, basic), `AnonymousAuthenticationFilter`, `ExceptionTranslationFilter`, and `AuthorizationFilter` last. CORS is before CSRF and authentication so preflight requests are answered without credentials.

**Follow-up**
4. **How do you add a custom filter and where?**
   Use `addFilterBefore`, `addFilterAfter` or `addFilterAt` relative to a known filter class. A filter that needs the authenticated user goes after the authentication filters; a filter that performs authentication (a custom API-key filter) goes before `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` or `AuthorizationFilter` and sets the context itself.
5. **Why can declaring a custom filter as a `@Component` be a problem?**
   Spring Boot registers every `Filter` bean with the servlet container, so it runs in the container chain and again inside the security chain where you added it. Either create it with `new` inside the config or disable container registration with a `FilterRegistrationBean`.
6. **How do multiple `SecurityFilterChain`s work?**
   Each chain has a `securityMatcher`; `FilterChainProxy` picks the first matching chain by `@Order`. Exactly one chain handles a request, so rules in a later chain are invisible for requests that an earlier chain matched.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **Users intermittently see another user's data in a custom thread pool. What could be the cause?**
   Someone set the security context on a pooled thread (for example with `MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL` or a manual `setContext`) and never cleared it, so the next task on that thread runs as the previous user. `FilterChainProxy` only clears the request thread. Use `DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor`, which sets and clears around each task.
8. **A `POST /api/orders` returns 403 even for an admin, while `GET` works. Why?**
   Most likely `CsrfFilter`: CSRF protection is on by default and rejects state-changing requests without a token, with a 403 that looks like an authorization failure. TRACE logging shows "Invalid CSRF token found". For a stateless bearer-token API, disable CSRF; for a cookie session app, send the token.
9. **Does Spring Security protect error pages and `/error`?**
   Yes. Since 6.0 the filter chain also applies to `ERROR` and `FORWARD` dispatches. That is why an unauthenticated exception in a controller can turn into a 401 instead of the expected 500 body if `/error` is not permitted; many apps add `requestMatchers("/error").permitAll()`.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you can trace a request through the container, the proxy and the filters, and debug 401/403 problems instead of guessing.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Custom filter as `@Component` and also added to the chain | Runs twice, once without security context | Instantiate in config or disable container registration |
| Catch-all chain with lower order than specific chains | Specific chain never runs | Specific chains get `securityMatcher` and lower `@Order` |
| Custom auth filter placed after `AuthorizationFilter` | Requests are rejected before your filter runs | Place it before the authorization step |
| Forgetting to clear a manually set context on pooled threads | User data leaks between requests | Use delegating executors or `try/finally` with `clearContext()` |
| Debugging 403 by changing rules randomly | Rules become insecure | Enable TRACE logging for `org.springframework.security` |

### Best practices
- Keep one chain per security style (stateless API, session web UI, actuator), each with an explicit `securityMatcher`.
- Use TRACE security logging in development; it prints the chosen chain and each filter.
- Extend `OncePerRequestFilter` for custom filters and keep them free of business logic.
- Remember that headers (`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Cache-Control: no-store`) come for free from `HeaderWriterFilter`; do not disable them.

### Compare with
| Concept | Layer | Sees | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Servlet filter (Spring Security) | Servlet container, before `DispatcherServlet` | Every request, including static files and errors | Authentication, CORS, CSRF, headers |
| `HandlerInterceptor` | Spring MVC, around handler methods | Only requests mapped to handlers | Logging, locale, request timing |
| `@PreAuthorize` (AOP) | Bean method call | Method arguments and return values | Business-level authorization |
| API gateway filter | Network edge | Requests to all services | Token validation, rate limiting |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
In OrderHub, add an `ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter` for a reporting client that calls `GET /api/reports/**` with header `X-API-Key`. A valid key (from `orderhub.reporting.api-key` in `application.yml`) authenticates a principal `reporting-client` with authority `ROLE_REPORTING`. Put reports in their own `SecurityFilterChain` with `@Order(1)`.

Acceptance criteria:
- `GET /api/reports/daily` with the right key returns 200; with a wrong key or no key returns 401.
- The filter is not a `@Component`.
- The rest of the API is unaffected.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.core.authority.SimpleGrantedAuthority;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContext;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

public class ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private final byte[] expectedKey;

    public ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter(String expectedKey) {
        this.expectedKey = expectedKey.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        String key = request.getHeader("X-API-Key");
        // constant-time comparison avoids timing attacks
        if (key != null && MessageDigest.isEqual(expectedKey, key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            var auth = UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated(
                "reporting-client", null, List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_REPORTING")));
            SecurityContext context = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
            context.setAuthentication(auth);
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(context);
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);   // no key: stays anonymous, AuthorizationFilter returns 401
    }
}
```

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.security.web.access.intercept.AuthorizationFilter;
import org.springframework.security.web.authentication.HttpStatusEntryPoint;

@Configuration
public class ReportingSecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    @Order(1)
    SecurityFilterChain reportingChain(HttpSecurity http,
                                       @Value("${orderhub.reporting.api-key}") String apiKey) throws Exception {
        return http
            .securityMatcher("/api/reports/**")
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().hasRole("REPORTING"))
            .addFilterBefore(new ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter(apiKey), AuthorizationFilter.class)
            .exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(new HttpStatusEntryPoint(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)))
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .build();
    }
}
```

```yaml
orderhub:
  reporting:
    api-key: ${REPORTING_API_KEY}   # injected from the environment, never committed
```
The `HttpStatusEntryPoint` returns a bare 401 for anonymous requests. The main API chain keeps a higher `@Order` number, so it handles everything that is not `/api/reports/**`.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What is the role of DelegatingFilterProxy in Spring Security?
A: It is a servlet-container filter that delegates to the Spring bean `springSecurityFilterChain` (the `FilterChainProxy`), bridging the container and the Spring context.

Q: How does FilterChainProxy choose which SecurityFilterChain to run?
A: It tries the chains in `@Order` and runs only the first whose `securityMatcher` matches the request.

Q: Which Spring Security filter turns an AccessDeniedException into a 401 or 403?
A: `ExceptionTranslationFilter`: entry point (401) for anonymous users, access denied handler (403) for authenticated users.

Q: Why is CorsFilter placed before CsrfFilter and the authentication filters?
A: So CORS preflight `OPTIONS` requests, which carry no credentials or CSRF token, can be answered before they are rejected.

Q: Why should a custom Spring Security filter usually not be a @Component?
A: Spring Boot also registers `Filter` beans with the servlet container, so the filter would run twice.

Q: Which filter is last in a Spring Security 6 filter chain and what does it do?
A: `AuthorizationFilter`, which asks the `AuthorizationManager` whether the current authentication may access the request.

**Related:** [[Authentication vs Authorization]] · [[SecurityFilterChain Configuration]] · [[JWT Stateless Authentication]]

# SecurityFilterChain Configuration

**Level: Intermediate | Phase 14 | Priority: MUST | Since: Spring Security 5.4 (SecurityFilterChain bean); lambda DSL 5.2; WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter removed 6.0**

> **30-second interview answer:** In Spring Security 6 you configure security by declaring a `SecurityFilterChain` `@Bean` built from `HttpSecurity` with the lambda DSL: `authorizeHttpRequests` for URL rules (evaluated top to bottom, first match wins), an authentication mechanism such as `oauth2ResourceServer`, `httpBasic` or `formLogin`, `sessionManagement` for stateful or stateless, and `csrf`, `cors`, `headers` and `exceptionHandling` for the rest. The old `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` is gone. If you declare no chain, Spring Boot creates a default one that secures everything with form login and HTTP Basic.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
The rule book at a nightclub door.

| Nightclub door | SecurityFilterChain configuration |
|---|---|
| The rule book the bouncer reads top to bottom, stopping at the first rule that fits | `authorizeHttpRequests` with ordered `requestMatchers` |
| "Bar area: everyone", "VIP lounge: VIP wristband", "Everything else: must have a ticket" | `permitAll()`, `hasRole("VIP")`, `anyRequest().authenticated()` |
| How guests prove they paid: ticket scan or wristband | Authentication mechanism (`oauth2ResourceServer`, `httpBasic`) |
| Hand stamp that lets you come back in without paying again | Session (`JSESSIONID`); stateless means no stamp, show your ticket each time |
| What the bouncer says when he turns you away | `exceptionHandling` (entry point and access denied handler) |
| The club's standard house rules if the owner wrote nothing | Spring Boot's default chain |

### What it is
- **`HttpSecurity`:** a builder, prototype-scoped per chain, that collects configurers and produces a `DefaultSecurityFilterChain`.
- **Lambda DSL:** each feature takes a `Customizer<T>` lambda, for example `.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())` or `.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())`. Since 6.1 the non-lambda methods and `.and()` are deprecated; in `Boot 4` (Spring Security 7) they are removed.
- **`authorizeHttpRequests`:** builds the `AuthorizationFilter` and its `RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager`. Rules: `permitAll`, `denyAll`, `authenticated`, `anonymous`, `hasRole`, `hasAnyRole`, `hasAuthority`, `hasAnyAuthority`, `access(AuthorizationManager)`.
- **`requestMatchers()`:** chooses requests by path pattern and optionally HTTP method. With Spring MVC on the classpath, patterns are matched the same way MVC matches them.
- **`securityMatcher()`:** decides whether this whole chain applies (different from `requestMatchers`, which choose rules inside a chain).
- **`SessionCreationPolicy`:** `IF_REQUIRED` (default), `ALWAYS`, `NEVER` (use one if it exists), `STATELESS` (never create or use a session for security).
- **`AuthenticationEntryPoint` / `AccessDeniedHandler`:** produce the 401 and 403 responses.

### Why it exists
The adapter style hid configuration in overridden methods and made multiple configurations awkward. A bean-based configuration is plain Spring: you can have several chains, inject other beans, test them, and compose them with `@Order`. The lambda DSL makes the scope of each setting obvious and removes the confusing `.and()` chains where it was unclear which feature a method belonged to.

## 2. How It Works
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["@Bean SecurityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http)"] --> B["Configurers registered: authorize, csrf, cors, oauth2ResourceServer"]
    B --> C["http.build()"]
    C --> D["Each configurer init() then configure(): adds its filter"]
    D --> E["Filters sorted by FilterOrderRegistration"]
    E --> F["DefaultSecurityFilterChain(matcher, filters)"]
    F --> G["FilterChainProxy holds all chains"]
```

Rule evaluation inside `AuthorizationFilter`:
```text
Request: DELETE /api/products/7, user alice [ROLE_CUSTOMER]

1. requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()                 no match
2. requestMatchers(GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()        no match (method is DELETE)
3. requestMatchers("/api/products/**").hasRole("ADMIN")         MATCH -> alice lacks ROLE_ADMIN -> DENY
4. requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")            never evaluated
5. anyRequest().authenticated()                                 never evaluated

Result: AccessDeniedException -> ExceptionTranslationFilter -> AccessDeniedHandler -> 403
```
First match wins, so put the most specific rules first and the catch-all last. Spring Security 6 throws at startup if `anyRequest()` is not the last rule.

What Spring Boot auto-configures:
- `SecurityAutoConfiguration` imports `SpringBootWebSecurityConfiguration`, which creates a default chain (`anyRequest().authenticated()`, `formLogin()`, `httpBasic()`) **only if you have not declared any `SecurityFilterChain` bean**. Your bean replaces it completely; nothing is merged.
- `SecurityFilterAutoConfiguration` registers `DelegatingFilterProxy` with the servlet container.
- `UserDetailsServiceAutoConfiguration` creates the generated in-memory user only if no `UserDetailsService`, `AuthenticationProvider`, `AuthenticationManager` or OAuth2 resource server configuration exists.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
The OrderHub base configuration that the JWT topic will complete: URL rules, stateless sessions, JSON error bodies in RFC 9457 Problem Details format (Phase 11), security headers, and a custom `AuthorizationManager`.

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.security.web.AuthenticationEntryPoint;
import org.springframework.security.web.access.AccessDeniedHandler;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

/** Writes 401 and 403 as application/problem+json, matching the API's other errors. */
@Component
public class ProblemDetailsSecurityHandlers {

    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public ProblemDetailsSecurityHandlers(ObjectMapper mapper) { this.mapper = mapper; }

    public AuthenticationEntryPoint entryPoint() {
        return (request, response, ex) ->
            write(response, HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Authentication required", request.getRequestURI());
    }

    public AccessDeniedHandler accessDeniedHandler() {
        return (request, response, ex) ->
            write(response, HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN, "You do not have permission for this action", request.getRequestURI());
    }

    private void write(HttpServletResponse response, HttpStatus status, String detail, String path) throws IOException {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, detail);
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(path));
        response.setStatus(status.value());
        response.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
        mapper.writeValue(response.getOutputStream(), pd);
    }
}
```

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import java.util.function.Supplier;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.authorization.AuthorizationDecision;
import org.springframework.security.authorization.AuthorizationManager;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.security.web.access.intercept.RequestAuthorizationContext;
import org.springframework.security.web.header.writers.ReferrerPolicyHeaderWriter;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain apiSecurity(HttpSecurity http, ProblemDetailsSecurityHandlers handlers) throws Exception {
        http
            .securityMatcher("/api/**", "/error")
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/error").permitAll()                                   // let error responses through
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/login", "/api/auth/register").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/products/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/customers/{id}/**").access(sameCustomerOrAdmin())
                .anyRequest().authenticated())                                           // deny by default
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                  // no cookies are used for auth in this API
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())               // uses the CorsConfigurationSource bean
            .headers(h -> h
                .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'"))
                .referrerPolicy(r -> r.policy(ReferrerPolicyHeaderWriter.ReferrerPolicy.NO_REFERRER)))
            .exceptionHandling(e -> e
                .authenticationEntryPoint(handlers.entryPoint())
                .accessDeniedHandler(handlers.accessDeniedHandler()))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());         // replaced by oauth2ResourceServer in the JWT topic
        return http.build();
    }

    /** /api/customers/{id}/** is allowed for ADMIN or for the customer whose id is in the path. */
    private AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext> sameCustomerOrAdmin() {
        return (Supplier<Authentication> authentication, RequestAuthorizationContext ctx) -> {
            Authentication auth = authentication.get();
            boolean admin = auth.getAuthorities().stream()
                                .anyMatch(a -> a.getAuthority().equals("ROLE_ADMIN"));
            if (admin) return new AuthorizationDecision(true);
            String pathId = ctx.getVariables().get("id");
            boolean owner = auth.getPrincipal() instanceof com.orderhub.user.OrderHubUserDetails u
                            && u.customerId() != null
                            && u.customerId().toString().equals(pathId);
            return new AuthorizationDecision(owner);
        };
    }
}
```

```yaml
logging:
  level:
    org.springframework.security.web.access: DEBUG   # logs every authorization decision
```

### Walkthrough
- `securityMatcher("/api/**", "/error")` scopes the chain; a separate chain could serve `/actuator/**`.
- Rules are ordered from specific to general. `GET /api/products/**` is public, but any other method on products falls to the next line and needs `ADMIN`. If the `hasRole("ADMIN")` line came first, browsing products would require admin.
- `"/api/customers/{id}/**"` uses a path variable; `RequestAuthorizationContext.getVariables()` exposes it to the custom `AuthorizationManager`. This is URL-level ownership; [[Method Security with @PreAuthorize]] shows the more common method-level way.
- `STATELESS` stops Spring Security from creating or reading an `HttpSession`, so every request must carry credentials.
- CSRF is disabled because authentication will use the `Authorization` header, which a malicious site cannot make a browser send automatically.
- Custom headers add a strict Content Security Policy and no referrer. Default headers (`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store`) stay on.
- The handlers return Problem Details JSON instead of Spring's default empty 401 or HTML pages, which frontends can parse.

### Output
```http

Authorization: Basic YWxpY2U6YWxpY2UtcGFzcw==

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer

{"type":"about:blank","title":"Forbidden","status":403,"detail":"You do not have permission for this action","instance":"/api/products/7"}
```
```http
GET /api/orders

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type":"about:blank","title":"Unauthorized","status":401,"detail":"Authentication required","instance":"/api/orders"}
```
DEBUG log for the 403:
```text
o.s.s.w.a.AuthorizationFilter : Authorizing DELETE /api/products/7
o.s.s.w.a.i.RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager : Checking authorization on DELETE /api/products/7 using AuthorityAuthorizationManager[authorities=[ROLE_ADMIN]]
o.s.s.w.a.ExceptionTranslationFilter : Sending UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken [Principal=alice] to access denied handler since access is denied
```

### Compare
```java
// OLD: Spring Security 5.x, removed in 6.0. Do not write this in an interview.
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter;

@Configuration
public class OldConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {
    @Override
    protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeRequests()
                .antMatchers("/api/products/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            .and()
            .httpBasic()
            .and()
            .csrf().disable();
    }
}
```
| Old | New |
|---|---|
| Extend `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` | Declare `SecurityFilterChain` `@Bean` |
| Override `configure(AuthenticationManagerBuilder)` | Declare `UserDetailsService` and `PasswordEncoder` beans |
| `authorizeRequests` + `antMatchers` / `mvcMatchers` | `authorizeHttpRequests` + `requestMatchers` |
| `.and()` between features | One lambda per feature |
| `web.ignoring()` to skip static files | `permitAll()` rules (ignoring also drops headers and context) |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **How do you configure Spring Security in Spring Boot 3?**
   Declare a `SecurityFilterChain` bean that takes `HttpSecurity`, configure it with the lambda DSL and return `http.build()`. Users come from a `UserDetailsService` bean and passwords from a `PasswordEncoder` bean. There is no adapter class to extend.
2. **What happens if you add the security starter and configure nothing?**
   Boot creates a default chain: every request requires authentication, with form login and HTTP Basic, plus a generated in-memory user `user` whose password is printed at startup. CSRF and security headers are enabled.
3. **In what order are `requestMatchers` rules evaluated?**
   Top to bottom, and the first matching rule decides. Put specific rules before general ones and finish with `anyRequest()`, which must be last or startup fails.

**Follow-up**
4. **What is the difference between `securityMatcher` and `requestMatchers`?**
   `securityMatcher` decides whether the whole chain applies to a request; it is how multiple chains split the URL space. `requestMatchers` inside `authorizeHttpRequests` choose which authorization rule applies within that chain.
5. **What does `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` do and when do you use it?**
   Spring Security neither creates nor uses an `HttpSession` to store the security context, so each request must authenticate itself, typically with a bearer token. Use it for token-based REST APIs; use the default for browser apps with form login.
6. **How do you return JSON instead of the default 401 and 403 responses?**
   Configure `exceptionHandling` with a custom `AuthenticationEntryPoint` and `AccessDeniedHandler` that write a body, ideally a `ProblemDetail`. A `@ControllerAdvice` will not catch these, because the exceptions happen in filters before the `DispatcherServlet`.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **Why does `@ControllerAdvice` not handle `AccessDeniedException` from URL rules, but does from `@PreAuthorize`?**
   URL rules are enforced by `AuthorizationFilter`, outside Spring MVC, so only `ExceptionTranslationFilter` sees the exception. `@PreAuthorize` throws inside the controller or service call, which is within MVC, so an `@ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)` would catch it first. If you handle it there, rethrow or return 403 deliberately, or let it propagate so Spring Security's handler is used consistently.
8. **Someone uses `web.ignoring().requestMatchers("/api/public/**")`. What is the risk?**
   Ignored paths bypass the entire security filter chain: no security headers, no CSRF, no `SecurityContext`, no firewall. Spring logs a warning recommending `permitAll()` instead. Use ignoring only for truly static resources, if at all.
9. **After adding your own `SecurityFilterChain`, the H2 console and Swagger UI stop working. Why?**
   Your bean replaced Boot's default chain, so those paths are now covered by your `anyRequest().authenticated()`. Add explicit `permitAll()` rules for `/swagger-ui/**` and `/v3/api-docs/**` (and frame options `sameOrigin` plus CSRF ignore for the H2 console in development only).

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you write modern configuration, understand ordering and statelessness, and know which parts happen in filters versus MVC.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Catch-all rule before specific rules | Specific rules never apply | Specific first, `anyRequest()` last |
| Forgetting HTTP method in a public rule | `POST /api/products` becomes public too | Use `requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**")` |
| Expecting `@ControllerAdvice` to format filter errors | Default empty 401 or 403 | Custom entry point and access denied handler |
| Using `web.ignoring()` for API paths | No headers or context on those paths | `permitAll()` |
| Ending with `anyRequest().permitAll()` | New endpoints are public by accident | Deny by default with `authenticated()` |
| Copying old `antMatchers` and adapter code | Compilation errors on Boot 3 | Lambda DSL and `requestMatchers` |

### Best practices
- One `SecurityConfig` per chain with a clear `securityMatcher`; keep rules readable and grouped by resource.
- Deny by default and write a MockMvc test per rule; security rules are code and regress like code.
- Keep URL rules coarse (public, authenticated, admin area) and push business rules ("own orders only") to method security.
- Return consistent error bodies; never leak stack traces or which rule failed.

### Compare with
| Configuration style | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` | Removed in 6.0 | Interview red flag if written today |
| `SecurityFilterChain` bean, non-lambda | Deprecated since 6.1 | Works on Boot 3, removed in `Boot 4` |
| `SecurityFilterChain` bean, lambda DSL | Current | Use this |
| Kotlin DSL `http { }` | Current | Same features for Kotlin projects |
| XML namespace `<http>` | Legacy but supported | Old enterprise apps |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
Write OrderHub's rules for these requirements and a test class that proves them:
- `POST /api/auth/**` is public, `GET /api/products/**` is public.
- Creating, updating and deleting products requires `ADMIN`.
- `GET /api/admin/reports/**` requires `ADMIN` or `REPORTING`.
- `/actuator/health` is public, other actuator endpoints need `ADMIN`.
- Anything else requires authentication; 401 and 403 are Problem Details JSON.

Acceptance criteria: tests with `@WithMockUser` cover at least one allowed and one denied case per rule.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class OrderHubRules {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain rules(HttpSecurity http, ProblemDetailsSecurityHandlers handlers) throws Exception {
        return http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/products/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/admin/reports/**").hasAnyRole("ADMIN", "REPORTING")
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(handlers.entryPoint())
                                     .accessDeniedHandler(handlers.accessDeniedHandler()))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .build();
    }
}
```

```java
package com.orderhub.security;

import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.delete;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.content;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class OrderHubRulesTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @Test void productsArePublic() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/products")).andExpect(status().isOk());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "CUSTOMER")
    void customerCannotDeleteProduct() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(delete("/api/products/1"))
           .andExpect(status().isForbidden())
           .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON));
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")
    void adminCanDeleteProduct() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(delete("/api/products/1")).andExpect(status().isNoContent());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "REPORTING")
    void reportingCanReadReports() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/admin/reports/daily")).andExpect(status().isOk());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "REPORTING")
    void reportingCannotUseOtherAdminEndpoints() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/admin/users")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    @Test void healthIsPublic() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/actuator/health")).andExpect(status().isOk());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "CUSTOMER")
    void metricsNeedAdmin() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/actuator/metrics")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    @Test void anonymousGetsProblemJson401() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/api/orders"))
           .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized())
           .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON));
    }
}
```
`@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` puts an authenticated user with `ROLE_ADMIN` into the test's security context without any login. The order of the `/api/admin/reports/**` rule before `/api/admin/**` is what lets `REPORTING` in.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: How is Spring Security configured in Spring Boot 3 without WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter?
A: By declaring a `SecurityFilterChain` `@Bean` built from `HttpSecurity` with the lambda DSL and returning `http.build()`.

Q: In what order does authorizeHttpRequests evaluate requestMatchers rules?
A: Top to bottom; the first matching rule decides, and `anyRequest()` must be last.

Q: What is the difference between securityMatcher and requestMatchers in Spring Security?
A: `securityMatcher` selects whether a whole chain applies; `requestMatchers` select an authorization rule within the chain.

Q: What does SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS do in Spring Security?
A: It stops Spring Security from creating or using an HTTP session for the security context, so each request must carry credentials.

Q: Why can't @ControllerAdvice format 401 responses from Spring Security URL rules?
A: They are produced in the filter chain before the `DispatcherServlet`; use a custom `AuthenticationEntryPoint` instead.

Q: What does Spring Boot do when you declare your own SecurityFilterChain bean?
A: It backs off its default chain entirely; your chain is the only configuration.

**Related:** [[Security Filter Chain Architecture]] · [[JWT Stateless Authentication]] · [[CSRF, CORS and Common Vulnerabilities]]

# Modern auth

**Shared analogy: a festival wristband system.** At a big festival you show your ticket once at the gate and get a tamper-proof wristband (a JWT): every stage checks the wristband instead of calling the ticket office. Some people buy through a ticket partner instead of the festival itself, and the festival trusts the partner's stamp (OAuth2 and OpenID Connect). Inside, some areas check more than the wristband colour: the artist lounge checks that your name is on that night's list (method security with `@PreAuthorize`). And the festival must stop tricksters who make you unknowingly sign things (CSRF) and decide which partner sites may sell its tickets (CORS). This group turns OrderHub into a token-based API that can also trust an external identity provider.
