# Auto-Configuration Internals

**Level: Advanced | Phase 18 | Priority: MUST | Since: Spring Boot 1.0 (spring.factories), Boot 2.7 (@AutoConfiguration and AutoConfiguration.imports), Boot 3.0 (spring.factories no longer read for auto-config)**

> **30-second interview answer:** `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, which imports `AutoConfigurationImportSelector`. That selector reads the class names listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` from every jar, quickly filters them using precomputed metadata (`@ConditionalOnClass` and friends), and hands the survivors to Spring as configuration classes. Because it is a `DeferredImportSelector`, auto-configuration is processed after your own configuration, so conditions like `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` see your beans and back off. You can see every decision with `--debug` or the `/actuator/conditions` endpoint.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
A wedding planner with a checklist.

| Wedding planner | Auto-configuration |
|---|---|
| A thick binder with every possible service (music, catering, flowers) | All auto-configuration classes listed in `AutoConfiguration.imports` |
| "Only if there is a dance floor" | `@ConditionalOnClass(DispatcherServlet.class)` |
| "Only if the couple has not hired their own band" | `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` |
| "Only if the couple ticked 'fireworks: yes'" | `@ConditionalOnProperty` |
| The planner waits until the couple's own arrangements are known | `DeferredImportSelector`: user config first |
| Catering must be booked after the venue | `@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` |
| The planner's notes on what was booked and why not | The condition evaluation report |

### What it is
- **Auto-configuration class:** a `@AutoConfiguration` class (a `@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)` with ordering attributes) containing `@Bean` methods guarded by conditions. Example: `DataSourceAutoConfiguration`, `JacksonAutoConfiguration`.
- **`AutoConfiguration.imports`:** a plain text file, one fully qualified class name per line, at `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`. Boot 2.7 introduced it; Boot 3.0 stopped reading auto-configurations from `spring.factories`.
- **`@Conditional`:** core Spring (4.0) annotation that takes a `Condition` class with `matches(ConditionContext, AnnotatedTypeMetadata)`. Spring Boot adds `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingClass`, `@ConditionalOnBean`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, `@ConditionalOnProperty`, `@ConditionalOnResource`, `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`, `@ConditionalOnSingleCandidate`, `@ConditionalOnExpression`, `@ConditionalOnJava`, `@ConditionalOnCloudPlatform`, `@ConditionalOnThreading` (Boot 3.2, virtual threads), `@ConditionalOnBooleanProperty` (Boot 3.5).
- **Condition evaluation report:** a record of every condition outcome, printed with `debug=true` and served at `/actuator/conditions`.

### Why it exists
Before Boot, every Spring app copied the same 200 lines of configuration for a data source, transaction manager, Jackson, MVC and so on. Boot ships that configuration once, but only activates the pieces your classpath and properties ask for, and always lets your own beans win. "Opinionated defaults that back off" is the whole design.

## 2. How It Works

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["@SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @ComponentScan + @EnableAutoConfiguration"] --> B["@Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector) - a DeferredImportSelector"]
    B --> C["ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses YOUR config and scanned components first"]
    C --> D["Deferred selectors run: ImportCandidates.load reads every AutoConfiguration.imports on the classpath (about 150 to 200 classes)"]
    D --> E["Remove exclusions: exclude, excludeName, spring.autoconfigure.exclude"]
    E --> F["AutoConfigurationImportFilter fast pass using spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties: OnClassCondition, OnWebApplicationCondition, OnBeanCondition (no class loading)"]
    F --> G["Sort by @AutoConfiguration(before, after), @AutoConfigureOrder"]
    G --> H["Each survivor parsed as a configuration class; full @Conditional evaluation on class and on each @Bean method"]
    H --> I["Bean definitions registered; report records match or no-match with reasons"]
```

**Step details**
1. **Deferred:** `DeferredImportSelector` runs after all other `@Configuration` classes in the current processing round are parsed. That is what lets `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` see the `DataSource` you defined yourself.
2. **Candidate loading:** `ImportCandidates.load(AutoConfiguration.class, classLoader)` reads all files. Lines starting with `#` are comments.
3. **Fast filtering:** at build time, Boot's annotation processor (`spring-boot-autoconfigure-processor`) writes `META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties` containing entries like `...JacksonAutoConfiguration.ConditionalOnClass=com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper`. The filter checks these strings against the classpath without loading the auto-configuration class itself, which removes most candidates cheaply.
4. **Ordering:** `@AutoConfiguration(after = ..., before = ...)` (or `@AutoConfigureAfter`, `@AutoConfigureBefore`, `@AutoConfigureOrder`) controls the order in which auto-configurations are *parsed*. Order matters for `@ConditionalOnBean`, which only sees bean definitions registered so far.
5. **Full evaluation:** for each class, `ConditionEvaluator.shouldSkip` evaluates conditions in two phases. `PARSE_CONFIGURATION` conditions (like `OnClassCondition`) decide whether the class is parsed at all. `REGISTER_BEAN` conditions (`OnBeanCondition` is a `ConfigurationCondition` with this phase) decide whether each bean definition is registered, after more definitions are known.
6. **Class-level then method-level:** a class-level condition failing skips the entire class; method-level conditions can skip individual `@Bean`s.

**How `@ConditionalOnClass` can reference a missing class:** the annotation's value is read from bytecode by ASM metadata reading (no class loading) during the filter and parse phases, so referencing `ObjectMapper.class` is safe even when Jackson is absent. That only works on the class-level annotation of a top-level or nested configuration class, which is why Boot uses nested static `@Configuration` classes for optional dependencies.

**Condition evaluation order inside one class**

| Order | What | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Class-level conditions, cheapest first (`OnClassCondition` before `OnBeanCondition`, via `@Order` on condition classes) | `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)` |
| 2 | Nested configuration classes, each with their own conditions | `DataSourceConfiguration.Hikari` |
| 3 | `@Bean` method conditions, at bean registration phase | `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on `dataSource()` |

**Key rule:** `@ConditionalOnBean` and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` are only reliable in auto-configuration classes (processed last, in a known order). In your own `@Configuration` they depend on scanning order and may give wrong answers.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
OrderHub inspects and overrides auto-configuration.

```java
// file: src/main/java/com/orderhub/OrderHubApplication.java
package com.orderhub;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.task.TaskSchedulingAutoConfiguration;

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = TaskSchedulingAutoConfiguration.class)  // we do our own scheduling
public class OrderHubApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderHubApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

```java
// file: src/main/java/com/orderhub/config/JsonConfig.java
package com.orderhub.config;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.SerializationFeature;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jackson.Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.converter.json.Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class JsonConfig {

    // Option A (preferred): customise the auto-configured ObjectMapper, keep Boot's defaults
    @Bean
    Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer orderHubJson() {
        return builder -> builder.featuresToDisable(SerializationFeature.WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS);
    }

    // Option B: define your own ObjectMapper; JacksonAutoConfiguration's
    // @ConditionalOnMissingBean then backs off entirely. Uncomment to see the report change.
    // @Bean
    // ObjectMapper objectMapper(Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder builder) {
    //     return builder.build();
    // }
}
```

A simplified copy of how Boot itself writes an auto-configuration (based on `JacksonAutoConfiguration` and `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` patterns):

```java
// Not OrderHub code: how Boot's auto-configurations are structured
package org.example.autoconfigure;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnClass;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnMissingBean;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnProperty;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.http.HttpMessageConvertersAutoConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

@AutoConfiguration(before = HttpMessageConvertersAutoConfiguration.class) // parse before the converters
@ConditionalOnClass(ObjectMapper.class)                                    // PARSE phase, read via ASM
@EnableConfigurationProperties(ExampleJsonProperties.class)
public class ExampleJsonAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                                  // REGISTER_BEAN phase: user bean wins
    @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "example.json", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
    ObjectMapper exampleObjectMapper(ExampleJsonProperties props) {
        ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        mapper.findAndRegisterModules();
        return mapper;
    }
}
```

```text
# file: META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (inside the jar)
org.example.autoconfigure.ExampleJsonAutoConfiguration
```

```yaml
# application.yml
debug: false                      # true prints the CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT at startup
spring:
  autoconfigure:
    exclude:
      - org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.mail.MailSenderAutoConfiguration
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: conditions,beans
```

### Walkthrough
- `exclude` on `@SpringBootApplication` and `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` both remove candidates before any condition runs. Use the property when the decision differs per environment.
- Option A uses a customizer: Boot's auto-configured `ObjectMapper` still exists with all its defaults (modules, property binding of `spring.jackson.*`), plus your tweak. Option B replaces it, so you lose `spring.jackson.*` properties unless you build from `Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder` as shown.
- The example auto-configuration shows the canonical shape: class-level `@ConditionalOnClass` to avoid loading anything if the library is absent, bean-level `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` so user beans win, properties to switch features, and ordering relative to related auto-configs.
- The `.imports` file is the registration. Without it, the class is just an unused class in a jar (unless component scanning picks it up, which must never happen for auto-configurations).

### Output
Running with `--debug`:
```text
============================
CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT
============================

Positive matches:
-----------------
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource', 'org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.embedded.EmbeddedDatabaseType' (OnClassCondition)

   JacksonAutoConfiguration.JacksonObjectMapperConfiguration#jacksonObjectMapper matched:
      - @ConditionalOnMissingBean (types: com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper; SearchStrategy: all) did not find any beans (OnBeanCondition)

Negative matches:
-----------------
   MongoAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'com.mongodb.client.MongoClient' (OnClassCondition)

Exclusions:
-----------
   org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.task.TaskSchedulingAutoConfiguration
   org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.mail.MailSenderAutoConfiguration

Unconditional classes:
----------------------
   org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.context.ConfigurationPropertiesAutoConfiguration
```
With Option B enabled, the Jackson entry moves to negative matches:
```text
   JacksonAutoConfiguration.JacksonObjectMapperConfiguration#jacksonObjectMapper:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnMissingBean (types: com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper; SearchStrategy: all) found beans of type 'com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper' objectMapper (OnBeanCondition)
```

### Compare
| Boot 2.6 and earlier | Boot 2.7 to 3.x |
|---|---|
| `META-INF/spring.factories` key `org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=a.B,c.D` | `META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports`, one class per line |
| `@Configuration` + `@AutoConfigureAfter` | `@AutoConfiguration(after = ...)` |
| Still read in Boot 2.7 (deprecated) | Not read for auto-config in Boot 3.0+ (still used for listeners, failure analyzers, environment post-processors) |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?**
   `@EnableAutoConfiguration` imports `AutoConfigurationImportSelector`, which loads candidate classes from every `AutoConfiguration.imports` file, filters them by conditions and exclusions, orders them, and registers them as configuration classes after the user's configuration. Each auto-configuration creates beans guarded by `@Conditional` annotations, mainly "class present" and "bean missing".
2. **Where are auto-configuration classes registered in Spring Boot 3?**
   In `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`, one fully qualified class name per line. `spring.factories` is no longer read for auto-configuration since Boot 3.0.
3. **How do you disable a specific auto-configuration?**
   `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = X.class)`, `excludeName` for classes not on the classpath, or the `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` property. Often better: define your own bean so `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` backs off, or set the feature's property.

**Follow-up**
4. **Why are auto-configurations processed after user configuration?**
   `AutoConfigurationImportSelector` is a `DeferredImportSelector`, run after the regular configuration classes are parsed. That ordering lets `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` detect user-defined beans so Boot's defaults back off.
5. **How can `@ConditionalOnClass(SomeClass.class)` work if `SomeClass` is not on the classpath?**
   Spring reads annotation metadata from the class file with ASM instead of loading the class, so the class literal is just a name in the bytecode. Additionally, the import filter uses precomputed `spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties` and never loads the auto-configuration class when the dependency is missing.
6. **Why should you avoid `@ConditionalOnBean` in normal `@Configuration` classes?**
   It only sees bean definitions registered so far. In user configuration, processing order depends on scanning and is not guaranteed, so the result can change between environments. In auto-configuration, order is controlled with `after` and `before`.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **You added `spring-boot-starter-data-redis` and the app now fails to start because it cannot connect to Redis in tests. Why, and what are your options?**
   The starter puts Lettuce and Spring Data Redis on the classpath, so `RedisAutoConfiguration` and repositories auto-configuration match and create beans; something then connects eagerly (for example a health indicator or a repository init). Options: provide Redis with Testcontainers and `@ServiceConnection`, exclude the Redis auto-configurations in the test profile, or disable the specific feature via properties (`management.health.redis.enabled=false`).
8. **Your own `DataSource` bean is defined, but Boot still creates a second one and you get "expected single matching bean but found 2". How?**
   Your bean is probably not of type `DataSource` at definition level (for example a `@Bean` method returning `Object` or a `FactoryBean` whose type cannot be determined early), so `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` did not see it. Declare the most specific return type on `@Bean` methods; the conditions report shows exactly what was searched.
9. **How do you find out why a bean you expected is missing?**
   Start with `--debug` or `/actuator/conditions` and search for the auto-configuration: the report states the failed condition (missing class, property value, existing bean). `/actuator/beans` shows what exists. For property conditions, check spelling and relaxed binding.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether "Boot is magic" is replaced by a precise mental model you can use to debug missing or duplicate beans.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Putting auto-configurations in a package covered by component scanning | They are processed as user config: wrong order, conditions unreliable | Keep them out of scanned packages; register only via `.imports` |
| Using `@ConditionalOnBean` in user configuration | Results depend on order | Use it only in auto-configuration with explicit ordering |
| `@Bean` methods returning a broad type (`Object`) | `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` cannot match the real type | Return the specific type |
| Excluding auto-configuration instead of customising | You must rebuild everything Boot did, losing properties support | Prefer customizers and properties |
| Forgetting `.imports` after migrating from Boot 2 | Auto-configuration silently not applied | Move entries from `spring.factories` to `AutoConfiguration.imports` |

### Best practices
- When a bean behaves unexpectedly, read the auto-configuration's source; it is short and states exactly when it applies and what it reads.
- Customise with `*Customizer` beans (`Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer`, `WebServerFactoryCustomizer`, `RestClientCustomizer`) and properties before replacing beans.
- Use `ApplicationContextRunner` to test conditions of your own auto-configurations.
- Keep `debug=true` out of production configs; use `/actuator/conditions` (secured) instead.

### Compare with
| Mechanism | Who writes it | When processed | Backs off? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@Configuration` in your app | You | First | Not by design |
| `@AutoConfiguration` | Library authors | After user config, ordered | Yes, via conditions |
| `@Import(SomeConfig.class)` | You | With the importing class | Only if it has conditions |
| `@Enable*` annotations | Library | When you add the annotation | No; explicit opt-in |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
In OrderHub, prove the back-off behaviour with a test. Acceptance criteria: an `ApplicationContextRunner` test loads `JacksonAutoConfiguration`; case 1 asserts that exactly one `ObjectMapper` exists and that it has the bean name `jacksonObjectMapper`; case 2 registers a user configuration with its own `ObjectMapper` named `orderHubMapper` and asserts that only that bean exists; case 3 sets a `spring.jackson.serialization.indent-output=true` property and asserts the auto-configured mapper honours it.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```java
// file: src/test/java/com/orderhub/config/JacksonBackOffTest.java
package com.orderhub.config;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.SerializationFeature;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfigurations;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jackson.JacksonAutoConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.runner.ApplicationContextRunner;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

class JacksonBackOffTest {

    private final ApplicationContextRunner runner = new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(JacksonAutoConfiguration.class));

    @Test
    void autoConfiguredMapperByDefault() {
        runner.run(ctx -> {
            assertThat(ctx).hasSingleBean(ObjectMapper.class);
            assertThat(ctx).hasBean("jacksonObjectMapper");
        });
    }

    @Test
    void userMapperWins() {
        runner.withUserConfiguration(UserMapperConfig.class).run(ctx -> {
            assertThat(ctx).hasSingleBean(ObjectMapper.class);
            assertThat(ctx).hasBean("orderHubMapper");
            assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean("jacksonObjectMapper");
        });
    }

    @Test
    void propertiesApplyToAutoConfiguredMapper() {
        runner.withPropertyValues("spring.jackson.serialization.indent-output=true").run(ctx ->
                assertThat(ctx.getBean(ObjectMapper.class)
                        .isEnabled(SerializationFeature.INDENT_OUTPUT)).isTrue());
    }

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    static class UserMapperConfig {
        @Bean
        ObjectMapper orderHubMapper() { return new ObjectMapper(); }
    }
}
```
`AutoConfigurations.of(...)` applies the same ordering and deferred semantics as a real Boot app, so `withUserConfiguration` beans are seen by `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: Which file registers auto-configuration classes in Spring Boot 3?
A: `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`, one class name per line.

Q: Why does Spring Boot auto-configuration back off when you define your own bean?
A: Auto-configuration is imported by a `DeferredImportSelector` after user configuration, and its beans use `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.

Q: How does Spring Boot evaluate @ConditionalOnClass without loading a missing class?
A: It reads annotation metadata from bytecode with ASM and pre-filters with `spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties`.

Q: How do you see why a Spring Boot auto-configuration did or did not apply?
A: Run with `--debug` (or `debug=true`) for the conditions evaluation report, or call `/actuator/conditions`.

Q: Why is @ConditionalOnBean unreliable in your own @Configuration classes?
A: It only sees bean definitions registered so far, and the processing order of user configuration is not guaranteed.

# Startup Performance, AOT and GraalVM Native Images

**Level: Advanced | Phase 18 | Priority: NICE | Since: Spring Boot 3.0 (AOT and native support), Boot 3.2 (CRaC), Boot 3.3 (CDS support), Java 24 AOT cache (marked Java 25+ here)**

> **30-second interview answer:** A Spring Boot JVM app typically starts in 2 to 10 seconds because it scans the classpath, evaluates hundreds of conditions, loads thousands of classes and creates beans by reflection. You can measure the cost with `/actuator/startup`, then reduce it with lazy initialization, Class Data Sharing (CDS), or Spring AOT, which moves configuration processing to build time by generating Java code for bean definitions. Taking AOT further, GraalVM compiles the app into a native executable that starts in tens of milliseconds and uses far less memory, at the cost of long builds, a closed-world assumption (no runtime classpath surprises, fixed profiles and conditions) and lower peak throughput without profile-guided optimisation.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
Opening a pop-up shop versus a prefabricated kiosk.

| Shop | Spring startup |
|---|---|
| Every morning you unpack boxes, read the floor plan, decide where shelves go | JVM startup: scan classpath, evaluate conditions, reflectively create beans |
| Only unpack a box when a customer asks for that product | Lazy initialization |
| Keep yesterday's shelf layout photo so unpacking is faster | CDS or the Java AOT cache: pre-parsed class data reused |
| The floor plan is decided at the factory and printed as step-by-step instructions | Spring AOT: generated code instead of runtime decisions |
| The whole kiosk is built at the factory and dropped in place, ready to open | GraalVM native image |
| But you cannot rearrange the kiosk once it arrives | Closed world: no runtime class generation, profiles fixed at build time |
| Freeze the shop mid-morning and thaw it tomorrow already running | CRaC checkpoint and restore |

### What it is
- **Startup time:** time from `java -jar` to `ApplicationReadyEvent`. **Time to first request** and **memory footprint (RSS)** are the related metrics that matter for scale-to-zero and serverless.
- **Lazy initialization:** `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` makes all beans lazy, created on first use.
- **CDS (Class Data Sharing):** a JVM feature that stores parsed class metadata in an archive mapped at startup. Boot 3.3+ helps create one (`-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit` on a training run, then `-XX:SharedArchiveFile`). Java 24 (JEP 483, marked `Java 25+` in this guide) adds the AOT cache, which also stores loaded and linked classes (`-XX:AOTCache`).
- **Spring AOT:** a build-time step (`spring-boot:process-aot`, Gradle `processAot`) that runs the application context's configuration phase at build time and writes Java source for bean definitions (`*__BeanDefinitions` classes), plus `RuntimeHints` (reflection, resources, proxies, serialization) as GraalVM config files.
- **GraalVM native image:** ahead-of-time compiler that does static analysis from `main`, includes only reachable code, initializes some classes at build time, and produces a platform-specific executable with the Substrate VM runtime.
- **Closed-world assumption:** everything that can run must be known at build time; reflection, resources, dynamic proxies and serialization need hints.
- **CRaC (Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint):** OpenJDK project (supported JDKs like Azul Zulu with CRaC) that snapshots a warmed-up JVM process and restores it in milliseconds. Boot 3.2 supports it (`-Dspring.context.checkpoint=onRefresh`).

### Why it exists
Containers, autoscaling and serverless functions start instances on demand. A 10 second start with 400 MB of memory is fine for a long-lived monolith but expensive when you scale from 0 to 50 pods during a traffic spike, or pay per millisecond on AWS Lambda. Spring had to compete with frameworks designed for fast startup (Quarkus, Micronaut), and Spring Boot 3 made AOT and native a first-class option.

## 2. How It Works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph JVM["Regular JVM run"]
        A1["Scan classpath, parse @Configuration"] --> A2["Evaluate conditions"] --> A3["Create beans by reflection"] --> A4["JIT warms up over minutes"]
    end
    subgraph AOT["Spring AOT at build time"]
        B1["Refresh context in AOT mode (no bean instances)"] --> B2["Generate __BeanDefinitions Java code"] --> B3["Generate reflect-config, resource-config, proxy-config"]
    end
    subgraph NATIVE["GraalVM native-image"]
        C1["Static analysis from main"] --> C2["Compile reachable code to machine code"] --> C3["Native executable: starts in ~50 ms"]
    end
    B3 --> C1
```

**What Spring AOT generates (for one bean)**

```java
// Generated at build time: target/spring-aot/main/sources/com/orderhub/order/OrderService__BeanDefinitions.java
import org.springframework.beans.factory.aot.BeanInstanceSupplier;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.BeanDefinition;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.support.RootBeanDefinition;

public class OrderService__BeanDefinitions {
  private static BeanInstanceSupplier<OrderService> getOrderServiceInstanceSupplier() {
    return BeanInstanceSupplier.<OrderService>forConstructor(OrderRepository.class, PaymentService.class)
            .withGenerator((registeredBean, args) -> new OrderService(args.get(0), args.get(1)));
  }

  public static BeanDefinition getOrderServiceBeanDefinition() {
    RootBeanDefinition beanDefinition = new RootBeanDefinition(OrderService.class);
    beanDefinition.setInstanceSupplier(getOrderServiceInstanceSupplier());
    return beanDefinition;
  }
}
```
No classpath scanning, no condition evaluation and no reflective constructor lookup at runtime: the decisions were frozen at build time. With AOT on the JVM (`-Dspring.aot.enabled=true`) you get a modest startup gain; in a native image it is mandatory.

**Typical numbers for a mid-size REST plus JPA service (indicative, measure your own)**

| Mode | Startup to ready | RSS memory at idle | Peak throughput | Build time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| JVM, default | 3.5 s | 350 MB | 100 percent (after JIT warm-up) | 30 s |
| JVM, lazy init | 2.2 s | 300 MB | 100 percent, first requests slower | 30 s |
| JVM plus CDS (or Java AOT cache) | 2.0 s (1.5 s) | 320 MB | 100 percent | 30 s plus training run |
| JVM plus Spring AOT | 2.8 s | 330 MB | 100 percent | 45 s |
| GraalVM native image | 0.08 s | 90 MB | 60 to 90 percent (better with PGO, Oracle GraalVM) | 3 to 8 min, 6 to 10 GB RAM |
| CRaC restore | 0.05 s | similar to JVM | 100 percent, already warm | Checkpoint step in pipeline |

**Restrictions in AOT and native mode**
- Profiles, `@ConditionalOnProperty` and `@ConditionalOnClass` are evaluated at build time. Changing `spring.profiles.active` at runtime does not add or remove beans (property *values* can still change).
- No `@Profile`-based bean sets chosen at runtime, no runtime-generated classes (CGLIB proxies are generated at build time by AOT instead), no `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` that registers beans based on runtime state.
- Reflection, resources and JDK proxies used by your code or libraries need `RuntimeHints`. Spring registers hints for its own annotations; libraries publish metadata in the GraalVM Reachability Metadata Repository.
- Mockito-based tests do not run in native mode; run the JVM test suite, plus `nativeTest` for smoke tests.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
OrderHub measures its startup, then gets a native build profile and runtime hints for a class read by reflection.

```xml
<!-- pom.xml: Boot parent already defines the 'native' profile; add the GraalVM plugin -->
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.graalvm.buildtools</groupId>
            <artifactId>native-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

```java
// file: src/main/java/com/orderhub/report/ReportFormatter.java
package com.orderhub.report;

// Loaded by class name from configuration, so GraalVM's static analysis cannot see it
public class ReportFormatter {
    public String format(String title, int orders) {
        return "%s: %d orders".formatted(title, orders);
    }
}
```

```java
// file: src/main/java/com/orderhub/report/ReportService.java
package com.orderhub.report;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class ReportService {
    private final Object formatter;

    public ReportService(@Value("${orderhub.report.formatter:com.orderhub.report.ReportFormatter}") String cls)
            throws ReflectiveOperationException {
        this.formatter = Class.forName(cls).getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();   // reflection
    }

    public String daily(int orders) throws ReflectiveOperationException {
        return (String) formatter.getClass().getMethod("format", String.class, int.class)
                .invoke(formatter, "Daily report", orders);
    }
}
```

```java
// file: src/main/java/com/orderhub/report/ReportHints.java
package com.orderhub.report;

import org.springframework.aot.hint.MemberCategory;
import org.springframework.aot.hint.RuntimeHints;
import org.springframework.aot.hint.RuntimeHintsRegistrar;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.ImportRuntimeHints;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@ImportRuntimeHints(ReportHints.Registrar.class)
public class ReportHints {

    static class Registrar implements RuntimeHintsRegistrar {
        @Override
        public void registerHints(RuntimeHints hints, ClassLoader classLoader) {
            hints.reflection().registerType(ReportFormatter.class,
                    MemberCategory.INVOKE_PUBLIC_CONSTRUCTORS, MemberCategory.INVOKE_PUBLIC_METHODS);
            hints.resources().registerPattern("reports/*.txt");      // classpath resources read at runtime
        }
    }
}
```

```java
// file: src/test/java/com/orderhub/report/ReportHintsTest.java
package com.orderhub.report;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.aot.hint.RuntimeHints;
import org.springframework.aot.hint.predicate.RuntimeHintsPredicates;

class ReportHintsTest {
    @Test
    void registersReflectionForFormatter() {
        RuntimeHints hints = new RuntimeHints();
        new ReportHints.Registrar().registerHints(hints, getClass().getClassLoader());
        assertThat(RuntimeHintsPredicates.reflection().onType(ReportFormatter.class)).accepts(hints);
        assertThat(RuntimeHintsPredicates.resource().forResource("reports/daily.txt")).accepts(hints);
    }
}
```

```bash
# 1. Measure the JVM baseline (needs actuator and BufferingApplicationStartup, see the startup lifecycle topic)
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/startup | jq '[.timeline.events[] | {name: .startupStep.name, ms: (.duration | sub("PT";"") )}] | sort_by(.ms) | reverse | .[0:5]'

# 2. Quick wins on the JVM: CDS training run, then run with the archive (Boot 3.3+)
java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/orderhub.jar extract --destination app
java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app/app.jsa -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh -jar app/orderhub.jar
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app/app.jsa -jar app/orderhub.jar

# 3. Native executable (needs GraalVM JDK 21+ installed) or a native container image (needs only Docker)
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile
./mvnw -Pnative spring-boot:build-image
./target/orderhub

# 4. Run the test suite inside a native image
./mvnw -PnativeTest test
```

```yaml
# application.yml: lazy init for local development only (not in production)
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: dev
  main:
    lazy-initialization: true
```

### Walkthrough
- **Measure first:** the startup endpoint lists the slowest steps; common winners are Hibernate metamodel building, Flyway migrations, eager remote clients and big component scans.
- **CDS:** the training run (`spring.context.exit=onRefresh` stops right after refresh) records loaded classes into `app.jsa`; later runs map the archive instead of parsing class files, typically 30 to 40 percent faster. The extracted layout is needed because CDS does not work with nested jars.
- **`ReportService`** loads a class by name, invisible to static analysis. On the JVM it works; in a native image without hints it fails at runtime with `ClassNotFoundException` or `NoSuchMethodException`.
- **`ReportHints`** registers the reflection and resource hints. Spring AOT collects all `RuntimeHintsRegistrar`s and writes `reflect-config.json` and `resource-config.json` under `META-INF/native-image`. `@RegisterReflectionForBinding` is a shortcut for DTOs serialised by Jackson outside of Spring MVC.
- **`ReportHintsTest`** proves the hints exist without building a native image (minutes saved per feedback loop).
- **Lazy init** is a dev-time helper: it hides wiring errors until first use and shifts latency onto the first requests, so do not use it blindly in production.

### Output
```text
JVM:     Started OrderHubApplication in 3.412 seconds (process running for 3.81)
JVM+CDS: Started OrderHubApplication in 2.107 seconds (process running for 2.36)
Native:  Started OrderHubApplication in 0.081 seconds (process running for 0.089)
```
```text
$ ps -o rss,cmd -C orderhub
  RSS CMD
92160 ./target/orderhub
```
Native run without the hints:
```text
java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: com.orderhub.report.ReportFormatter
	at org.graalvm.nativeimage.builder/com.oracle.svm.core.hub.ClassForNameSupport.forName(ClassForNameSupport.java:122)
```

### Compare
| Technique | Startup gain | Effort | Risks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fix slow beans found in `/actuator/startup` | Varies, often the biggest | Low | None |
| Lazy initialization | 20 to 40 percent | One property | Errors at first use, slow first requests |
| CDS or Java AOT cache | 30 to 50 percent | Training run in the Dockerfile | Archive must match JDK and classpath |
| Spring AOT on JVM | 10 to 20 percent | Build step | Profiles and conditions fixed at build time |
| GraalVM native | 95 to 98 percent, plus much less memory | High: hints, long builds, native tests | Lower peak throughput, library compatibility |
| CRaC | 95 percent, already warm | Checkpoint pipeline, supported JDK | Secrets and open sockets in the snapshot must be handled |

## 4. Interview Questions
**Basic**
1. **Why does a Spring Boot application start slowly compared to a native app?**
   At startup it scans the classpath, parses configuration classes, evaluates hundreds of auto-configuration conditions, loads thousands of classes, creates beans with reflection and generates proxies, and the JIT only optimises after warm-up. All of this happens every time the JVM starts.
2. **What is Spring AOT?**
   A build-time step that runs the context's configuration phase without creating beans and generates Java code for bean definitions plus GraalVM hint files. At runtime the generated code registers beans directly, skipping scanning, condition evaluation and reflection.
3. **What is a GraalVM native image?**
   A standalone executable produced by ahead-of-time compiling the reachable parts of the application and JDK into machine code. It starts in milliseconds and uses much less memory, but needs every reflective or dynamic access declared at build time.

**Follow-up**
4. **What is the closed-world assumption, and how does it affect Spring?**
   GraalVM assumes all code that can run is known at build time. For Spring, that means bean definitions, profiles and class conditions are fixed at build time, CGLIB proxies must be generated during AOT, and reflection, resources and proxies need `RuntimeHints`.
5. **When would you choose native over JVM?**
   For scale-to-zero, serverless, CLI tools, or many small instances where startup and memory dominate cost. For long-running, high-throughput services, the JVM's JIT usually wins on peak performance and the build stays simple.
6. **How do you make a library that uses reflection work in a native image?**
   Check the GraalVM Reachability Metadata Repository (applied automatically by the native build tools), otherwise register hints with a `RuntimeHintsRegistrar` and `@ImportRuntimeHints`, or `@RegisterReflectionForBinding`. Verify with a `RuntimeHintsPredicates` unit test and the native test profile; the tracing agent (`-agentlib:native-image-agent`) can record what is accessed at runtime.

**Tricky / scenario**
7. **Your service scales from 2 to 40 pods during flash sales, and new pods take 25 seconds to become ready, so requests fail. What would you try, in order?**
   First, profile startup and fix expensive beans (remote calls, migrations at startup, big scans). Then add CDS or the Java AOT cache in the Docker image and make readiness accurate. If still too slow, consider native or CRaC. In parallel, scale earlier using predictive or scheduled autoscaling and keep a warm minimum of pods.
8. **The native image works locally but in production it activates a `prod` profile and a bean is missing. Why?**
   Profiles that control bean registration are decided at AOT build time. The image was built with the default profile, so `@Profile("prod")` beans were not included. Build with the profile set at AOT time (`spring.profiles.active` configured for `process-aot`) or replace profile-based beans with property values.
9. **Your team turned on `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` in production to start faster; p99 latency spiked after each deploy and a missing bean only failed in production. Explain.**
   Lazy beans are created on first request, so the first users pay creation cost (and JIT is cold). Wiring errors that would fail startup now fail at first use. Use lazy init selectively with `@Lazy`, or exclude critical beans with `LazyInitializationExcludeFilter`, and warm up before readiness.

**What the interviewer is really testing:** whether you can reason about the startup cost model and choose a technique based on measured needs, not hype.

## 5. Pitfalls & Best Practices
### Common mistakes
| Mistake | What goes wrong | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Going native without measuring | Weeks spent on hints for a service that restarts once a month | Measure, then pick the cheapest technique that meets the goal |
| Using runtime profiles to switch beans in a native image | Beans missing in production | Fix profiles at build time or use properties |
| Reflection without hints | Native runtime `ClassNotFoundException` | `RuntimeHintsRegistrar` plus predicate tests |
| Only running JVM tests for a native app | Native-only failures in production | Run `nativeTest` in CI for smoke coverage |
| Global lazy init in production | Slow first requests, late failures | Use it in dev; warm up critical beans |

### Best practices
- Track startup time and memory as CI metrics so regressions are caught when a dependency is added.
- Keep constructors and `@PostConstruct` cheap; defer remote connections.
- For containers, prefer the layered jar plus CDS (or the Java AOT cache) as the low-risk default; reserve native for workloads where it pays off.
- Build native images in CI on a machine with enough memory and cache dependencies; local developers keep the JVM for fast feedback.

### Compare with
| Option | Startup | Peak throughput | Operational complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| JVM | Seconds | Best (JIT) | Lowest |
| JVM plus CDS or AOT cache | Faster seconds | Best | Low |
| Native image | Milliseconds | Good | Medium to high |
| CRaC | Milliseconds and warm | Best | Medium, JDK-specific |

## 6. Hands-on Exercise
Make OrderHub's Docker image start at least 30 percent faster without going native. Acceptance criteria: a multi-stage Dockerfile extracts the jar with the tools jar mode, performs a CDS training run during the build, and starts with the archive; the log of the old and new image shows the improvement; and the readiness probe only succeeds after `ApplicationReadyEvent`.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```text
# file: Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/orderhub.jar extract --destination /app

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app /app
# Training run: start the context and exit right after refresh, dumping the class archive
RUN java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh \
         -Dspring.profiles.active=cds-training -jar orderhub.jar || true
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa", "-jar", "orderhub.jar"]
```

```yaml
# file: src/main/resources/application-cds-training.yml
# The training run must not need a real database or broker
spring:
  autoconfigure:
    exclude:
      - org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.flyway.FlywayAutoConfiguration
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:training
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: none
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
```

```text
old image: Started OrderHubApplication in 3.402 seconds
new image: Started OrderHubApplication in 2.088 seconds   (39 percent faster)
```
The Kubernetes readiness probe targets `/actuator/health/readiness`, which reports `ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC` only after `ApplicationReadyEvent`. Since Boot 3.3 the `spring-boot:build-image` goal can do the same with `BP_JVM_CDS_ENABLED=true` for Paketo buildpacks.
</details>

## 7. Recall
Q: What does Spring AOT generate at build time?
A: Java source code for bean definitions (`__BeanDefinitions` classes) and GraalVM hint files for reflection, resources and proxies.

Q: What is the closed-world assumption in GraalVM native images?
A: All code, classes and dynamic accesses must be known at build time; anything not declared or reachable is excluded.

Q: Why can a Spring native image not switch bean-defining profiles at runtime?
A: Profiles and conditions are evaluated at AOT build time, so the bean set is frozen in the generated code.

Q: How do you register reflection hints for a Spring Boot native image?
A: Implement `RuntimeHintsRegistrar` and import it with `@ImportRuntimeHints`, or use `@RegisterReflectionForBinding`.

Q: What is a low-risk way to speed up Spring Boot startup on the JVM without going native?
A: Class Data Sharing (or the Java AOT cache in newer JDKs) with a training run, after fixing slow beans found via `/actuator/startup`.

**Related:** [[ApplicationContext Startup Lifecycle]] · [[Auto-Configuration Internals]] · [[Docker Images for Spring Boot]] · [[Virtual Threads]]

# Phase 19: Advanced Data and Caching (Advanced)

Phase 12 taught you to make the data layer *correct*: entities, relationships, transactions. This phase makes it *fast and scalable*. Most production performance incidents in Spring Boot services are data incidents: an exhausted connection pool, a missing index, an N+1 query, 50,000 single-row inserts, a cache that serves stale prices, a replica that lags behind. Senior interviews are full of these scenarios ("p99 went from 80 ms to 4 s after a release, what do you check?"), and the answers in this phase are the ones that impress: numbers, query plans and trade-offs.

OrderHub gains Redis caching for its catalog, tuned HikariCP settings, indexes driven by `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, batched order imports, a read replica for reports and a Spring Batch job for nightly invoicing.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Connection Pooling with HikariCP"] --> B["Query Performance and Indexes"]
    B --> C["Batch Inserts and Updates"]
    B --> D["Spring Cache Abstraction"]
    D --> E["Redis with Spring Boot"]
    D --> F["Hibernate Second-Level Cache"]
    A --> G["Multiple Datasources and Read Replicas"]
    C --> H["Spring Batch"]
```

**Prerequisites:** Spring Data JPA, entity relationships, fetching and N+1, transactions and propagation, Flyway (Phase 12); Testcontainers (Phase 13); `@Transactional` internals and proxies (Phase 18).

**The 5 questions from this phase that come up most often**
1. How do you size a HikariCP connection pool, and what happens when it is exhausted?
2. A query is slow in production. Walk me through how you find and fix the cause.
3. How does `@Cacheable` work, and how do you keep the cache consistent with the database?
4. Why are JPA inserts with `GenerationType.IDENTITY` not batched, and how do you insert 100,000 rows quickly?
5. How would you route read-only queries to a replica, and what problems does replication lag cause?

**Shared analogy: a busy restaurant kitchen.** Connections are the stoves: lighting a new stove for every order is slow, so you keep a fixed number lit (the pool), and if all are busy, orders wait in line. Every speed-up in this group reduces either waiting for a stove, searching for an ingredient, or trips back and forth.

name: Connection Pooling with HikariCP
description: Why pools exist, HikariCP settings and defaults, pool sizing, leak detection, exhaustion symptoms and metrics
content:
# Connection Pooling with HikariCP

**Level: Advanced | Phase 19 | Priority: MUST | Since: HikariCP default pool in Spring Boot 2.0**

> **30-second interview answer:** Opening a database connection costs a TCP handshake, TLS, authentication and server-side process creation, often 20 to 100 ms, so applications keep a pool of open connections and borrow them per transaction. Spring Boot uses HikariCP by default with `maximumPoolSize` 10 and `connectionTimeout` 30 seconds. The pool should be small: connections are limited by the database's CPU and disks, not by your request threads, so a common starting point is about `cores * 2` on the database side divided across all app instances. When every connection is busy, threads wait up to `connectionTimeout` and then fail with "Connection is not available, request timed out", usually caused by long transactions, leaks or remote calls inside transactions rather than by a pool that is too small.

## 1. Concept in Simple Words
### Analogy
A car rental desk at an airport.

| Car rental | Connection pool |
|---|---|
| Buying a new car for every trip is absurdly slow and expensive | Opening a new physical connection per request |
| The desk owns 10 cars; customers borrow and return them | `maximumPoolSize = 10` |
| If all cars are out, the next customer waits in line | Threads block in `getConnection()` |
| After 30 seconds of waiting, the customer gives up | `connectionTimeout` then `SQLTransientConnectionException` |
| A customer who never returns the car | Connection leak |
| Cars are retired after 30 minutes and replaced with fresh ones | `maxLifetime` |
| Quick check that a parked car still starts | `keepaliveTime` and validation |
| Adding more cars than the airport has parking spaces | Pool larger than the database can serve: everything slows down |

### What it is
- **Physical connection:** a TCP session plus a server process (PostgreSQL forks one backend process per connection, each using several MB of RAM).
- **Connection pool:** keeps physical connections open and hands out a wrapper (`HikariProxyConnection`); `close()` on the wrapper returns it to the pool instead of closing the socket.
- **HikariCP:** a small, very fast JDBC pool (lock-free `ConcurrentBag` with thread-local affinity). Boot auto-configures it when `com.zaxxer:HikariCP` is on the classpath, which `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` and `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` bring.
- **Key settings (Boot properties under `spring.datasource.hikari.*`):**

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maximum-pool-size` | 10 | Max connections, idle plus in use |
| `minimum-idle` | same as max | Keep this many idle; Hikari recommends a fixed-size pool (leave unset) |
| `connection-timeout` | 30000 ms | Max wait for a connection before an exception |
| `idle-timeout` | 600000 ms | Retire idle connections above `minimum-idle` (only if min is less than max) |
| `max-lifetime` | 1800000 ms | Retire any connection after this age; set a few seconds below database or firewall limits |
| `keepalive-time` | 120000 ms in current versions (0, disabled, in older ones) | Ping idle connections so firewalls do not drop them |
| `leak-detection-threshold` | 0 (off) | Log a stack trace if a connection is held longer than this |
| `validation-timeout` | 5000 ms | Max time for a connection aliveness check |
| `auto-commit` | true | Spring's transaction manager turns it off per transaction; JPA users may set `false` plus `hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true` to skip a round trip |
| `pool-name` | HikariPool-1 | Name in logs and metrics |

### Why it exists
Without pooling, every request opens and closes a connection: slow (tens of ms each), heavy on the database (process creation), and dangerous under load because a traffic spike becomes a connection storm that can take the database down. A pool caps concurrency at a level the database can handle and amortises connection cost to zero.

## 2. How It Works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as "Request thread"
    participant TM as "JpaTransactionManager"
    participant H as "HikariPool"
    participant DB as "PostgreSQL"
    T->>TM: "begin @Transactional"
    TM->>H: "getConnection()"
    alt "idle connection available"
        H-->>TM: "borrow (thread-local list first, then shared bag)"
    else "pool below max"
        H->>DB: "open new physical connection (async adder thread)"
        H-->>TM: "new connection"
    else "pool exhausted"
        H->>H: "wait up to connectionTimeout on a handoff queue"
        H-->>TM: "SQLTransientConnectionException after 30 s"
    end
    TM->>DB: "SQL statements"
    TM->>H: "commit, then close() = return to pool"
```

**How long a connection is held:** from transaction begin to transaction end. Without `@Transactional`, each repository call borrows and returns separately. With Open Session in View (`spring.jpa.open-in-view=true`, the default, with a warning at startup), the `EntityManager` stays open for the whole web request, and once it has acquired a connection (for lazy loading) it keeps it until the response is written.

**Pool sizing**

```text
Little's law:  connections needed = throughput (tx per second) x average connection hold time (s)
  example: 400 tx/s x 0.015 s = 6 connections busy on average; add headroom -> 10

Database-side rule of thumb (PostgreSQL wiki / HikariCP "About Pool Sizing"):
  total connections ~ (db_cores x 2) + effective_spindle_count
  example: 8-core DB with SSD -> about 17 to 20 connections in total

Distribute across instances:
  6 app pods x pool 10 = 60 connections  -> too many for that 8-core DB
  6 app pods x pool 3  = 18 connections  -> matches
```
Bigger pools often make latency *worse*: the database context-switches between more active queries, lock contention grows, and every query slows down. Request threads (Tomcat default 200) do not need one connection each, because most request time is spent outside the database.

**Pool deadlock:** if one request needs two connections at once (REQUIRES_NEW, or a second `DataSource` call outside the transaction), N concurrent requests holding their first connection can wait forever for a second. Rule: pool size must be at least `threads x (connections per request - 1) + 1`, or avoid nested connections.

## 3. Code Example
### Code
OrderHub tunes its pool, adds leak detection in staging, and exposes pool metrics.

```yaml
# file: src/main/resources/application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db:5432/orderhub
    username: orderhub
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      pool-name: orderhub-pool
      maximum-pool-size: 8            # 4 pods x 8 = 32 connections for a 16-core DB
      connection-timeout: 3000        # fail fast: 3 s, not 30 s, so callers can retry or shed load
      max-lifetime: 1740000           # 29 min, below the 30 min idle limit of the cloud proxy
      keepalive-time: 60000
      leak-detection-threshold: 0     # enabled per profile below
      data-source-properties:
        reWriteBatchedInserts: true   # PostgreSQL driver option, used in the batching topic
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false               # never hold a connection while rendering the response
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics,prometheus
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: staging
  datasource:
    hikari:
      leak-detection-threshold: 10000 # log any connection held longer than 10 s
```

```java
// file: src/main/java/com/orderhub/report/SlowReportService.java
package com.orderhub.report;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

@Service
public class SlowReportService {
    private final OrderStatsRepository stats;
    private final RestClient fxClient;

    public SlowReportService(OrderStatsRepository stats, RestClient.Builder builder) {
        this.stats = stats;
        this.fxClient = builder.baseUrl("https://fx.example.com").build();
    }

    // BAD: holds a pooled connection while waiting up to 2 s on a remote API
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public BigDecimal revenueInEurBad() {
        BigDecimal usd = stats.totalRevenueUsd();
        BigDecimal rate = fxClient.get().uri("/rate?from=USD&to=EUR").retrieve().body(BigDecimal.class);
        return usd.multiply(rate);
    }

    // GOOD: remote call first, then a short transaction (repository call is transactional by itself)
    public BigDecimal revenueInEur() {
        BigDecimal rate = fxClient.get().uri("/rate?from=USD&to=EUR").retrieve().body(BigDecimal.class);
        return stats.totalRevenueUsd().multiply(rate);
```
